passages.title: The clear Arabic Book and the best of stories
passages.tafsir:
**These three ayat are the surah introducing itself.** Before a single event of Yusuf's life is told, Allah names what the reader is holding: verses of a Book that is clear, sent down in Arabic so that people would understand it, and about to relate the best of stories — an account the Prophet ﷺ had no knowledge of before it was revealed to him. One claim runs through all three: what follows is not a story collected from somewhere. It is revelation — and, as the commentators will show, the telling of it is itself the proof.

## A surah told whole

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that, apart from four verses, Surah Yusuf is wholly Makkan, and that the story of Sayyidnā Yusuf (peace be upon him) is described here with continuity and order. The story appears in this surah alone; it is not repeated anywhere else in the whole Qur'an as such. In Surah al-Anʿām (6:84) and Surah al-Muʼmin, also called Ghāfir (40:34), only his name is mentioned, as a Messenger of Allah, in appropriate context.

That is particular to this story. Otherwise, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, the accounts of all the blessed prophets are introduced across the Qur'an with great wisdom — part by part, and repeatedly. These three opening ayat prepare us for the exception.

## Alif-Lām-Rā: a door left closed

The surah opens with *Alif Lām Rā* — the isolated letters, *al-ḥurūf al-muqaṭṭaʿāt*, of the Holy Qur'an. Ibn Kathir simply refers the reader back to what he set out at the beginning of Surah al-Baqarah, where he discussed the separate letters.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the position plainly: it is the universal verdict of the majority of the Ṣaḥābah (the Companions) and the Tābiʿīn (the generation that followed them) that these letters are a secret between Allah Taʿālā, the speaker, and the Prophet ﷺ, the addressee — something a third person cannot understand, and which it is not appropriate for anyone to exert himself and insist on finding out.

There is a discipline in that. On this view, the first response to these letters is not speculation but restraint: some of what has been revealed was not given to us to decode, and the sources themselves tell us to stop pressing.

## "The verses of the clear Book"

The Book is described as *al-Mubīn*. Ibn Kathir explains the phrase "These are the verses of the Book" as referring to the Clear Qur'an that is plain and apparent, and that explains, clarifies and makes known the unclear matters. So the word carries both directions at once: clear in itself, and clarifying of everything else.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān — rendering the phrase "the verses of the enlightening Book" — adds the practical edge. These are verses of the Book which delineate the delimitations and restrictions of what is lawful and unlawful, including those of other things in all departments of human life, and which thereby give people a simple, straight and moderate system of living: as promised in the Torah, and as already known to the Jews.

Hold that description against what is coming. The Book that draws the lines of lawful and unlawful is the same Book that is about to relate this narrative. The story is not set beside the guidance; it arrives as part of it.

## Sent down in Arabic

"Verily, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an in order that you may understand."

Ibn Kathir says the Arabic language is the most eloquent, plain, deep and expressive of the meanings that might arise in one's mind. He then lines up a whole chain of honour: therefore the most honourable Book was revealed in the most honourable language, to the most honourable Prophet and Messenger ﷺ, delivered by the most honourable angel, in the most honourable land on earth, and its revelation began during the most honourable month of the year, Ramadan. Therefore, he concludes, the Qur'an is perfect in every respect. Nothing about it is incidental — not even the language it arrived in.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān comes at the same words from another side. The ayah is indicative of the situation: those who had asked to be informed of what had happened to Sayyidnā Yusuf (peace be upon him) were the Jews of Arabia. So Allah Taʿālā revealed this story in their language, so that they might ponder over it, attest to the veracity of the Prophet ﷺ, and tune their lives in the light of the injunctions and instructions which emerge from this story. Arabic here is not ornament; it removes an excuse.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then draws attention to one word. *Laʿalla* has been brought in here in the sense of "so that" — and the reason given is that the mindset of these addressees was already known: that despite having the benefit of very clear verses before them, they would still doubt and delay their acceptance of the truth. The aim named in the ayah itself is not that you merely hear the account, but that you understand.

## Two requests, one answer

Two requests lie behind the third ayah in the sources, and they could not be more different in spirit.

Ibn Kathir reports, on the reason behind revealing this ayah, that Ibn Jarir aṭ-Ṭabarī recorded that ʿAbdullāh bin ʿAbbās said: "They said, 'O Allah's Messenger! Why not narrate to us stories?' Later on, this Ayah was revealed: *We relate unto you the best of stories...*"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that, according to some narrations, another reason could lie in what the Jews had said to the Prophet ﷺ. To test him, they had asked: if you are a true prophet, tell us why the family of Yaʿqūb moved from Syria to Egypt, and what had actually happened to Yusuf (peace be upon him). It was in answer to that that this whole story was revealed.

One request was simply a wish to be told an account; the other was laid as a trap. The same revealed narrative answered both — and, as we will see, it turned the test back on the testers.

## Why this story runs in order

The ayah names not only the matter but the manner: the best of stories is related "through Our revelations unto you, of this Qur'an."

So why is this one account given whole and in sequence, when the Qur'an elsewhere gives prophetic history part by part and repeatedly? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers on two levels.

**First, the Qur'an's usual method.** The truth of the matter, they say, is that world history and past experiences teach human beings what to do with their lives in the future. These have a natural effect of their own which acts better on minds and hearts than the pull of formal education; the effect is deeper and fairly effortless. Therefore the Holy Qur'an, sent for all peoples of the world as their last testament, takes up electively and pragmatically a marked portion of the history of the peoples of the world — the portion that serves as the master prescription for the betterment of the present and ultimate human condition. And it introduces even that portion in a style so unique and inimitable that the reader simply does not get the impression he is reading a book of history: whatever part of a story serves the need of driving home a lesson or tendering good counsel on a given occasion is just the part that finds mention in that setting, and should that part be needed again on another occasion, it is repeated. Sequential order, therefore, was not the consideration; at some places the earlier part of a story comes later, and the later part earlier.

From this, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a standing rule of guidance: reading or remembering world history and its past events is not an end by itself. Instead, the purpose of every human being should be to draw some lesson from every story, and to cull and deduce some good advice from every piece of information.

They frame it in a classical distinction. Human speech is classified into two forms: *khabar*, the descriptive — statements about what is — and *inshāʼ*, the imperative — words that call for something to be done. According to the knowledgeable scholars, it is the imperative that is the essential objective; description in itself is not an end. A wise man ought to learn an imperative from every description, and make use of it for correcting and reforming himself.

**Second, why this surah runs differently.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān suggests the story may have been narrated in sequence here because historiography is a discipline, with particular rules of guidance for its practitioners: for instance, the narration should not be so brief as to make understanding it impossible, nor so long as would make reading and remembering it difficult — which becomes clear, they say, from the Qur'anic treatment of this story.

## "And before this, you were among those who knew nothing about it"

The third ayah closes by turning to the Prophet ﷺ himself: before this, he was among the unaware.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads this as chastening the Jews. They had tried to test the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and it proved to be in vain, for its effect turned out to be the reverse of what they had intended: it only went on to prove his excellence and authenticity in a far more evident manner. He was an *ummiyy* — one who was not taught by anyone, who had never read a book, and who had lived in Makkah practically his whole life — and he had no knowledge of world history. Yet he narrated all the events mentioned in the Torah correctly, and in fact told them of what was not mentioned in the Torah. That he came to know this needs an explanation, and there can be no explanation except that he was divinely educated and blessed with revelation as a prophet of Allah Taʿālā.

Notice that Allah states this to him directly, and does not soften it. His prior unawareness is not an embarrassment tucked out of sight; it is placed in the ayah as part of the argument. The account's force as proof rests on the fact that its narrator had no access to it.

## From the Sunnah: this Book is enough

Ibn Kathir says there is a hadith that is relevant upon mentioning this honourable ayah — one which praises the Qur'an and demonstrates that it is sufficient, removing the need for all books besides it.

Imam Ahmad recorded a narration from Jābir bin ʿAbdullāh that ʿUmar bin al-Khaṭṭāb came to the Prophet ﷺ with a book that he had taken from some of the People of the Book. ʿUmar began reading it to the Prophet ﷺ, who became angry and said: "Are you uncertain about it, Ibn al-Khaṭṭāb? By the One in Whose Hand is my soul! I have come to you with it white and pure. Do not ask them about anything, for they might tell you something true and you reject it, or they might tell you something false and you believe it. By the One in Whose Hand is my soul! If Musa were living, he would have no choice but to follow me."

Imam Ahmad also recorded a narration from ʿAbdullāh bin Thābit, who said: "ʿUmar came to Allah's Messenger and said, 'O Messenger of Allah! I passed by a brother of mine from the tribe of Qurayẓah, so he wrote some comprehensive statements from the Tawrah for me — should I read them to you?' The face of Allah's Messenger changed with anger. So I said to him, 'Don't you see the face of Allah's Messenger?'" ʿUmar said, "We are pleased with Allah as our Lord, Islam as our religion, and Muhammad as our Messenger." So the anger of the Prophet ﷺ subsided, and he said: "By the One in Whose Hand is Muhammad's soul, if Musa appeared among you and you were to follow him, abandoning me, then you would have strayed. Indeed you are my share of the nations, and I am your share of the Prophets."

Sitting where they do, these two narrations are pointed. A question about Yusuf had been put by those who held the earlier scriptures; the answer came directly from Allah to a man who had never read a book. "White and pure" is exactly the contrast — you have been handed the account clean, and the warning that follows is precisely against going to them for such things, since what they tell you may be true and rejected, or false and believed.

## Living it

**Know where to stop asking.** The letters that open the surah are, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports from the majority of the Ṣaḥābah and Tābiʿīn, a secret between the One who spoke them and the one to whom they were spoken — and it is not appropriate to exert oneself and insist on finding it out. Not every door in revelation was given us a key to, and it is no loss to leave it closed.

**Read with your mind engaged.** The second ayah states the purpose: *in order that you may understand*. To recite Surah Yusuf without following what is being said falls short of the aim Allah named for it — and the doubting and delaying of people who had very clear verses in front of them is exactly the failing Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the wording anticipates.

**Take an imperative out of every description.** This is Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's standing rule: description is not an end in itself; a wise person learns an imperative from every description and uses it to correct and reform himself. As this surah unfolds, the question to keep asking is not "what happened?" but "what does this require of me?"

**And read it as revelation, not literature.** The third ayah tells you the one relating it had no knowledge of it beforehand. What is being read did not come up to the Prophet ﷺ from human memory; it came down to him.

passages.title: Joseph's dream and his father's counsel
passages.tafsir:
A boy tells his father a dream; the father, reading it instantly, tells him to keep it to himself — and then tells him what it means for his future. What holds the passage together is a single thread: **a true dream is a communication from Allah, and what a wise man does with such a communication is guard it.**

## Ayah 4: the dream

Ibn Kathir begins with the command behind the telling. Allah is saying, in effect, *"Mention to your people, O Muhammad, among the stories that you narrate to them, the story of Yusuf."*

The address is warm. Yusuf says **yā abati** — rendered "O my dear father" — and in ayah 5 Yaʿqub answers with **yā bunayya**, "O my dear son." Before any of the drama of this surah begins, we are shown a household where a son brings his inner life to his father, and a father receives it without dismissing it.

Yusuf is the son of Yaʿqub, son of Ishaq, son of Ibrahim — peace be upon them all.

**What he saw.** Eleven stars, and the sun, and the moon, prostrating to him. ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbbas explained the imagery: the eleven stars are his eleven brothers, and the sun and the moon are his father and mother. Ibn Kathir records this same explanation from Ibn ʿAbbas, ad-Dahhak, Qatadah, Sufyan ath-Thawri and ʿAbdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam.

**A note on "his mother."** Al-Qurtubi observes that Yusuf's mother had already died before this. In her place his father had married her sister. A maternal aunt naturally carries for her sister's children the love a mother has, and once she becomes the father's wife she is customarily called the mother.

**Why this dream counts as revelation.** Ibn ʿAbbas stated the principle plainly: *the dreams of Prophets are revelations from Allah.* That is the frame in which the father's reply should be read — not a child's imagination, but news.

**When it came true.** Ibn Kathir says the vision became reality forty years later — or, some say, eighty — when Yusuf raised his parents to the throne and his brothers stood before him, and the Qur'an itself records the moment: *"and they fell down before him prostrate. And he said: 'O my father! This is the interpretation of my dream aforetime! My Lord has made it come true!'"* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites Tafsir al-Qurtubi's report from ʿAbdullah ibn Shaddad ibn al-Had that the interpretation was fulfilled after forty years, and draws the practical lesson: **an interpretation does not have to actualise immediately.** A true dream may be a forty-year appointment.

## What a dream actually is

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes Qadi Thanaʼullah in Tafsir Mazhari, who explains the reality of a dream this way: when the human self, through sleep or unconsciousness, is released from managing the active body, it comes to see forms through the faculty of imagination.

On this explanation, those forms come in **three kinds**, two false and one true:

1. **Self-suggestion** (*Hadith an-Nafs*) — what one has been seeing while awake, returning transformed in sleep.
2. **The seductive input of the Shaytan** (*Taswil ash-Shaytan*) — forms, situations and events Shaytan introduces into a person's mind, whether pleasing or terrifying.
3. **The true kind** — a species of *ilham*, inspiration: out of His unseen treasures Allah puts things into a servant's mind and heart, to warn him or to give him glad tidings.

The first two, Maʿārif says bluntly, have no substance or reality, and cannot be interpreted in any actual sense.

Maʿārif adds that three kinds of dreams have been reported from the Prophet ﷺ, the third kind, correct and true, being the forty-sixth part of the ingredients of prophethood — that is, an inspiration from Allah.

Even the true kind is fragile. Maʿārif is careful: other contingents can intermingle with a true dream and make it defective and unreliable; some true dreams cannot be interpreted because the actuality of the event is not clear; and where the interpretation is wrong, the event itself ends up different. So a dream is a proven *ilham* from Allah only when it originates from Allah's command, is free of discordant elements, *and* has been interpreted correctly.

**The prophets are the exception.** All the dreams of the blessed prophets are of that pure kind — which is why their dreams carry the status of *wahy* (revelation). The dreams of ordinary believing Muslims are not free of these many probabilities. Maʿārif states the consequence directly: **they are not a binding argument or proof for anyone**, not for the dreamer and not for anyone else. Sometimes such dreams get mixed up with temperamental or self-oriented elements; sometimes the after-effects of sins overtake a true dream in the form of dark and murky silhouettes, making it unreliable.

Maʿārif names the error: people who, after such a dream, start taking it as a sign of having become a saint, or who give what they got out of it the status of the injunctions of the Sharīʿah. Both approaches, it says, are baseless. A true dream is glad tidings or a warning — no more, and no less.

**A dream as conversation with one's Lord.** Reported by al-Tabarani with a sound chain of authorities, and cited in Tafsir Mazhari, the Prophet ﷺ said that the dream of a believer is a dialogue in which he has the honour of talking to his Rabb.

## "A part of prophethood" — and what that does not mean

The true dream has been declared a part of *nubuwwah* in authentic prophetic traditions, and the narrations differ on the fraction: a fortieth, a forty-sixth, a forty-ninth, a fiftieth, a seventieth. Maʿārif reports that these narrations were compiled together in Tafsir al-Qurtubi, where, following the investigative judgment of Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr, it was established that there is no contradiction among them — each is correct in its place, because the number depends on the condition of the one seeing the dream. Whoever is armed with truth, trust, honesty and perfection of faith — his dream is the fortieth part; whoever ranks somewhat lesser in those qualities, the forty-sixth or fiftieth; whoever is lesser still, the seventieth.

Why a *fortieth*? Tafsir Mazhari offers a calculation: revelation came to Muhammad al-Mustafa ﷺ over twenty-three years. During the first half-year period it kept coming in the form of dreams; during the remaining forty-five half-year periods it was communicated through the angel Jibraʼil al-Amin. Accounted for in this manner, true dreams turn out to be the fortieth part of prophetic revelation. As for narrations where the numbers vary higher or lower, Maʿārif says they either carry approximative statements or stand dropped for lack of sound authority.

Imam al-Qurtubi explains the phrase differently: there are occasions when a person sees in a dream what does not lie within his control — flying high in the skies, or things from the Unseen he had no access to. That cannot come about by any means other than divine support and inspiration, which is in reality an intrinsic attribute of prophethood. Hence it was declared *a part* of it.

**Maʿārif then closes a door.** Some have taken the survival of this "part" of prophethood as the survival of prophethood itself — the deception of the Qadiyani imposter. This, Maʿārif says, is against the definite, categorical statements of the Qur'an, against countless sound and authentic ahadith, and squarely against the collective belief of the entire Ummah in *khatm an-nubuwwah*, the finality of prophethood. The reasoning error is elementary: the presence of a part of something does not mean the presence of that thing in full. A single nail or strand of hair belonging to a person, found somewhere, does not mean the person is present.

The decisive text appears in the **Sahih of al-Bukhari**: the Prophet ﷺ said that no part of *nubuwwah* will remain except *al-mubashshirat* — and when the noble Companions asked what these were, he said: **true dreams.** What remains is only that small part, not prophethood in any kind or form.

**True dreams are not a certificate of piety.** Maʿārif points out that it stands proved from the Qur'an, from Hadith, and from experience that sinners, and even disbelievers, may see true dreams. Within Surah Yusuf itself are the true dreams of Yusuf's two prison mates and of the king of Egypt, none of the three of them Muslims. Mentioned in Hadith is the dream of Kisra about the coming of the Prophet ﷺ, which turned out true though Kisra was not a Muslim; the paternal aunt of the Prophet ﷺ, ʿAtikah, saw a true dream about him while she was still a disbeliever; and the dream of the disbelieving king of Babylon, Nebuchadnezzar, interpreted by Sayyidna Daniyal, peace be upon him, was a true dream. The customary practice of Allah is that the dreams of true and good people are generally true, and those of sinners generally self-suggestion or satanic input — but occasionally the opposite can happen, so a true dream is no proof of the dreamer's piety, or even of his being Muslim.

## Ayah 5: the father's counsel

*"O my dear son! Relate not your vision to your brothers, lest they should arrange a plot against you. Verily, Shaytan is to man an open enemy!"*

Ibn Kathir reads Yaʿqub's mind for us. The vision indicated that the brothers would be under Yusuf's authority — subjugated to it so completely that they would prostrate before him in respect, honour and appreciation. Yaʿqub feared that if Yusuf narrated his vision to any of them, they would envy him and conspire evil plots against him. And Ibn Kathir does not soften what "plot" means here: **"They might arrange a plot against you that causes your demise."** The father is not worried about hurt feelings; he is worried about his son's life.

Then the diagnosis: **"Surely, Satan is an open enemy for mankind."** Maʿārif adds the mechanism — he seduces people to take such action for the sake of worldly wealth and power. The brothers are not exonerated, but the deeper adversary is named.

**From the Sunnah, on telling and not telling.** Ibn Kathir cites a confirmed hadith: if one of you sees a vision he likes, let him narrate it; if he sees a dream he dislikes, let him turn onto his other side, blow to his left three times, seek refuge with Allah from its evil, and not tell it to anyone — and it will not harm him. Maʿārif reports the same counsel from the hadith of **Sahih Muslim** and explains why it works: some dreams are composed of satanic seductions, and this action removes them; and if the dream is true, it can be hoped that its evil portion is eliminated too.

Maʿārif also reports, from **Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah**, that the Prophet ﷺ said a dream is of three kinds: glad tidings from Allah; self-suggestions; and satanic inputs. So if a person sees a dream he feels good about, he may relate it to others if he wishes; and if he sees something bad in it, let him tell no one — instead let him rise and offer Salah.

Ibn Kathir then cites a hadith collected by **Imam Ahmad and the collectors of the Sunan**, from Muʿawiyah bin Haydah al-Qushayri, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"The dream is tied to a bird's leg, as long as it is not interpreted. If it is interpreted, it comes true."* From this Ibn Kathir draws a rule of life: **conceal the prospect of a coming bounty until it comes into existence and becomes known.** He supports it with the Prophet's ﷺ words — reported in both tafsirs without a named collection — that one should earn help for fulfilling one's needs by being discreet about them, *for every owner of a blessing is envied.*

**Jami' al-Tirmidhi**, quoted in Maʿārif, joins the threads: a true dream is one of the forty parts of *nubuwwah*; a dream stays in suspension until it is related to someone; when it is related and interpreted by the listener, it actualises as interpreted. Hence the instruction — relate a dream only to someone knowing and wise, or at minimum a friend and a well-wisher.

**Why an interpretation can shape the outcome.** Tafsir Mazhari explains that some matters of destiny are not absolutely pre-decided; they remain in a state of suspension — contingent destiny, where if something is done the impending misfortune goes away, and if it is not done, it comes. In such a case a bad interpretation makes things turn bad and a good one makes them come out well. There is a second reason too: when a person hears a bad interpretation, he finds himself overwhelmed by the thought that misfortune is about to hit him — and it appears in Hadith that Allah said, *"I am with the opinion of My servant about Me"*: whatever a servant believes Allah to be for him, that He becomes for him.

## What this asks of us

Maʿārif draws out several rulings from ayah 5:

- **Do not relate a dream before someone who is not a well-wisher, or who is no expert in interpretation.** This is the plain lesson of Yaʿqub's prohibition.
- **The prohibition on relating a distressing dream is advice, not law.** Maʿārif is explicit that the hadith narrations indicate this is not a legal prohibition but affectionate, sympathetic counsel, and should not be taken as something the Sharīʿah made unlawful; relating such a dream is no sin. Al-Qurtubi's proof is striking: at the time of the Battle of Uhud the Prophet ﷺ said that he had seen in a dream that his sword, Zulfaqar, had broken, and had seen cows being slaughtered — interpreted as the martyrdom of Sayyidna Hamzah, may Allah be pleased with him, and many other Muslim mujahidin, a grave misfortune indeed. He related it before the Companions anyway.
- **Warning someone of a danger to them is not backbiting.** Yaʿqub disclosed to Yusuf that there was a danger to his life at the hands of his brothers. Maʿārif generalises: if you learn that A intends to rob or kill B, you should forewarn B. Being an effort to offset an evil design, this does not fall under the *ghibah* that is forbidden.
- **Do not display blessings before someone likely to envy them.** If Allah has blessed you and you apprehend that your listener will be jealous, do not mention wealth, status and the like before him — for every holder of a blessing is envied in this world.

**One more thing this passage establishes.** Reading ayah 5 together with what follows — the plotting, the well, the disobedience to their father — Maʿārif, citing al-Qurtubi, concludes that Yusuf's brothers were **not prophets or messengers of Allah**. The blessed prophets have to be free of all sins and protected from them, and such men would not have stooped to conspiring to kill a brother, lowering him into a desolate well, and then disobeying their father. Their reference as prophets in the book of al-Tabari, it says, is not correct.

## Ayah 6: the promise

*"Thus will your Lord choose you and teach you the interpretation of Ahadith, and perfect His favour on you and on the offspring of Yaʿqub, as He perfected it on your fathers, Ibrahim and Ishaq aforetime! Verily, your Lord is All-Knowing, All-Wise."*

Yaʿqub does not merely warn; he interprets. Ibn Kathir renders his reasoning: *just as Allah chose you to see the eleven stars, the sun and the moon prostrate before you in a vision, thus will your Lord choose you* — that is, designate and assign you to be a Prophet from Him. Maʿārif reads the choosing more broadly as being chosen for Allah's blessings and favours, something which manifested itself when wealth, recognition and power came into his hands in Egypt. Both readings are given by the sources; both are fulfilled in the surah.

**"And teach you the interpretation of *al-ahadith*."** Mujahid and several other scholars, Ibn Kathir reports, take this as referring to the interpreting of dreams. Maʿārif says *al-ahadith* here means the dreams of people — Allah will teach him how to interpret them — and notes what follows from it: **interpreting dreams is a standing area of expertise, bestowed by Allah on a chosen few. Everyone is not fit to have it.** The very problem of the earlier section — people over-reading their own dreams — has its answer here: this is a science, and it is given, not assumed.

**"And perfect His favour on you."** Ibn Kathir: by His Message and revelation to you. Maʿārif agrees — it refers to the bestowal of prophethood. And the comparison Yaʿqub reaches for is his own lineage: *as He perfected it aforetime on your fathers, Ibrahim* — Allah's intimate friend — *and Ishaq*, Ibrahim's son. Maʿārif adds a quiet observation: what is said here also indicates that the skill of interpreting dreams given to Yusuf had been taught to Ibrahim and Ishaq, peace be upon them both.

**"Verily, your Lord is All-Knowing, All-Wise."** Ibn Kathir's comment is one line and it settles everything: *Allah knows best whom to choose for His Messages.* Maʿārif expands it: teaching an art to someone is not difficult for Him, nor, as His wisdom would have it, does He teach this art to just anyone — instead He elects someone, in His wisdom, and lets him have this expertise.

**The shape of the passage, in one line.** A boy is shown his future; his father recognises the source, shields him from envy, and names the enemy behind it — then tells him that the same Lord who showed him the dream will choose him, teach him, and complete upon him what He began with Ibrahim and Ishaq. Forty years lay between the dream and its fulfilment. The promise in ayah 6 was true the whole time.

passages.title: The brothers' envy and the plot against Joseph
passages.tafsir:
Ayat 7–10 move from Allah's own framing of the story to the first human act inside it. Ayah 7 announces that in Yusuf and his brothers there are signs "for those who ask"; ayat 8–10 then let us listen in on the conversation that follows — ten older brothers talking themselves from resentment of a favoured child, to a proposal to kill him, to a compromise that drops him alive into the bottom of a well. What holds the four ayat together is that Allah first tells us this is a sign, and only then shows us the scene.

## Ayah 7: a warning not to read this as a story

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads ayah 7 as a notice of warning: the account of Yusuf, peace be upon him, is not to be taken as a common tale. Ibn Kathir puts the same point positively — Allah is saying that there are *āyāt*, lessons and wisdom, in the story of Yusuf and his brothers "for those who ask about their story and seek its knowledge," and that their story is unique and worthy of being narrated.

**Who are "those who ask"?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives two readings.

The first is historical. According to a narration, while the Prophet ﷺ was in Makkah al-Muʿazzamah, news of him reached Madinah. The Jews living there sent a group of their men to Makkah to investigate and to test his claim to prophethood. They framed their question deliberately vaguely: if you are a true prophet of Allah, tell us about the prophet one of whose sons was taken from Syria to Egypt — an event that had left the father blind from constant weeping during his son's absence.

They chose that event precisely because it was obscure. It was not widely known, and no one in Makkah was aware of it; at that time there was no member of the People of the Book living in Makkah from whom any part of the account as found in the Torah and Injīl could have been ascertained. It was following this very question that the whole of Sūrah Yūsuf was revealed — relating the entire history of Sayyidunā Yaʿqūb and Yūsuf, peace be upon them, in a detail that does not appear even in the Torah and Injīl. So when the Prophet ﷺ described it, it was an open miracle shown at his blessed hands.

The second reading is that the event in itself, quite apart from the question of the Jews, is full of signs of the perfect power of Allah and full of guidance. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Qurṭubī and Mazharī) invites the reader to picture it: a child thrown into a pit, and then the power of Allah taking over — carrying him from one stage to the next, guarding him all the way from childhood into youth; then Allah blessing him with a divine colour as He does with His special servants, so that he stands steadfast as a servant against trials that make obedience difficult. It is all the more difficult when a man is young and challenged by opportunities — yet here he is, armed with the fear of Allah, holding his ground, controlling himself from desiring the undesirable, walking out clean from the stranglehold of temptation. And then the story tells us how Allah rewards a person who takes righteousness and fear of Allah as his conscious and determined way of life: making him rise higher than his adversaries in power and recognition, until they stand subdued before him. These are lessons and truths that can be realised by anyone who cares to look and find out.

## The family behind the quarrel

The "brothers" of ayah 7 are the twelve sons of Sayyidunā Yaʿqūb, peace be upon him, counting Yūsuf himself. Each of them had children; their families prospered; and because Yaʿqūb's title was Isrāʾīl, these twelve families came to be known as the Banū Isrāʾīl — the children of Isrāʾīl.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Qurṭubī, fills in the detail that makes ayah 8 intelligible. The eldest ten sons were from Yaʿqūb's first wife, Sayyidah Layyā, daughter of Layyān. After her death he married her sister Rāḥīl (Rachel), and she became the mother of his two sons, Yūsuf and Benyamīn (Benjamin). Rāḥīl died during Yūsuf's childhood, at the time of Benjamin's birth. So Benjamin was Yūsuf's only real brother; the other ten were half-brothers from the father's side — and the two youngest were motherless.

## Ayah 8: how envy talks

Ibn Kathir notes the force of their speech: they swore, according to their false thoughts, that Yūsuf and his brother Binyamīn — Yūsuf's full brother — were dearer to their father than they were.

**"while we are ʿuṣbah."** Ibn Kathir glosses *ʿuṣbah* simply as "a group"; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that in Arabic the word is used for a band of five to ten. The whole grievance is packed into that one word. Their reasoning, in Ibn Kathir's paraphrase: how can he love these two more than the group? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān expands the unspoken argument — we are ten, we are older, we have the ability and group strength to manage the family's affairs, while those two are small children who cannot do much. Our father should have noticed this. Notice what they are really claiming: that love is owed to usefulness, and that the strong have a better claim on a father's heart than the weak.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also raises the possibility that they had somehow found out about Yūsuf's dream, and that the prospect of his coming rise in status is what unsettled them and fed the envy.

**"Truly our father is in plain error."** This is the sentence a reader has to handle carefully. *Ḍalāl* lexically means the error of straying, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is emphatic that it cannot mean religious error here. Yaʿqūb, peace be upon him, is an exalted prophet of Allah, and such a thought in his case would be absolute kufr — it would make all of the brothers disbelievers.

That cannot be, and the Qurʼān itself shows why: later in the surah the brothers admit their crime and request their father to pray for their forgiveness, and he accepts to do so. Their mistake, then, was forgiven — and that is only possible if they were believers, since praying for the forgiveness of a disbeliever is not permissible. On this Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports no difference of opinion: the brothers were believers. So *ḍalāl* here is uttered in the sense that their father does not treat his sons equally in the matter of their rights. Ibn Kathir reads it the same way: "our father is in a plain error" *because* he preferred them and loved them more than us.

**Were the brothers prophets?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that the ʿUlamāʾ differed on this, while agreeing they were believers. Its own position, argued at ayah 9, is that they were not: the plan described here involves many major sins at once — the intention to kill someone innocent, disobedience to their father and causing him pain, contravention of a pledge, conspiracy — and by Muslim consensus the noble prophets, peace be upon them, cannot commit such sins even before they are ordained to prophethood.

## Ayah 9: the plot, and the sin planned in advance

Ibn Kathir reconstructs their thinking bluntly: remove Yūsuf, who competes with you for your father's love, from in front of your father's face, so that his favour is yours alone. Either kill him or banish him to a distant land, so that you are rid of his trouble and you alone enjoy the love of your father. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes it as an exchange of opinions — some suggesting killing, others opting for throwing him into a desolate pit — the aim in either case being that the thorn in their side be removed and they become the sole recipients of their father's attention.

Notice what both commentaries say they are competing for. Not land, not inheritance: their father's love, his face, his attention.

**"and after that you will be a righteous people."** This is the most chilling phrase in the passage. Ibn Kathir's comment is one line, and it is enough: they were thus intending repentance *before* committing the sin. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports this same understanding — the sin they would earn by killing him or throwing him into a pit was something to be taken care of later, when they could repent for what they did and so become righteous — and mentions two further readings: that things would simply come out right for them afterwards, once their father's attention was no longer fixed on Yūsuf; or that after apologising to their father they would become normal as they were before.

Whichever reading one takes, the disease is visible. A sin budgeted for in advance, with repentance filed as a later expense, is not repentance at all — it is a way of quieting the conscience just long enough to get the thing done.

## Ayah 10: one voice pulls back

**Who spoke?** The Qurʼān says only "one from among them," and the early authorities differed on his identity. Ibn Kathir reports that Qatādah and Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq said he was the oldest among them, Rūbīl (Reuben); As-Suddī said he was Yahūdhā (Judah); Mujāhid said it was Shamʿūn (Simeon). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names the adviser as their eldest brother Yahūdā (Judah), while noting that some narrations report Rūbīl as the eldest and as the one who gave this advice — and identifies him as the same person mentioned later, who, when Benjamin was detained in Egypt, came forward and said that he could not face his father without him and would not go back to Canaan.

His words, "kill not Yūsuf," mean — in Ibn Kathir's gloss — do not let your enmity and hatred towards him reach this level, of murder.

**"the bottom of the well."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up *ghayābat al-jubb*. *Ghayābah* literally means everything which hides something in or makes it disappear — which is why a grave, too, is called a *ghayābah*. And *jubb* refers to a well without raised sidings. Hear that and the "mercy" in this proposal shrinks: he is offering to make the boy disappear, into something the Arabic itself also uses for a grave.

**"some caravan will pick him up."** The verb *yaltaqiṭhu* is from *iltiqāṭ*, a derivation from *luqṭah*. A *luqṭah* is something left or dropped which is found by someone without having had the desire to have it. If the found thing is inert it is *luqṭah*; if it is alive, the Muslim jurists call it *laqīṭ* — and a human being is called *laqīṭ* only when he is a child, not yet rational and not yet of age. It is from this very word that al-Qurṭubī proves that Yūsuf, peace be upon him, was a non-pubert child when he was thrown into the well. He adds to it Yaʿqūb's own words in ayah 13, "I fear lest a wolf should devour him" — a fear that can only be imagined in the case of a child. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that, as reported by Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Shaybah, his age at that time was seven years.

Keep that number in mind as you re-read the plan. And notice the adviser's calculation: this way it serves their purpose without killing him, and without the trouble of travelling with him to some far-out place — some caravan passing that way would itself carry him off to a distant destination. "If you must do something" means, as Ibn Kathir says: if you still insist on getting rid of him.

## What Allah was doing while they planned

Ibn Kathir makes the decisive point here, and it changes how the whole scene reads. Their plot to kill Yūsuf would not have succeeded — because Allah the Exalted willed that Yūsuf fulfil a mission that must be fulfilled and completed: he would receive Allah's revelation and become His Prophet, and Allah willed him to be a powerful man in Egypt and to govern it. Consequently, Allah did not allow them to persist in their intent against Yūsuf — and the means He used was that brother's words, his advice that they throw him instead to the bottom of a well.

The rescue and the ruin arrive in the same sentence. The advice that saves Yūsuf's life is also the advice that lowers him into the pit; the very well they choose to hide him in becomes the road to Egypt. This is how Allah's decree runs through human choices without excusing them: they are fully guilty of what they intended, and Allah is doing something else entirely with what they did.

## Ibn Isḥāq on what they were really doing

Ibn Kathir closes with a passage from Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq ibn Yasār, collected by Ibn Abī Ḥātim from the route of Salamah ibn al-Faḍl from Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq, which names the crime layer by layer. They agreed, he says, to a particularly vicious crime: it involved cutting the relation of the womb; undutiful treatment of parents; and harshness towards the young, helpless and sinless. It was also harsh towards the old and weak, who have the rights of being respected, honoured and appreciated, who are honoured with Allah and who have parental rights over their offspring. They sought to separate the beloved father — who had reached old age and whose bones had become weak, yet who had a high status with Allah — from his beloved young son, in spite of the boy's weakness, tender age, and his need of his father's compassion and kindness. And then Ibn Isḥāq says something worth sitting with: *may Allah forgive them, and indeed He is the Most Merciful among those who have mercy* — for what they intended to carry out was a grave error.

## Living it

**Envy begins as arithmetic.** "We are a group; they are two." "We are ten, older, more capable." Every step of ayah 8 is reasonable-sounding, and the conclusion is that a prophet of Allah is in plain error. When your grievance is forcing you to conclude that someone far better than you has lost his judgement, the fault is more likely at your end.

**Never bank on later repentance.** Ayah 9's "after that you will be a righteous people" is the sinner's oldest instalment plan. Ibn Kathir's phrase — intending repentance before committing the sin — is a diagnosis, not a description of piety.

**Speak up even if you can only slow it down.** The brother of ayah 10 did not save Yūsuf from injustice; he only reduced it. Yet Ibn Kathir teaches that Allah did not allow them to persist in their intent precisely through those words. The partial objection you are tempted to swallow because it will not fix everything may be exactly what Allah uses.

**Finally, from the word *luqṭah* itself.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that Imām al-Qurṭubī takes this word as an occasion to set out the rulings on lost property, and draws from it a principle of Islamic society: the protection of people's life and property, and the upkeep and cleanliness of walkways and streets, are not left in the sole charge of government departments — every individual is obligated. So one who finds lost property is not merely obliged to refrain from stealing it: he must pick it up as an article of trust, keep it safe, make an announcement, look for the owner, and hand it over once the owner's description of it satisfies him. If, despite announcement and search, the owner remains untraced and one becomes convinced he is not going to look for it anymore, then a finder who is himself poor may use it personally, and one who is not should give it in charity to the poor and needy — counting in both cases as ṣadaqah from the owner, its reward reaching him as though it were deposited in his name in the Treasury of the Heavens. In the same spirit, removing thorns, nails, broken glass or rocks from public thoroughfares is not the sole responsibility of a city council but the business of every believing Muslim, urged in a mode of persuasion with the promise of great reward; and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites a stern warning in the Hadith against those who make things difficult for passers-by by crowding, lingering, or dumping their belongings on public walkways — that such a person's jihād is not acceptable. These are golden principles of public service and social self-help, laid on every individual of an Islamic society: only if Muslims would understand their religion and act on it, the whole world would notice them with surprise at how easily and effectively they accomplish what big government departments fail to accomplish at enormous cost.

passages.title: Persuading Jacob to let Joseph go out
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is.** These four ayat are a single conversation: the brothers come to their father and ask him to let Yusuf come out with them for a day, and Ya'qub — peace be upon him — resists, then is talked round. Nothing violent happens here. The whole passage is speech, and that is the point: as Ibn Kathir describes it, the brothers "started executing their plan by this introductory statement." The plot does not begin with a hand raised. It begins with a carefully chosen sentence.

What holds the unit together is the back-and-forth itself — request (ayah 11), sweetened offer (ayah 12), a father's refusal and his fear (ayah 13), and the brothers' closing argument (ayah 14). Read as one scene, it shows how a bad intention dresses itself in good words, and how a prophet's love, wisdom and restraint respond to it.

## The plan came first, the request came second

Ibn Kathir sets the scene plainly: **when Yusuf's brothers had already agreed to take him and throw him down the well** — taking the advice of their elder brother Rubil — **then** they went to their father Ya'qub, peace be upon him, and said, "Why is it that you do not trust us with Yusuf?"

So by the time ayah 11 is spoken, the decision has already been made. Ibn Kathir says they "started executing their plan by this introductory statement, even though they really intended its opposite, out of envy towards Yusuf for being loved by his father." Every word in ayat 11 and 12 is therefore doing two jobs at once — one on the surface, another underneath. That is the tension the reader is meant to feel throughout.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a detail easy to miss: **the tone of the request suggests this was not the first time they had asked.** An earlier request had been made and not accepted by their father, and so this time they press with added effort and insistence. What we are reading is a second attempt, better prepared than the first.

## Ayah 11 — "Why do you not trust us?"

Notice the shape of the sentence. They do not begin by asking for anything. They begin with a question that puts their father in the position of having to explain himself: *why do you not trust us with Yusuf?* Ibn Kathir's word for it is telling — this is an **introductory statement**, the opening move of a plan already agreed on.

Then comes the reassurance: **"though we are indeed his well-wishers."** They present themselves as those who want nothing but his good. Ibn Kathir's comment cuts through it: they "really intended its opposite." And he names the engine — envy towards Yusuf for being loved by his father.

There is something worth pausing over here for anyone who deals with people. The most dangerous words in this passage are not threats. They are the words *we wish him well*. Truthful-sounding language is the ordinary packaging of harm, and the Qur'an shows it to us in the mouths of men who had already agreed to throw a child into a well.

## Ayah 12 — "so that he may enjoy himself and play"

The request is now made concrete and made small: **"Send him with us tomorrow."** Not forever — tomorrow. Not for anything serious — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the wording as going out with the freedom to enjoy eating and drinking, and to play together. Ibn Kathir reports the same sense from **Qatadah, Ad-Dahhak and As-Suddi**: "so that we all enjoy ourselves and play."

Then the guarantee: **"and verily, we will take care of him."** Ibn Kathir glosses it: "we will protect him and ensure his safety for you." They offer precisely the thing they intend to withhold.

**A ruling drawn from this ayah.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out something the wording quietly establishes. What the brothers asked permission for was an outing with eating and playing — and **Ya'qub did not disallow that at all.** His reluctance, in the next ayah, is entirely about sending *Yusuf* with *them*. From this, the commentary concludes that going out to enjoy oneself and play is allowed within permissible limits; it notes that authentic Ahadith too seem to indicate its justification. The condition attached is firm: in such fun and games there must be no transgression of the limits set by the Sharīʿah — the sacred law — nor should it be mixed up with anything impermissible (Qurtubi and others).

That is a genuinely useful point. Recreation is not treated here as a weakness to be apologised for. It is permitted — with a boundary around it, not a suspicion over it.

## Ayah 13 — a father who says exactly what is true, but not everything that is true

Ya'qub's answer has two parts, and Ibn Kathir treats them separately.

**First: "Truly, it saddens me that you should take him away."** Ibn Kathir explains that it was hard on him simply to be separated from Yusuf for the duration of the trip, until they came back. And he draws out why: this "demonstrates the deep love that Ya'qub had for his son, because he saw in Yusuf great goodness and exalted qualities with regards to conduct and physical attractiveness associated with the rank of prophethood."

Read that carefully. In Ibn Kathir's explanation, Ya'qub's love is not the arbitrary favouritism of a doting parent; it is a father responding to what he saw in this child. The brothers, by Ibn Kathir's account of them, saw only that Yusuf was loved by his father — and envied him for it.

**Second: "I fear lest a wolf should devour him, while you are careless of him."** Ibn Kathir renders the sense: 'I fear that you might be careless with him while you are tending the cattle and shooting, then a wolf might come and eat him while you are unaware.' Ibn Kathir also notes that the request was to send Yusuf with them to the desert to tend their cattle — so this is not an idle worry about an imaginary danger, it is a father picturing the actual place his son is being taken to.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān summarises Ya'qub's two reasons together: he remains uncomfortable without Yusuf in his sight, and he fears that out in the wilderness they will become neglectful at some moment and a wolf will eat him.

**Where did the wolf come from?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers two possibilities: either wolves were simply abundant in Canaan, or — and this is the striking one — Ya'qub had seen a dream. In it he was standing on top of a hill and Yusuf was on the slope below him. All of a sudden ten wolves surrounded Yusuf and tried to attack him, but one of the wolves came forward to rescue him from the rest; once released, Yusuf took refuge inside the terrain.

The interpretation of that dream manifested later: **the ten wolves were the ten brothers**, the wolf that defended Yusuf and saved him from being killed was his elder brother Yahuda (Judah), and his hiding under the land was the depth of the pit.

And here is the piece that reframes the whole exchange. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites a narration from **Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās**, may Allah be pleased with him, that because of this dream Ya'qub felt the danger of an unfortunate situation coming at the hands of these brothers. **They were the ones he had alluded to as wolves** — but, in consideration of his wisdom, he did not lay the truth bare (Qurtubi).

Read ayah 13 again with that in mind. The father names the danger without naming the guilty. He tells the truth, and stops short of the accusation.

## Ayah 14 — the argument that ends the discussion

The brothers seize on the word. **"If a wolf were to devour him, while we are an ʿusbah — a group — then surely we are the losers."**

Ibn Kathir puts their meaning like this: 'If a wolf should attack and devour him while we are all around him in a strong group, then indeed we are the losers and weak.' Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sharpens it further: they told their father his apprehension was strange, given a strong group of ten of them there to protect Yusuf. If a wolf could be expected to eat Yusuf while they stood guard, their very presence around him would be totally senseless — they could not be taken as good for anything.

And Ibn Kathir points out the sting in it: **"They heard these words from his mouth and used them in their response for what they did afterwards."** The word that came from the father's own lips became, later, a tool in the hands of the very people he had been warning.

## Why Ya'qub let him go

If he sensed the danger came from them, why did he agree? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the reasons directly. Ya'qub, acting with the elegance of the great prophet he was, did not say plainly before his children that it was *they* about whom he feared foul play, for two reasons: first, it would have been a painful statement to make against all of them; and second, there was the danger that such a statement from their father would have increased their enmity to higher proportions — so that even if they abandoned the idea of killing him now, they might return to it later under some other excuse. **"For this reason, he allowed them to go."**

So he let them go. But he did not let them go carelessly. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that **he made sure the brothers gave him a solemn pledge** that they would see no harm came to Yusuf, and as an added precaution he **entrusted him to his elder brother** — Ruebel (Rueben) or Yahuda (Judah) — so that his needs would be specially taken care of out there and he would return soon and safe. The brothers lifted Yusuf up on their shoulders, taking turns carrying him, and Ya'qub followed them a certain distance to bid them farewell.

That final image — a father carrying his fear quietly, walking a little further than he needs to before turning back — is where ayah 14 leaves us.

## What the historical narrations add

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then relates, on the authority of **Al-Qurtubi following historical narrations**, what happened once they were out of Ya'qub's sight. These are historical reports, not part of the Qur'anic text, and are worth knowing as commentary rather than as certainty.

The brother on whose shoulders Yusuf was perched threw him down on the ground. He started walking by himself, but being too small he could not keep pace, and when he turned to one brother after another for help, each remained cold. They told him he had better call for help those **eleven stars, the sun and the moon** he had seen prostrating to him — *they* should help him. From this, Al-Qurtubi concludes that the brothers had somehow found out about Yusuf's dream, and that the dream became the cause of their extreme hostility.

Finally Yusuf appealed to Yahuda as his elder brother, telling him of his plight: he was weak and small and needed protection, at least for the sake of their old father, to whom they had given the pledge. Yahuda was moved and told him that as long as he was alive he would not let the brothers hurt him. Allah placed mercy in Yahuda's heart and the ability to do what was right, and he told his brothers that killing someone sinless was an extremely grave sin — they should fear Allah and take the innocent child back to his father; and to make things easier on them, they could take a pledge from Yusuf that he would not complain in any way about their behaviour.

They answered with a threat: *we know what you mean — you wish to rise higher than us in the sight of our father — and if you do anything to resist our intention, we shall kill you too.* Realising he alone could do nothing against his nine brothers, Yahuda proposed the compromise that saved Yusuf's life: an old well nearby, thick with wild growth and home to many lethal crawlers. Put him there. If a snake or scorpion bit and killed him, they would have what they were looking for and remain free of the blame of shedding his blood with their own hands; and if he still lived, a caravan might come that way, lower its bucket for water and find him instead, and carry him off to some other country — which, to their minds, also achieved their objective.

Note that Ibn Kathir places the agreement to throw Yusuf into the well *before* the brothers ever approached their father, on Rubil's advice, while these narrations related from Al-Qurtubi place Yahuda's proposal of the well on the journey itself. The reports differ on this detail; the ayat before us do not settle it, and neither should we.

## Living it

**Judge requests by the one making them, not by how well they are phrased.** Ya'qub was given a flawless argument — safety in numbers, sincere well-wishing, an innocent day out — and Ibn Kathir tells us the men making it "really intended its opposite."

**You can speak the truth without exposing everyone.** Ya'qub named the danger without naming the guilty. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān shows him weighing what his words would *do* — the pain of such a statement against all his sons, and the risk of driving their enmity higher — and choosing accordingly. That is prophetic manners, and it is rarer than plain speaking.

**Do the precautions anyway.** He sensed danger, and he still let them go — but he took a solemn pledge from them and entrusted Yusuf to his elder brother, and walked with them part of the way. A misgiving he could not act on openly did not become a reason to do nothing at all.

**And guard your heart from envy.** Ibn Kathir names it as the root of everything in this scene: envy at a brother being loved by his father. It began as a feeling, dressed itself up as concern, and ended at the mouth of a well.

passages.title: Cast into the well, the shirt of false blood
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is.** Ayat 15–18 carry the plot against Yusuf from intention to execution and then home again: the brothers take him out, throw him into the well, and come back that night to their father with a rehearsed story and a bloodstained shirt. What holds the four ayat together is a contrast. Down in the pit, Allah's word reaches Yusuf — a promise of a day when he will stand over these events rather than under them. Up at the tent, a story is being assembled to bury him. Revelation in one place; fabrication in the other.

## Ayah 15: "and they all agreed"

Ibn Kathir draws attention to the phrase *wa ajmaʿū an yajʿalūhu fī ghayābati'l-jubb* — "they all agreed to throw him down to the bottom of the well." He says this part of the ayah magnifies their crime: it was not one hot-headed brother, it was a settled, shared decision. And this, he adds, was their intent all along; yet when they asked their father for permission they pretended otherwise, so that he would send Yusuf with a good heart, at ease and comfortable with his decision. Ibn Kathir reports that when Yaʿqub sent him off with them, he embraced Yusuf, kissed him, and supplicated to Allah for him.

As-Suddi said the interval between the pretence of well-wishing and the harm was no longer than it took them to stray out of their father's sight. Then the verbal abuse began — cursing — and the beating.

The two commentaries describe the well itself with slightly different details, and both are worth having.

**Ibn Kathir's account:** when they reached the well they had agreed on, they tied him with a rope and lowered him. When Yusuf begged one of them, that brother would smack him and curse him. When he tried to hold on to the sides of the well, they struck his hand. At half the distance down they cut the rope. He fell into the water and went under — but he was able to climb onto a stone that was in the well and stood on it.

**Qurtubi and other commentators, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates them:** as they began, Yusuf clung to the outer edge of the well. They pulled his shirt off him and tied his hands with it. He pleaded for mercy once more, and got the same answer as before: *call those eleven stars that prostrate to you — let them help you.* Then they put him in a bucket and lowered him, and at half the depth cut the rope for a free fall. But Allah is the protector of His prophet: he fell into the water unhurt, and a rock jutted out close by, and he sat on it safe and sound. According to some narrations, Jibrīl was commanded to place him on the rock. Maʿārif adds that Yusuf remained in the well three days, and that his brother Yahūdā secretly brought him food and water each day, lowering it down in a bucket.

Notice what their answer to his pleading contains. The taunt about the eleven stars shows they knew exactly what they were trying to bury: not a brother only, but a dream. The thing they mocked him with was the very thing they were afraid of.

## "And We revealed to him" — where the sentence actually lands

There is a grammatical point here that changes how the ayah reads. Qurtubi (cited in Maʿārif) says the *wāw* — the "and" — in *wa awḥaynā ilayhi* is *zāʼidah*: an extra letter carrying no meaning of its own. *Wa awḥaynā ilayhi* is not a new sentence tacked on; it is the main clause answering the opening "when" — "**when** they took him away and agreed to put him in the bottom of the well, **We revealed to him**…" The entire build-up of the crime is a subordinate clause. The point the sentence exists to make is that Allah spoke to him.

Ibn Kathir says that in this ayah Allah mentions His mercy and compassion, and the compensation and the relief He sends in times of distress. The revelation came during that distressful time to comfort Yusuf's heart and strengthen his resolve. Ibn Kathir renders its sense: *do not be saddened by what you have suffered; you will surely have a way out of this distress and a good end, for Allah will aid you against them, elevate your rank and raise your grade — and later on, you will remind them of what they did to you.*

On the closing words *wa hum lā yashʿurūn* ("while they do not perceive"), Ibn ʿAbbas commented: "You will remind them of this evil action against you, while they are unaware of your identity and unable to recognize you." Maʿārif puts the glad tidings the same way — a future meeting in which Yusuf would be free of any need of help from these brothers, holding rather the upper hand, and able to call them to account while they knew nothing of who he was.

## What kind of revelation was this — and when did it come?

The scholars differed on both questions, and the differences are worth stating honestly rather than settling.

**On its kind. Tafsir Mazhari** holds that this revelation, coming to Yusuf in childhood, was not the ordinary *waḥy* given to prophets — because that is conferred at the age of forty. It was rather a revelation of the kind sent to the mother of Musa (peace be upon him). On this view the usual prophetic channel opened only after Yusuf reached Egypt and attained maturity, as the Qur'an says in ayah 22: *"And when he reached the prime of his age, We gave him wisdom and knowledge."*

**Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and others**, as Mazhari reports, took this to be prophetic revelation proper, though granted in an exceptional way — as ʿĪsā (peace be upon him) was invested with prophethood during his childhood.

**On its timing.** Qurtubi offers two possibilities and does not decide between them. (1) It came after Yusuf was thrown into the well, to comfort him in that state and give him the good news of deliverance soon. (2) Allah had oriented Yusuf well before the well — telling him in advance what he would face, that he would come out of this death-trap safely, and that a day would come when he would admonish these brothers while they did not even recognise him.

Either way, the consolation is the same: before the pit had finished swallowing him, the outcome was already spoken.

## The silence that follows for years

One detail here quietly answers a question every reader of this surah eventually asks: why, once Yusuf was safe — out of prison, holding the government of Egypt — did he never send word to his grieving father that he was alive?

ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbbas said (as Qurtubi transmits it) that after Yusuf reached Egypt, **Allah forbade him by revelation to report his circumstances back home.** His silence was not neglect. It was obedience.

Maʿārif then asks who could know the wisdom hidden behind that arrangement, and offers a reflection tentatively, not as a verdict: perhaps among the many considerations was that Yaʿqub be gently sounded out that such boundless love for someone other than Allah was not ideally favour-worthy — and that in eventually making the brothers come to Yusuf in need there was a mild censure of the father's conduct as well as the sons'.

## Ayat 16–17: nightfall, tears, and a story

They come *ʿishāʼan* — at nightfall. Ibn Kathir describes them returning during the darkness of the night, crying, showing sorrow and grief for losing Yusuf. Maʿārif fills in the scene: hearing the sound of their crying, Yaʿqub came out and asked what had happened — was the flock of your goats attacked by someone? And where is Yusuf?

Their answer in ayah 17 has three moving parts, and Ibn Kathir takes each in turn:

- *innā dhahabnā nastabiqu* — "we went racing with one another," or, he notes, had a shooting competition.
- *wa taraknā Yūsufa ʿinda matāʿinā* — "and we left Yusuf by our belongings," guarding the clothes and the luggage.
- *fa-akalahu'dh-dhiʼb* — "and a wolf devoured him" — which, Ibn Kathir points out, is exactly what their father had told them he feared for Yusuf and warned them against. They took his own stated fear and handed it back to him as the explanation.

Then the shrewdest line of all: *wa mā anta bi-muʼminin lanā wa law kunnā ṣādiqīn* — "but you will never believe us, even if we are telling the truth." Ibn Kathir explains what they were doing: they were trying to lessen the impact of the grave news. In effect they said, *we know you will not believe this even if you consider us truthful — so what about when you suspect we are not? Especially since you feared the wolf, and the wolf is what happened.* They pre-empted his disbelief by naming it themselves, and reframed the very implausibility of their story as an unlucky coincidence rather than a symptom of lying.

## A ruling drawn from the word *nastabiq*

Because the brothers said they went out racing, the jurists take up the question of racing itself. Ibn al-ʿArabi in *Aḥkām al-Qurʼān* (via Maʿārif) says racing one another is legitimate in the Sharīʿah — a good habit that comes in handy in jihād. The Prophet ﷺ personally took part in such races, as established by authentic hadith reports, and racing horses against each other is likewise established. Among the Companions, Salamah ibn al-Akwaʿ ran a one-on-one race against a man and won it.

So racing horses is permissible, and so is competition in running, archery and other fields. A prize given **by a third party** to the winner is permissible too. But fixing an amount in a bilateral agreement whereby the loser pays the winner is *qimār* — gambling — which the Qur'an has declared unlawful. Maʿārif's conclusion for our own day is blunt: none of the prevailing forms of horse racing is free of gambling and *qimār*, so all of them are unlawful.

## Ayah 18: the shirt they forgot to tear

*Wa jāʼū ʿalā qamīṣihi bi-damin kadhib* — "and they brought his shirt with false blood on it." Ibn Kathir says they did this to help prove the plot they had all agreed on. According to Mujahid, As-Suddi and several other scholars, they slaughtered a sheep and stained Yusuf's shirt with its blood; Maʿārif has it as a kid goat. Then they claimed this was the shirt he was wearing when the wolf devoured him.

The blood on the cloth was real blood. What was false was the story it was made to tell — and the story collapsed on one overlooked detail. **They forgot to tear the shirt.** Ibn Kathir says plainly that this is why Allah's Prophet Yaʿqub did not believe them. Maʿārif puts it as an act of Allah: He had His own way of exposing the lie, and He made them neglect the one further thing they should have done. Had they torn it, the shirt would have supported the wolf story. Instead they arrived with an intact garment soaked in blood, and Maʿārif preserves the father's reply: *My sons, certainly wise was this wolf, who ate Yusuf in a way that his shirt was not torn from anywhere.*

## Yaʿqub's answer

His response, still in ayah 18, is three short movements — and what he does *not* do is as instructive as what he does.

**"Bal sawwalat lakum anfusukum amran."** Ibn Kathir: "your own selves have made up a tale"; Maʿārif: "your inner desires have seduced you to something." He does not name a crime, accuse them of any particular deed, or demand a confession. He names the source: their own *nufūs*, their own selves. The tale did not come from a wolf; it came from inside them.

**"Fa-ṣabrun jamīl."** Beautiful patience — "patience is most fitting." Ibn Kathir gives the sense: *I will firmly observe patience for this plot on which you agreed, until Allah relieves the distress with His aid and compassion.* This is not resignation and it is not numbness. It is patience with an expectation attached to it.

**"Wa'llāhu'l-mustaʿānu ʿalā mā taṣifūn."** And Allah alone is the One whose help is sought — against, as Ibn Kathir explains, the lies and the unbelievable incident they claimed had occurred. A father who knows he has just been lied to by his own sons turns, in that same breath, to Allah rather than to them.

## Two rulings the scholars take from this ayah

**1. Circumstantial evidence counts.** Yaʿqub used the intact shirt as evidence that his sons were lying. From this, Qurtubi (in Maʿārif) draws a principle of judgement: a *qāḍī*, a judge, should keep an eye on circumstantial evidence alongside the claims and arguments of the parties before him. Truth often shows itself in the detail nobody thought to arrange.

Al-Māwardi adds a remarkable observation: the shirt of Yusuf is a wonder of the world in its own right, because three great events of prophetic history are connected with it — (i) this one, the shirt smeared with false blood, the deceiving of a father, and the shirt itself becoming the evidence that established the lie; (ii) the episode with Zulaikha, where the shirt appears as conclusive evidence; and (iii) the return of Yaʿqub's eyesight, where the shirt stands out as the cause of that miracle. A garment sits at the centre of a deception, of a vindication, and of a healing.

**2. Even a prophet's personal opinion can be mistaken.** Some scholars note that Yaʿqub says these same words — *bal sawwalat lakum anfusukum* — a second time, in ayah 83, when the brothers come back reporting that Benyamin has been detained in Egypt on a charge of theft. Both times he was speaking from his own opinion. The first judgement turned out to be true. The second did not, because in that case the brothers were not to blame.

Maʿārif draws the lesson carefully: this shows that a wrong personal opinion is possible even from prophets initially — though they are not left standing on that opinion, for divine revelation corrects them. And Qurtubi's conclusion is for the rest of us: if an error of opinion can be committed by the highest of the high, then every man and woman of opinion should treat their own opinion as suspect, and never become so rigid about it that they will not listen to what others have to say.

## Living it

- **Agreement is not innocence.** Ibn Kathir's reading of *ajmaʿū* is that shared consent made the crime worse, not lighter. A wrong decided together is still a wrong.
- **Help can arrive inside the pit.** The revelation in ayah 15 does not lift Yusuf out of the well. Relief in Allah's dealing often begins as strength given in the middle of the trial rather than removal from it.
- **Lies leave a torn edge missing.** They managed the blood and forgot the tear. It is worth remembering how small a thing exposes a constructed story — and how patiently Allah lets that small thing do its work.
- **Grief has somewhere to go.** *Ṣabrun jamīl* and *wa'llāhu'l-mustaʿān* are one gesture: carry the pain, and carry it to Allah, rather than into war with the people who caused it.

passages.title: Drawn from the well, sold, and settled in Egypt
passages.tafsir:
**Yusuf is lifted out of the pit and carried into Egypt.** In four ayat he travels from the bottom of a well to the household of the most powerful minister in the land — pulled up by a stranger, sold for the price of a trinket, and settled in exactly the house he needed to be in. What holds the passage together is a claim the Qur'an makes twice, each time right beside the wrongdoing: *"and Allah was fully aware of what they were doing"* (ayah 19), and *"Allah is dominant over His affair, but most people do not know"* (ayah 21). Every turn here looks like coincidence or misfortune. The Qur'an keeps telling you it is neither.

## A caravan that had lost its way

Ayah 19 opens with three quiet words of vocabulary that carry the whole scene. **Sayyāra** (سَيَّارَة) means wayfarers — a caravan on the move. The **wārid** (وَارِد) is the man who goes ahead of the caravan as its vanguard, responsible for its needs, water above all. **Adlā** (أَدْلَىٰ) is precisely the act of letting a bucket down into a well. So: travellers arrive, the water-man goes ahead, the bucket goes down.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, drawing on Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī, fills in what the ayah leaves unsaid: this caravan was travelling from Syria to Egypt, lost its bearings, and strayed into that desolate place — and only then sent men to draw water from that particular abandoned well. Ibn Kathīr reports from Abū Bakr bin ʿAyyāsh that Yusuf had been in the well three days by then; Muḥammad bin Isḥāq says the brothers had stayed around it the rest of that first day, watching to see what would become of him.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses here on purpose. A caravan wanders off its route, arrives at that exact spot, and chooses that exact dead well — people call such a sequence accidental, philosophers call it contingent, and both, it says, rest on not understanding how the system of the universe actually runs. It was the Creator and Protector of Yusuf who moved that caravan off its road and brought it there. Allah is, as He says of Himself, **فَعَّالٌ لِّمَا يُرِيدُ** — *"Doer of whatever He intends"* (85:16). When the visible chain of events refuses to line up, a person shrugs and calls it chance.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names the water-carrier as **Mālik ibn Duʿbar**. He lowered the bucket — and Yusuf, seeing help descending from above, took hold of the rope. Up it came with no water, but with a boy.

## "What good news — a boy!"

**يَا بُشْرَىٰ هَـٰذَا غُلَامٌ** — *"What good news! Here is a boy."* The man's cry is instinctive delight before it is calculation. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes a face whose beauty and evident promise struck him at once. On the beauty of Yusuf, it cites the ḥadīth of the Night of Miʿrāj in the Ṣaḥīḥ of Muslim, in which the Prophet ﷺ said that when he met Yusuf, he saw that Allah had given him half of the beauty of the whole world, the other half being spread over everything else.

Hold that against the fact that this is a boy being fished out of a hole in the ground, about to be priced like livestock. The Qur'an is showing you how completely people can fail to see what is in front of them.

## Who hid whom?

**وَأَسَرُّوهُ بِضَاعَةً** — *"and they hid him as merchandise."* The commentators read the hidden subject of "they" in two ways, and both are preserved.

**First: the brothers.** Al-ʿAwfī reports from Ibn ʿAbbās that it was Yusuf's brothers who concealed the fact that he was their brother. Yusuf himself kept it hidden too — fearing that if he spoke, his brothers might kill him — and preferred being sold to being killed. On this reading, the brothers told the water-drawer about the boy, the man called out to his companions, *"What good news! A boy"* — a slave we can sell — and so Yusuf's own brothers sold him.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the narration that fills in the mechanics: Yahūdā had been bringing food to Yusuf each day while he was in the well. On the third day he found him gone, told his brothers, and together they traced him to the caravan. They said: this boy is our runaway slave, and you have done wrong to keep him. Mālik ibn Duʿbar and his men, afraid of being taken for thieves, opened negotiations to buy him. On this telling, it is the brothers who turned their own brother into "merchandise."

**Second: the water-carrier.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also allows that Mālik ibn Duʿbar, after his first surprised shout, thought better of it and decided to keep the boy hidden from the rest of the caravan — because if they knew, every man in it would claim a share of the money he could fetch.

Either way the word **biḍāʿa** — merchandise — lands like a verdict on everyone involved. A prophet of Allah has become stock.

## Allah knew

**وَاللَّهُ عَلِيمٌ بِمَا يَعْمَلُونَ** — *"and Allah was fully aware of what they were doing."* Ibn Kathīr is precise about what this means: Allah knew what the brothers did and what the buyers did; He was able to stop them and prevent it; and out of His perfect wisdom He decreed otherwise. He let them do what they did so that His decision would prevail and His appointed destiny would run its course — as He says, **أَلَا لَهُ الْخَلْقُ وَالْأَمْرُ ۗ تَبَارَكَ اللَّهُ رَبُّ الْعَالَمِينَ**, *"Surely His is the creation and the command; blessed is Allah, Lord of all the worlds"* (7:54).

Notice what is being affirmed and what is not.
