Allah's knowledge and power are complete — the crime happened under His gaze and within His decree — and the brothers are still the ones who did it, still guilty of it. The Qur'an does not soften their act by pointing to the decree; it simply tells you Who is running the story.

**And there is a word here for the Prophet ﷺ himself.** Ibn Kathīr reads this sentence as a reminder to Allah's Messenger ﷺ, in the middle of the persecution his own people were inflicting on him: nothing they do is outside Allah's knowledge, and nothing is beyond His power to stop. He chose to give them respite — and then to grant Muhammad ﷺ victory and make him prevail over them, exactly as He gave Yusuf victory over his brothers. For the Prophet ﷺ, hearing this while his own people pressed against him, this was not an old story about Egypt. It was his own situation, told back to him with the ending already visible.

## Sold for a price that was no price

Ayah 20: **وَشَرَوْهُ بِثَمَنٍ بَخْسٍ دَرَاهِمَ مَعْدُودَةٍ**.

The verb is deliberately open. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that in Arabic the root **shirāʾ** (شِرَاء) covers both buying and selling. If the pronoun refers to the brothers, they *sold* him; if to the caravan, they *bought* him. Both are possible, and both come to the same shabby result: a paltry price for a counted few coins.

**Bakhs** (بَخْس) means *decreased, cut short*. Ibn Kathīr points to its use in **فَلَا يَخَافُ بَخْسًا وَلَا رَهَقًا** — the believer "fears no *bakhs*," no shortchanging of his reward (72:13). So the price was not merely low; it was a price that shortchanged what was sold. Mujāhid and ʿIkrimah say it refers to the brothers selling him for a trifle. Ibn Kathīr adds the sting: he was so worthless in their eyes that had the caravan simply asked for him free, they would have handed him over free.

**Maʿdūda** means *counted out*. Al-Qurṭubī explains the trading custom behind the word: Arab merchants settled large sums by weighing the silver, and only counted coins individually when the number was forty or fewer. So "counted dirhams" itself signals a sum under forty. Ibn Kathīr, on the authority of ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd, reports the figure as twenty dirhams; the same is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, Nawf al-Bikālī, as-Suddī, Qatāda and ʿAṭiyya al-ʿAwfī, with the detail that the ten brothers split it among themselves — two dirhams each. Other narrations in Ibn Kathīr give twenty-two and forty.

**وَكَانُوا فِيهِ مِنَ الزَّاهِدِينَ** — *"and they had no interest in him."* The word **zāhidīn** comes from **zuhd**, which literally means indifference or lack of appetite, and which in normal religious usage is a virtue: turning away from wealth and property. Here the same detachment is a disgrace. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out why they were so indifferent to the money: profit was never the point. Their aim was to get Yusuf away from their father, and a low price bought that just as well as a high one. Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk explains their blindness at its root — they undervalued him "because they had no knowledge of his prophethood and his glorious rank with Allah."

They were still not finished. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites the report from Mujāhid (via Ibn Kathīr) that the brothers, afraid the caravan might let him slip away and that he would find his way home and expose them, travelled some distance alongside it, warning the traders that this boy was in the habit of running off — better to keep him bound. So the caravan carried its priceless cargo into Egypt tied up, with no idea what it had.

## What the Qur'an leaves out

Between ayah 20 and ayah 21 an entire journey disappears. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points to this as an example of the Qur'an's eloquent brevity: the stages of the road to Egypt and the sale itself are simply not narrated, because a reader can supply them. According to Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī, when the caravan reached Egypt and put him up for sale, the bidding climbed until men were offering his own weight in gold, in musk, in silk — and the ʿAzīz of Egypt outbid them all.

## "Make his stay honourable"

Ayah 21: **وَقَالَ الَّذِي اشْتَرَاهُ مِن مِّصْرَ لِامْرَأَتِهِ أَكْرِمِي مَثْوَاهُ عَسَىٰ أَن يَنفَعَنَا أَوْ نَتَّخِذَهُ وَلَدًا**.

**Akrimī mathwāh** — *make his stay graceful*, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it; *make his stay comfortable*, in Ibn Kathīr's wording. And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān spells out what the instruction amounted to in practice: provide good lodging for Yusuf, do not treat him as common slaves are treated, and see that good arrangements are made for him. Ibn Kathīr frames the whole verse as Allah's favour to Yusuf: He made the man who bought him take care of him, provide him a comfortable life, instruct his wife to be kind to him, and hope for his future — and Ibn Kathīr notes the reason the man had such hopes: Yusuf's firm, righteous conduct was already visible.

Ibn Kathīr identifies the buyer as the minister of Egypt, whose title was **ʿAzīz**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, on Ibn Kathīr's authority, that his office was what we would call finance minister, and that his name is cited as Qiṭfīr or ʿIṭfīr; the king of Egypt then was Ruyyān ibn Usayd, an Amalekite who — according to Mazharī — later accepted Islam at Yusuf's hands and died a Muslim in Yusuf's lifetime. The ʿAzīz's wife is named as Rāʿīl, or Zulaykhā.

**On reading a person rightly.** Ibn Kathīr records, through Abū Isḥāq from Abū ʿUbayda, that ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd said: three people had the sharpest insight into others — the ʿAzīz of Egypt, when he said *"make his stay comfortable"*; the woman who said to her father, **يَا أَبَتِ اسْتَأْجِرْهُ**, *"O my father, hire him"* (28:26, the daughter of Shuʿayb, speaking of Mūsā); and Abū Bakr aṣ-Ṣiddīq, when he appointed ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb as Khalīfa after him, may Allah be pleased with them both. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the same three, adding that the ʿAzīz discovered Yusuf's inner excellence from his outward appearance. The contrast writes itself: a stranger who had owned him for a matter of hours read him correctly at a glance, while the ten brothers who handed him over had just priced him at two dirhams a head.

## Established in the land

**وَكَذَٰلِكَ مَكَّنَّا لِيُوسُفَ فِي الْأَرْضِ** — *"and thus We established Yusuf in the land,"* meaning Egypt (Ibn Kathīr), and Ibn Kathīr ties it directly to the rescue: just as He saved him from his brothers, so He settled him here. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it as advance good news — the boy entering the ʿAzīz's house as a slave will one day be the highest man in the country, with the governance of Egypt in his hands.

**وَلِنُعَلِّمَهُ مِن تَأْوِيلِ الْأَحَادِيثِ** — *"and that We might teach him the interpretation of events."* Mujāhid and as-Suddī explain this as the interpretation of dreams. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that if the opening *wāw* is taken as a conjunction, a clause is understood before it, giving a fuller sense: We established him in the land so that he would bring peace through equity and justice and work for the people's welfare — *and* so that We would teach him to put things where they belong. On that reading, "interpretation of events" takes in grasping divine revelation, putting it into practice, mastering the knowledge that supports it, and reading dreams correctly.

**وَاللَّهُ غَالِبٌ عَلَىٰ أَمْرِهِ** — *"and Allah is dominant over His affair."* Ibn Kathīr: if He wills a thing, there is no averting His decision, no stopping it, no contradicting it; He has full power over everything and everyone. Saʿīd bin Jubayr's comment is one line — *"He does whatever He wills."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that when Allah wills something, the whole visible chain of causes falls into line behind His will; it cites a ḥadīth to that effect, that when Allah intends something He readies the worldly causes to act accordingly. (The source quotes this without naming a collection.)

**وَلَـٰكِنَّ أَكْثَرَ النَّاسِ لَا يَعْلَمُونَ** — *"but most people do not know."* Ibn Kathīr: they have no knowledge of Allah's wisdom in His creation, His compassion, and His doing what He wills. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it as a habit of the eye: people look at apparent causes, take them for the whole of reality, and chase them endlessly — that there is a Causer behind all causes, holding absolute power, is a thought they rarely stop for. That, exactly, is the reader's temptation in this passage: to see only a lost caravan, a cheap sale, and a lucky buyer.

## When he came of age

Ayah 22: **وَلَمَّا بَلَغَ أَشُدَّهُ آتَيْنَاهُ حُكْمًا وَعِلْمًا**. **Ashudd** is the prime of a man's age; Ibn Kathīr glosses it as being sound in mind and perfect in body. The commentators differ on the age: Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and Qatāda say thirty-three; aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk says twenty; Ḥasan al-Baṣrī says forty.

They agree, however, on what was given. **Ḥukm wa ʿilm** — wisdom and knowledge — here means **nubuwwa**, the station of prophethood (Ibn Kathīr; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws an important conclusion from this: Yusuf received prophethood well *after* he arrived in Egypt, which means the revelation given to him earlier in the depths of the well was not *waḥy* in the technical, prophetic sense. It was revelation in the literal sense — the kind that can also be given to those who are not prophets, as with the mother of Mūsā and with Maryam.

**وَكَذَٰلِكَ نَجْزِي الْمُحْسِنِينَ** — *"and thus do We reward the doers of good."* Ibn Kathīr's reason is simple: because Yusuf used to do good in obedience to Allah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it as a stated rule, not a one-off: his rescue from destruction and his rise to the office of power and honour flowed from his righteousness, his fear of Allah and his good deeds — and whoever acts as he did will receive Allah's blessings in the same way.

## Living it

Three things this passage asks of a believer.

**Stop calling it coincidence.** The wrong turn, the stranger who happened to be there — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's insistence is that the machinery is coordinated, not random. That is no licence to guess at Allah's purposes; it is a reason not to despair when the sequence makes no sense.

**Do not price people by what you can see.** Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk located the brothers' cheapness precisely: they did not know his rank with Allah.

**Keep doing good in obscurity.** Between the well and the wisdom lay years of being someone else's property, and ayah 22 closes the account: *thus do We reward the doers of good.*

passages.title: The attempted seduction and the torn shirt
passages.tafsir:
**One bolted room, one torn shirt, one verdict.** Ayat 23–29 are one unbroken scene with one theme under it: **Allah protects His chosen servants, first from the sin, then from the disgrace.**

## "The one in whose house he was" (ayah 23)

The Qur'an could simply have said "the wife of the ʿAzīz seduced him." Instead: **الَّتِي هُوَ فِي بَيْتِهَا** — "she in whose house he was." Maʿārif ul Qurʾān draws out the hint — this puts the *pressure* in front of us rather than the person. Yusuf lived in her house, under her protection, which made refusing her advance no easy thing.

Ibn Kathir fills in the background: the master of this house had told his wife to take care of Yusuf and be generous to him. Yusuf was, in Ibn Kathir's words, very handsome, filled with manhood and beauty; she beautified herself for him, closed the doors — bolted them, in Maʿārif ul Qurʾān's rendering — and called him.

Her words are **هَيْتَ لَكَ** (*hayta laka*), read two ways. Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and others took it as a summons; al-Bukhari relates from ʿIkrimah that it means "come on, O you" in the Aramaic language (Ibn Kathir notes this was transmitted without a chain of narration). Others recited it as "I am ready for you," reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī, Abū Wāʾil, ʿIkrimah and Qatādah.

## The first move is not willpower — it is refuge

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān makes this the heart of ayah 23. Yusuf's first act was not to grit his teeth. It was **مَعَاذَ اللَّهِ** — "I seek refuge in Allah." He took shelter in his Lord *first*, and only then spoke with the wisdom and counsel of a prophet, urging her to fear Allah and give up her intention. Whoever has Allah's protection cannot be moved off the straight path by anyone.

Then he reasons with her: **إِنَّهُ رَبِّي أَحْسَنَ مَثْوَايَ** — "he is my master; he has made my lodging good." Ibn Kathir, reporting from Mujāhid, al-Suddī, Muhammad ibn Isḥāq and others, explains that in that culture a chief and master was called *rabb*: *your husband is my master, he gave me comfort and kindness — I will never betray him with his own wife.* Maʿārif ul Qurʾān adds the barb inside the argument: if I honour his rights after a shorter time in his care, what of you, his wedded wife of years?

**A creedal footnote.** Maʿārif ul Qurʾān notes that our Sharīʿah does not permit calling any created being *rabb*, since such words either raise a suspicion of shirk (associating partners with Allah) or resemble the speech of those who commit it. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says: let no slave call his master his *rabb*, and let no master call his slave his *ʿabd*. This is a distinguishing mark of Islam's law: whatever might become a conduit to shirk is prohibited too. Yusuf's usage was correct in its own place. The commentary also allows that the pronoun in **إِنَّهُ** may refer to Allah — "He is my Lord, He made my lodging good," and disobedience to Him is the greatest injustice.

**A scene the early commentators preserved.** Al-Suddī, Ibn Isḥāq and others report that she praised his looks to soften his resistance. *How beautiful your hair is!* He said: after death, this hair will be the first to part from my body. *How beautiful your eyes!* After death they will become water and flow down my face. *How beautiful your face!* All this will be eaten up by the earth below. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān's comment: Allah had set the concern for the Ākhirah upon him in the prime of his youth, and it made every charm of mortal life turn to dust before him. That concern is what can keep any human being protected from evil, wherever they may be.

## The two *hamm*s (ayah 24)

**وَلَقَدْ هَمَّتْ بِهِ وَهَمَّ بِهَا لَوْلَا أَن رَّأَىٰ بُرْهَانَ رَبِّهِ** — "And she certainly desired him, and he would have desired her had he not seen the proof of his Lord."

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān explains that Arabic **هَمّ** (*hamm*, "thought") carries two meanings: (1) to intend and be determined upon something — this falls under sin and is accountable; and (2) a simple scruple in the heart, a thought appearing beyond one's control with no intention of acting on it, like the natural turn of thought towards cool water during a summer fast. The second is not accountable. Al-Qurtubi established both usages from Arab speech and poetry.

Her *hamm* was the first kind; his the second. The commentary points to the wording: had the two been identical, the Qur'an could have used the dual — *hammā*, "the two of them desired." Instead it separates them, **هَمَّتْ بِهِ** then **وَهَمَّ بِهَا**, and attaches the emphatic **لَقَدْ** to *hers alone*.

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān states the point of creed with attribution (*Musāmarah*): the majority of the Ummah holds that the prophets are protected from sins minor and major — a major sin can be committed by them neither intentionally nor through inadvertence or mistake, and although the bare probability of a minor sin through inadvertence exists, they are not left on it; they are warned and made to move away from it. So every prophet is *maʿṣūm* (sinless or infallible; protected by Allah). This is rationally necessary too: if prophets could sin, no one could place trust in the religion and revelation they brought.

Ibn Kathir reports from al-Baghawī that this ayah concerns thoughts that merely cross the mind, and al-Baghawī brings here the hadith of Abū Hurayrah from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: *Allah the Exalted said — if My slave intends to perform a good deed, record it for him as one good deed; if he performs it, record it for him multiplied tenfold. If he intends to commit an evil act but does not commit it, record it for him as one good deed, for he left it for My sake; but if he commits it, write it as one evil deed.* Ibn Kathir notes it was also collected in the Two Sahihs using various wordings; Maʿārif ul Qurʾān cites the same on the authority of Abū Hurayrah in the Sahihayn. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān also cites, via al-Qurtubi, a hadith in the Sahih of al-Bukhari that Allah has forgiven this Ummah the scruple and thought of sin so long as it is not put into practice; and a hadith in the Sahih of Muslim that when Yusuf faced this test the angels submitted before Allah that this sincere servant was thinking of sin, and Allah said: wait — if he commits it, write it; if he abstains, do not record it a sin but enter a good deed, for he has surrendered his desire only out of fear of Me.

Ibn Kathir mentions a further reported meaning: that Yusuf was about to beat her. And Maʿārif ul Qurʾān records that some commentators reorder the clause — *he would have desired her had he not seen the proof from his Lord* — so that the proof came first and he remained safe from the thought altogether. Other commentators declared that construction contrary to the rules of Arabic grammar; and on the first reading Yusuf's taqwā and his chastity rise higher still, since he stayed safe from sin *despite* the pull of human instinct.

## What was the *burhān*?

The Qur'an does not clarify, and the commentators differ. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān lists the reports: that Allah made the face of his father Yaʿqūb appear before him, finger in mouth, in warning (from ʿAbdullāh ibn Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Mujāhid, Muhammad ibn Sīrīn, Hasan al-Baṣrī and others); that it was the face of the ʿAzīz of Misr; that he looked towards the ceiling and saw written there *do not go near adultery — it is a grave act of immodesty and a very evil way*; that Zulaikha threw a curtain over an idol in her house, saying *this is my object of worship, I cannot dare sin before it*, and Yusuf answered that his Lord deserves far more modesty, for no curtain can stop His seeing; and that his station of prophethood and his knowledge of the Divine were themselves the proof.

Ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī said the correct opinion is simply that he saw one of Allah's signs which repelled the thought that crossed his mind, and since there are no clear proofs supporting any one of these in particular, it should be left vague, as Allah left it. Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʾān both adjudge this the most-favoured and doubt-free view.

## "That We might turn away from him evil and immorality"

**كَذَٰلِكَ لِنَصْرِفَ عَنْهُ السُّوءَ وَالْفَحْشَاءَ.** Maʿārif ul Qurʾān, citing Mazharī, reads **السُّوء** as minor sin (*ṣaghīrah*) and **الْفَحْشَاء** as major sin (*kabīrah*) — he was kept protected from both kinds.

A fine observation on word order: the ayah says Allah turned *evil and lewdness away from Yusuf*, not that He turned *Yusuf away from evil and lewdness*. The hint is that Yusuf, by his great station of prophethood, was already removed from it; it was evil and immodesty that had encircled *him*, and Allah broke that trap apart.

**إِنَّهُ مِنْ عِبَادِنَا الْمُخْلَصِينَ** — "he was one of Our chosen servants." Ibn Kathir glosses *mukhlaṣīn* as chosen, purified, appointed, righteous. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān notes that such servants have Allah's own security shield around them — Shaytan himself admitted he cannot touch them, swearing to put all humans on the wrong track *except Your servants, the ones chosen by You*. In some recitations the word appears as **الْمُخْلِصِين** (*mukhliṣīn*), those who obey and worship Allah with *ikhlāṣ* — sincerity, genuine and unalloyed, meaning that no worldly or personal desire intrudes into one's obedience. On that reading the ayah carries a promise: whoever is absolutely sincere in his deeds and worship, Allah will help him remain safe from sins.

## The race to the door (ayah 25)

**وَاسْتَبَقَا الْبَابَ** — they raced for the door. Ibn Kathir: Yusuf running away from her, she running after him to bring him back, catching hold of his shirt from the back and tearing it so terribly that it fell off his back — and at the front door, her master, her husband.

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān draws two rulings from this race. **First:** a place where there is a danger of getting involved in sin must be abandoned outright. **Second:** in matters requiring obedience to Allah's commands one should not let his effort taper off, even when no tangible result seems to be coming. Historical accounts mention the door was locked from the inside; Yusuf spent his maximum strength running for it anyway, and the lock opened up by itself and dropped down. Results rest in the hands of Allah, and when a servant has done his best, help from Allah is witnessed frequently.

## Speaking up when you are falsely accused (ayah 26)

She strikes first: **مَا جَزَاءُ مَنْ أَرَادَ بِأَهْلِكَ سُوءًا** — what is the recompense for one who intended an evil design against your wife, except that he be put in prison or a painful torment? Ibn Kathir reads this as deceit and evil plotting — trying to exonerate herself and implicate him — and takes "painful torment" as being tormented severely with painful beating.

**هِيَ رَاوَدَتْنِي عَن نَّفْسِي** — "It was she who sought to seduce me." Maʿārif ul Qurʾān observes that his prophetic gentleness might perhaps have kept her secret undisclosed; it was her charge sheet of false accusation that compelled him to tell the truth. And it derives a ruling: **when a person is falsely accused, speaking out in defence is the way of the prophets — the Sunnah of the Anbiyāʾ.** Remaining silent at such a time, and letting oneself be declared a criminal, is no act of piety or of trust in Allah (*tawakkul*).

## The witness, and the shirt (ayat 26–27)

Who was the *shāhid* — the witness? Ibn Kathir records the disagreement. ʿAbd al-Razzāq reports from Ibn ʿAbbās that he was "a bearded man," meaning an adult male; al-Thawrī reports through Jābir, from Ibn Abī Mulaykah, from Ibn ʿAbbās, that he was from the king's entourage; Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, al-Hasan, Qatādah, al-Suddī, Muhammad ibn Isḥāq and others also said an adult male. But al-ʿAwfī reports from Ibn ʿAbbās that he was "a babe in the cradle," and the like was reported from Abū Hurayrah, Hilāl ibn Yasāf, al-Hasan, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Muzāḥim — a young boy who lived in the ʿAzīz's house. **Ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī preferred this view**, and Maʿārif ul Qurʾān follows it, noting a hadith of the Prophet ﷺ reported by Imam Ahmad in his *Musnad*, Ibn Ḥibbān in his *Sahih* and al-Ḥākim in the *Mustadrak*, which they rated sahih (sound), that Allah blessed four children with the power of speech while still in their cradle.

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān sets it in a pattern: Allah has His own ways of saving His honoured servants from disgrace, and usually it is infants — not expected to talk at all — who are given speech to unfold the truth. So it was when people accused Sayyidah Maryam: Allah gave the day-old ʿĪsā the ability to speak, and through his tongue manifested his mother's sanctity. So too when a like accusation was made under a major conspiracy against Jurayj, a pious elder among the Banī Isrāʾīl — a new-born child testified to his innocence. Here, a child lying in a cradle in that house — and it is *that* mouth Allah opens.

Then the *content* of the testimony. The child does not merely assert Yusuf's innocence — Maʿārif ul Qurʾān notes that even that much would have been no less than a miracle. Instead he says something farsighted: **if the shirt is torn from the front, her word is true and his could be otherwise (26); if from the back, then there remains no other probability — she has lied and he is truthful (27).** Ibn Kathir spells out the logic: had Yusuf called her and she refused, she would have pushed him away and torn the shirt in front; since he was fleeing and she pulling him back, the tear is behind. When the direction was checked, the tear was at the back.

**Two points of fiqh** from Maʿārif ul Qurʾān. First, on the word *shāhid*: in common juristic usage a witness relates an event he personally observed, whereas this child related no observation but hinted at a device for arriving at a decision. Such terms were coined by later scholars and jurists for convenience of teaching; the Qur'an is not bound by them. He is called a witness in the sense that his statement did for the judge exactly what a witness's statement does. Second: **circumstantial evidence can be taken into consideration in deciding disputed cases.** All jurists agree that signs and indicators should be used to determine the truth — but signs alone cannot be given the status of sufficient proof. Here it is the miraculous speech of the child that really proves the innocence; the signs serve to confirm it.

## "Mighty is your plot" (ayah 28)

The ʿAzīz became certain. **إِنَّهُ مِن كَيْدِكُنَّ ۖ إِنَّ كَيْدَكُنَّ عَظِيمٌ.** Ibn Kathir: *this false accusation, staining the young man's reputation, is but one plot of many that you women have.* Maʿārif ul Qurʾān, citing Mazharī, explains why such guile is called great: it is difficult to understand and not easy to get out from, because an outward impression of softness and delicacy disarms a non-discerning onlooker — and where wisdom and honesty are lacking, that can become a web of deception.

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān cites, from a narration of Abū Hurayrah appearing in the Tafsir of al-Qurtubi, that the Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said the guile of women is stronger than the guile of Shaytan — since Allah called Shaytan's guile weak (4:76) while of this one He said it is great (12:28). And it immediately adds the qualification: **not all women are meant here** — only those involved in practising such guile and excuses.

## The strange calm of the ʿAzīz (ayah 29)

**يُوسُفُ أَعْرِضْ عَنْ هَٰذَا** — "Yusuf, turn away from this." Ibn Kathir: do not mention to anyone what has happened. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān: do not speak of it before others, so that no disgrace comes of it. Then to his wife: **وَاسْتَغْفِرِي لِذَنبِكِ** — seek forgiveness for your sin, both the desire she wanted to satisfy and the false accusation she then invented. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān notes this obviously means forgiveness from her husband, and could also mean from Yusuf.

It is surprising that a husband shown open proof of such immodesty and breach of trust would not be agitated but go on talking with perfect peace of mind. Ibn Kathir's reading is that the ʿAzīz was an easy man, or gave his wife an excuse because she had seen in Yusuf an appeal she could not resist. Imam al-Qurtubi suggests one reason may be that he was someone lacking that kind of sense of shame. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān offers a second possibility: just as Allah arranged to save Yusuf first from the sin and then from the disgrace, part of the same arrangement was that He did not let the ʿAzīz become enraged — for such an occasion customarily leads a man to physical assault without bothering to investigate, and something might then have been done to Yusuf unbefitting his august station.

Yusuf's own contribution was small and within reach of any of us: he said *maʿādha Llāh*, refused to betray a trust, ran for the door, and told the truth when lies began about him. Everything else — the proof from his Lord, the lock that dropped open, the infant given speech, the shirt torn in the one direction that exonerated him, the temper that never ignited — was Allah's doing, for one of His **mukhlaṣīn**. These are the wonders of divine power, which openly show how those who stand steadfast in obedience to their Lord are protected at every step they take in His way.

passages.title: The women's banquet and prison chosen over sin
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** The private incident in the house of the ʿAzīz has become the talk of Egypt. The women of the city sneer at his wife; she answers with a banquet designed to humiliate them — and it works so completely that she uses her victory to threaten Yūsuf openly, in front of them all. Cornered now by a whole room rather than by one woman, Yūsuf (peace be upon him) turns to the only refuge left and asks for prison rather than sin. Allah answers him. And then, in the last ayah of the passage, the men who *knew* he was innocent send him to prison anyway.

What holds these six ayat together is a single movement: **exposure → pressure → prayer → rescue → an unjust sentence that is itself the rescue.** Read as one unit, the passage is about what a believer does at the exact moment when refusing wrong stops being private and starts being costly.

**One thing to carry in from just before.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to how strangely calm the ʿAzīz had been on discovering his wife's betrayal — he simply told Yūsuf to let the matter drop and told her to seek forgiveness for her sin. Imam al-Qurṭubī suggested one reason may have been that the man lacked that kind of sense of shame; and it is also possible, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, that just as Allah arranged supernaturally to save Yūsuf first from the sin and then from disgrace, part of that same arrangement was that the ʿAzīz was not allowed to fly into a rage — for an enraged husband would customarily strike first and investigate later, and might have done something to Yūsuf unbefitting his noble station. Keep that in view for all six ayat: from the first verse to the last, the visible actors think they are managing a scandal. Someone else is managing them.

## Exposure: the talk that was already a plot (ayat 30–31)

Ibn Kathīr says the news of what happened between the ʿAzīz's wife and Yūsuf spread through the city — that is, through Egypt — and people talked. These are not idle neighbours. Ibn Kathīr specifies that the speakers were **women of chiefs and princes**, criticising and admonishing the wife of the ʿAzīz; and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that some commentators identify them as five women, all wives of officials close to the ʿAzīz (citing Qurṭubī and Mazharī). The scandal has reached the households that matter.

**"Her *fatā*."** The word used for Yūsuf is فَتَاهَا, "her young man". Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the usage: in customary speech a boy slave while small is called a *ghulām*; once he is in his youth he is called a *fatā*. Why "*her*" slave, when the husband was the buyer? Qurṭubī gives two possible reasons: what the husband owns is customarily spoken of as the wife's too, and/or she had taken Yūsuf from her husband as a gift. Either way the word sharpens the mockery — a woman of her rank, chasing a household boy.

**"He has pierced her heart with love."** قَدْ شَغَفَهَا حُبًّا — Ibn Kathīr glosses it: *her love for him filled her heart and engulfed it*. On that reading this is nothing like a passing interest; the heart has been filled and swallowed by it. And their verdict, إِنَّا لَنَرَاهَا فِي ضَلَالٍ مُّبِينٍ, "we see her in plain error" — Ibn Kathīr says they meant her loving him and trying to seduce him.

**But the talk itself was not innocent.** The next ayah calls what they said مَكْر — a scheme: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَتْ بِمَكْرِهِنَّ. Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq, quoted by Ibn Kathīr, says plainly: *they had heard of Yūsuf's beauty and wanted to see him, so they said these words in order to get a look at him.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers a second reading of the word: even though they had obviously planned no trick against her, because they spoke ill of her *secretly*, their talk was itself identified as *makr*. Both readings deserve to sit in the reader's mind. Backbiting dressed up as moral concern is already a kind of scheming — and sometimes it is not concern at all.

This is why the whole passage begins where it does. Nothing that follows — not the banquet, not the threat, not the prison — happens without this first, seemingly harmless step: people talking about someone else's sin.

## Pressure: the banquet, and the threat it made possible (ayat 31–32)

Everything in her preparation is deliberate. مُتَّكَأً, which Ibn Kathīr's rendering gives as "a banquet" and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān as "a comfortable place", is explained by Ibn ʿAbbās, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan and as-Suddī (as Ibn Kathīr reports) as **a sitting room** — couches, pillows to recline on, and food that requires knives to cut, such as citron. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the arrangement included special pillows placed for hand and back rest.

Then وَآتَتْ كُلَّ وَاحِدَةٍ مِّنْهُنَّ سِكِّينًا — she gave each one a knife. Outwardly, for the fruit. Ibn Kathīr says the knives were **part of her plan of revenge for their plot to see Yūsuf**; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the obvious purpose was cutting fruit, but what was concealed in her heart was exactly what followed. She had already worked out what one look would do to them.

Yūsuf was in another quarter of the house — she had put him there. اخْرُجْ عَلَيْهِنَّ, "come out before them." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that **he was not aware of her vain intention**; he came out simply because he was told to.

**أَكْبَرْنَهُ** — "they exalted him". Ibn Kathīr: they thought highly of him and were astonished at what they saw. And وَقَطَّعْنَ أَيْدِيَهُنَّ — they cut their hands. The reports Ibn Kathīr relays say they were slicing at the citron while their eyes were elsewhere, so the blades ran across their own hands without their noticing. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes it the same way — the knife ran over the hand unconsciously, as happens when one's thought is diverted to something else. Another report in Ibn Kathīr fills in the scene: after they had eaten and settled, she asked them, "Would you like to see Yūsuf?" They said yes; she made him come and go so they saw him from every side; he had gone back in and they were *still* cutting. Only when the pain reached them did they start screaming — and she said: *"You did all this from one look at him, so how can I be blamed?"*

**حَاشَ لِلَّهِ** — "How perfect is Allah!" Mujāhid and others read their words as "We seek refuge from Allah." Then: مَا هَٰذَا بَشَرًا إِنْ هَٰذَا إِلَّا مَلَكٌ كَرِيمٌ — "This is no human being; this is none other than a noble angel." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains what they meant: one exuding such light can only be an angel. Ibn Kathīr says they told her outright, *we do not blame you any more after the sight that we saw* — and notes they had never seen anyone like him, for Yūsuf, peace be upon him, was given half of all beauty. Ibn Kathīr cites an authentic hadith that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ passed by Yūsuf during the Night of Isrāʾ in the third heaven and remarked that he had been given half of all beauty; he does not name the collection at that point, and neither will we.

Notice what has just happened to the moral high ground. The room that came to judge her has convicted itself. A circle of women with sliced hands is in no position to lecture anyone about self-control — and she says so.

**Which is exactly what she does next.** فَذَٰلِكُنَّ الَّذِي لُمْتُنَّنِي فِيهِ — "So this is the one you blamed me over." Ibn Kathīr says she spoke these words so that they would excuse her behaviour: a man who looks this beautiful and perfect, she thought, is worthy of being loved.

Then comes an admission that will matter enormously later: وَلَقَدْ رَاوَدتُّهُ عَن نَّفْسِهِ فَاسْتَعْصَمَ — "I did try to seduce him, **and he refused**." Ibn Kathīr renders it "he refused to obey me"; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, "he abstained". In front of the most influential women in the city, the one person able to accuse him instead clears him. And some scholars, Ibn Kathīr reports, said that having shown them his outward beauty, she now told them of the inner beauty they did not know of — that he was chaste, beautiful inside and out. She is praising him even as she corners him.

Because cornering is what follows: وَلَئِن لَّمْ يَفْعَلْ مَا آمُرُهُ لَيُسْجَنَنَّ وَلَيَكُونًا مِّنَ الصَّاغِرِينَ — "if he does not do what I order, he shall certainly be cast into prison and be one of those who are disgraced." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out the shift: once she realised her secret lay disclosed before those women anyway, she stopped hiding and **threatened him openly, right in front of them**. And according to some commentators cited there, the women themselves then began telling Yūsuf that Zulaikhā was their benefactor, and he should not oppose her.

So the pressure has multiplied — one woman has become a room. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points to the wording of the next ayah as support for this: Yūsuf says يَدْعُونَنِي, "these women invite me", and كَيْدَهُنَّ, "*their* guile" — the statement is put in the plural, which is to say more than one woman is now pressing him. That is the situation into which he speaks his prayer.

## The prayer: "Prison is dearer to me" (ayah 33)

قَالَ رَبِّ السِّجْنُ أَحَبُّ إِلَيَّ مِمَّا يَدْعُونَنِي إِلَيْهِ. He does not argue with them; he turns and addresses his Lord. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the moment precisely: when Yūsuf saw that these women were also supporting Zulaikhā and there remained no other visible way to stay safe against their guile, he turned to his ultimate resort.

**What he is and is not saying.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful here: "prison is dearer to me" does not reflect any desire or wish to be detained in a prison. It is an expression that he would find that temporal hardship easier to face than falling into sin. He is weighing two evils and naming which one he can bear.

**The second half is the astonishing part.** وَإِلَّا تَصْرِفْ عَنِّي كَيْدَهُنَّ أَصْبُ إِلَيْهِنَّ وَأَكُن مِّنَ الْجَاهِلِينَ — "and unless You turn their guile away from me, I shall get inclined towards them and shall be among the ignorant." Ibn Kathīr unfolds the prayer: *If You abandon me and I am reliant on myself, then I have no power over myself, nor can I bring harm or benefit to myself, except with Your power and will. You are sought for each and everything, and our total reliance is on You alone. Please, do not abandon me and leave me to rely on myself.*

**Does this contradict a prophet's protection from sin?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the question directly. This is not contrary to the *ʿiṣmah* of prophethood — a prophet's state of being divinely protected from sin — because the very outcome of ʿiṣmah is that Allah arranges to keep the person safe from sin and so protects him from falling into it. Yūsuf had that protection by virtue of being a prophet, yet he was compelled to make this duʿāʾ because of the great awe he had for Allah in his heart. From this, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws two lessons, citing Qurṭubī: **no one can stay safe from sin without the help and support of Allah**; and every act of sin is caused by *jahālah*, ignorance — whose opposite is *ʿilm*, knowledge, and knowledge demands abstention from sins. That is why the word Yūsuf reaches for is not "sinful" but **"ignorant"**.

**A caution the scholars draw from his wording.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that according to some narrations, when Yūsuf was confined to the prison, a revelation from Allah told him: *you put yourself into the prison by what you yourself had said, "the prison is dearer to me"; had you asked for ʿāfiyah — wellbeing — you would have been blessed with perfect wellbeing.* The lesson drawn is that to stay safe from a major hardship, praying to be given some minor hardship instead is not appropriate; one should, under the threat of any hardship, pray to Allah for nothing but ʿāfiyah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān supports this with two reports: the Prophet ﷺ prohibited a man from praying for *ṣabr*, saying that ṣabr is what one does when distress and hardship come — so rather than praying for ṣabr, pray for ʿāfiyah (Tirmidhī); and that Sayyidnā al-ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him, the uncle of the Prophet ﷺ, asked to be taught a prayer and was told, "Pray for ʿāfiyah from your Lord" — and when he asked again after a period of time, "Pray to Allah for ʿāfiyah in this world and the hereafter" (Mazharī, from Ṭabarānī).

## The answer — and the shape the answer took (ayat 34–35)

فَاسْتَجَابَ لَهُ رَبُّهُ فَصَرَفَ عَنْهُ كَيْدَهُنَّ. The response follows immediately in the telling — the plot is turned away from him, in the very words he had used to ask.

Ibn Kathīr's comment on the whole episode is worth sitting with. Yūsuf, peace be upon him, was immune from error by Allah's will, and Allah saved him from accepting the advances of the ʿAzīz's wife; he preferred prison rather than accept her illicit call. **This, Ibn Kathīr says, indicates the best and most perfect grade in such a case** — because everything was stacked the other way. He was youthful, beautiful and full of manhood. She was his master's wife, the wife of the ʿAzīz of Egypt, herself very beautiful, wealthy, and of great social rank, and she was calling him to herself. He refused all of it, for he feared Allah and hoped to earn His reward.

The ayah then closes on two of Allah's names: إِنَّهُ هُوَ السَّمِيعُ الْعَلِيمُ — "Surely, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing." Sit with where they fall. Yūsuf had spoken his prayer with not one human ally in the room, and it was *heard*; the women's scheme had been wrapped inside a fruit party, and it was *known*.

**And then the sentence.** ثُمَّ بَدَا لَهُم مِّن بَعْدِ مَا رَأَوُا الْآيَاتِ لَيَسْجُنُنَّهُ حَتَّىٰ حِينٍ — "Then it occurred to them, after they had seen the signs, to imprison him for a time."

Ibn Kathīr titles this section *Yusuf is imprisoned without justification* and states it bluntly: they decided imprisonment was in *their* interest **even after they were convinced of his innocence and saw the proofs of his truth, honesty and chastity**. He judges — and Allah knows best — that they jailed him once the news of what happened had spread, wanting to pretend that Yūsuf was the one who had tried to seduce the ʿAzīz's wife and that they were punishing him for it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same from the other side: the ʿAzīz and his inner circle were already convinced of Yūsuf's piety, fear of Allah and chastity, but rumours of the incident had started circulating in the city, so they found it expedient to confine him for a period — so that no source of doubt remained in the family concerned, and the talk of the town would die out in due course. A reputation was being protected. It was not his.

And yet the previous ayah has just said that Allah *answered* him. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān joins the two directly: to protect Yūsuf from the guile of these women, **Allah made His own wise arrangements** — and the arrangement was the prison. That is the hardest and best lesson in the passage. Yūsuf had asked to be kept from the sin, not from the cost; the guile was turned away by removing him from that house entirely.

Ibn Kathīr adds the sequel that closes the circle: a long time afterwards, when Pharaoh asked Yūsuf to leave the jail, **he refused to leave until his innocence was ascertained and the allegation of his betrayal refuted** — and when that was successfully achieved, he left the prison with his honour intact, peace be upon him. The clearing he never got in ayah 35 came in the end.

## Living it

- **Yūsuf's refusal is the one the Prophet ﷺ named among the seven.** Ibn Kathīr records from the Two Ṣaḥīḥs that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that Allah will give shade to seven on the Day when there will be no shade but His, and among them: *a man who refuses the call of a charming woman of noble birth and says, "I am afraid of Allah."* Also named there: a just ruler; a youth brought up in the worship of Allah; a man whose heart is attached to the masjid from the time he leaves it until he returns; two who love one another only for Allah's sake, meeting and parting upon that; one who gives charity so secretly his left hand does not know what his right hand gave; and one who remembers Allah in seclusion and his eyes flood with tears. Yūsuf's private moment in an Egyptian house is the pattern behind a promise made to this ummah.
- **When you are cornered, speak to Allah, not to the room.** Yūsuf did not out-argue a room of hostile women. He turned away from them mid-scene and made duʿāʾ.
- **Never trust your own firmness.** A prophet, divinely protected, still said "unless You turn it away from me, I shall get inclined." If he prayed that, no one is above praying it.
- **Ask for ʿāfiyah.** Do not bargain for a smaller calamity. Ask Allah for wellbeing in this world and the hereafter.
- **Gossip about someone's sin can itself be the scheme.** The women's talk is called *makr* in the Qurʼān's own wording — and Ibn Isḥāq says the real motive was simply that they wanted a look at him.
- **Being cleared is not the same as being spared.** They saw the proofs and jailed him anyway. Allah's answer to a sincere prayer can look, from outside, exactly like a door closing.

passages.title: The prisoners' dreams and Joseph's call to tawhid
passages.tafsir:
These seven ayat take place entirely inside a prison. Two men are admitted alongside Yusuf (peace be upon him), each carrying a dream he cannot read. Before he interprets a single image, Yusuf calls them to the oneness of Allah; only then does he give them their answers, and only then does he ask one small favour of his own — which is promptly forgotten.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the frame: the Qur'an is no book of history, or of stories and tales. When it does relate an event, the sole objective is to provide a lesson, good counsel, or crucial guidance for some facet of human life. Yusuf's is the one story the Qur'an narrates continuously from beginning to end, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this supplementary episode too has its graces of guidance in abundance.

## The prison was an answered prayer

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān recalls the situation. Yusuf had been completely absolved of blame and his moral integrity strongly established, yet — to put an end to the disgrace of people talking about them — the ʿAziz of Misr and his wife decided to send him to prison for some time. In reality this was the fulfilment of Yusuf's own duʿa and wish, because defending his chastity while living in the ʿAziz's household had become extremely difficult for him.

Two other sentenced men were admitted with him. Qatadah said one was the king's distiller — his cup-bearer — and the other his baker. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that Ibn Kathir, citing major tafsir authorities, records that both were arrested on the charge of having tried to poison the king through food or drink, and were kept in prison while the case was under investigation.

Hold those details together: two men held over food and drink, two dreams about wine and bread, and the sign Yusuf will offer them is knowledge of food before it arrives.

## The man they chose to ask

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes how Yusuf conducted himself inside. Because of his prophetic morals, mercy and affection, he showed concern about all his fellow inmates and took care of them whenever needed. If anyone became sick, he would call on him and do whatever had to be done. For anyone he found sad or distressed, he had appropriate words of comfort; he would gently tell him to observe patience and made the hope of freedom come alive in his heart. He would think of bringing comfort to others at the cost of his own discomfort, and for whole nights he remained engaged in the worship of Allah. Seeing his endearing ways, all the inmates became convinced of his high spiritual status. Even the officer in charge was impressed, and said: *Had it been in my power, I would have let you go. Now, this much I can do, that you will face no inconvenience here.*

That is the background to how ayah 36 ends — **إِنَّا نَرَاكَ مِنَ الْمُحْسِنِينَ**, "we see you are a man of good deeds." From this statement Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a practical rule: the interpretation of a dream should be sought particularly from persons one trusts as righteous, good in deeds, and sympathetic.

A haunting note is preserved here from Ibn Kathir and Mazhari. When the officer in charge, or some of the inmates, told Yusuf that they loved him very much, he begged them not to — because whenever he had been loved by anyone, he had suffered one way or another. When he was a child his paternal aunt loved him, and he was blamed for theft. Then his father loved him, and it led to a term in a well at the hands of his brothers, then slavery, then expulsion from his home country. When the wife of the ʿAziz loved him, he landed in this prison.

## Did they really dream?

The commentators differ, and the difference changes how ayah 41 lands.

- **Ibn ʿAbbas** and some other leading authorities in tafsir said that the two men had really seen these dreams.
- **ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud** said there was no dream at all — they had simply made it up to test the spiritual excellence and veracity of Yusuf.

## He answers a question they did not ask

They ask for an interpretation. He gives them a sign instead: *no food will come to you as your provision but I will inform you of its interpretation before it comes to you.* Mujahid glossed "no food will come to you as your provision" as meaning *this day*, and As-Suddi said the same. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the picture: long before the food arrived — whether sent from their homes or from somewhere else — Yusuf could tell them its kind, its taste, its quantity and the time of its arrival, and it turned out exactly as predicted.

Then the disclaimer: **ذَٰلِكُمَا مِمَّا عَلَّمَنِي رَبِّي** — "this is of the knowledge my Lord has given me." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān stresses what he is ruling out. This has nothing to do with the art of divination through the computation of figures and lines (ʿilm al-jafr and ʿilm al-raml), nor soothsaying, nor any other occult act of conjuring. Instead of all that, this is what his Rabb tells him, and he passes on the information. It was an open miracle, proof positive of prophethood, and a major cause of confidence: Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that Yusuf was first building in their hearts a base of confidence in him.

And he immediately ties the gift to its cause: he was given this knowledge because he had abandoned the religion of a people who do not believe in Allah and are disbelievers in the Hereafter — people who, as Ibn Kathir puts it, neither hope for Allah's reward nor fear His punishment on the Day of Return.

Then: **وَاتَّبَعْتُ مِلَّةَ آبَائِي إِبْرَاهِيمَ وَإِسْحَاقَ وَيَعْقُوبَ** — the way of his fathers, Ibrahim, Ishaq and Yaʿqub. Ibn Kathir renders his meaning: *I have avoided the way of disbelief and polytheism, and followed the way of these honourable Messengers.* And from that, Ibn Kathir draws a general law. This, indeed, is the way of the one who seeks the path of guidance and follows the way of the Messengers while shunning the path of deviation. It is he whose heart Allah will guide, teaching him what he did not know beforehand; it is he whom Allah will make an Imam who is imitated in the way of righteousness, and a caller to the path of goodness.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds: alongside declaring his abhorrence for disbelief, he stresses that he is a member of the House of Prophets and a scion of the House of Ibrahim, Ishaq and Yaʿqub — and customarily this kind of inherited nobility is itself a source of creating confidence in a person.

Then: **مَا كَانَ لَنَا أَن نُّشْرِكَ بِاللَّهِ مِن شَيْءٍ** — it was never for us to associate any partners with Allah. Ibn Kathir identifies this as tawhid itself: affirming that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah alone, without partners.

And then the turn: this is **مِن فَضْلِ اللَّهِ عَلَيْنَا وَعَلَى النَّاسِ** — from the grace of Allah to us and to mankind. Ibn Kathir separates the two clauses. Upon *us*: He has revealed it to us and ordained it upon us. Upon *mankind*: to whom He has sent us as callers to tawhid. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it in terms of *tawfiq*, the enabling grace to act rightly — the ability to follow the true religion was nothing but the grace of Allah, for it was He who, by giving proper understanding, made the acceptance of truth easy. The same tongue that said "I abandoned… I followed" now says that the abandoning and the following were themselves a gift.

**وَلَٰكِنَّ أَكْثَرَ النَّاسِ لَا يَشْكُرُونَ** — "but most men thank not." Ibn Kathir explains the ingratitude precisely: they do not admit Allah's favour and blessing of sending the Messengers to them. Instead, as another ayah says of such people, they "changed the blessings of Allah into disbelief, and caused their people to dwell in the house of destruction" (14:28).

## Are many different lords better?

**يَا صَاحِبَيِ السِّجْنِ** — "O two companions of the prison." Then the question: **أَأَرْبَابٌ مُّتَفَرِّقُونَ خَيْرٌ أَمِ اللَّهُ الْوَاحِدُ الْقَهَّارُ** — are many different lords better, or Allah, the One, the Irresistible? Ibn Kathir describes Him as the One to Whose grace and infinite kingdom everything and everyone has submitted in humiliation.

Ayah 40 then dismantles the alternative. What they worship besides Him are **أَسْمَاءً سَمَّيْتُمُوهَا** — mere names which they and their fathers have named. Ibn Kathir: it is because of their ignorance that they worship these false deities and give them names, for the names were forged and are being transferred from one generation to the next, with no proof or authority supporting the practice. Hence **مَّا أَنزَلَ اللَّهُ بِهَا مِن سُلْطَانٍ** — Allah has sent down no *sulṭān* for them, which Ibn Kathir glosses as authority in the sense of proof and evidence.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays the logic out as a door with only two keys. **First**, an object of worship might have personal attributes deserving of the least fund of power — but these idols have none, because all of them are inert, something one can see with one's own eyes. **Second**, Allah might have sent down specific injunctions to worship them — and in that case, even if observation and reason had not been willing to accept their godhood, we would have set observation and reason aside and obeyed the command of Allah. But that is not there either: Allah sent down no argument or proof for their worship. What He sent was the opposite — **إِنِ الْحُكْمُ إِلَّا لِلَّهِ**, and Ibn Kathir affirms that the judgement, decision, will and kingdom are all for Allah alone, and He has commanded all of His servants to worship none but Him.

**ذَٰلِكَ الدِّينُ الْقَيِّمُ** — "that is the straight religion." Ibn Kathir renders Yusuf's meaning: *this tawhid of Allah, and directing all acts of worship at Him alone in sincerity, that I am calling you to, is the right, straight religion that Allah has ordained and for which He has revealed what He wills of proofs and evidences.* And then the refrain returns in a new key — **وَلَٰكِنَّ أَكْثَرَ النَّاسِ لَا يَعْلَمُونَ**, most men know not, and this, says Ibn Kathir, is why most of them are idolaters; as the surah itself says later, "most of mankind will not believe even if you eagerly desire it" (12:103).

## The answers, and what they cost him

Ibn Kathir marks the transition plainly: when Yusuf finished calling them, he started interpreting their dreams. One of them will pour out wine for his master to drink; the other will be crucified, and birds will eat from his head.

Ibn Kathir observes that Yusuf did *not* direct the first statement at the man it concerned, so as to lessen the grief of the other person. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets this out under the heading *An Example of Prophetic Compassion*, citing Ibn Kathir: though the two dreams were separate and the outcome already fixed — acquittal and reinstatement for the cup-bearer, crucifixion for the cook — out of prophetic compassion and clemency he did not specifically mention which of the two would be hanged, so that the man concerned would be spared becoming obsessed by the very thought of it from that moment on.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān turns this into a rule of speech. If what has to be communicated is painful or repugnant, yet its disclosure is necessary, then as far as possible it should be presented in the way that brings the least discomfort to the one receiving it.

**قُضِيَ الْأَمْرُ الَّذِي فِيهِ تَسْتَفْتِيَانِ** — "thus is the case judged concerning which you both did inquire." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: this interpretation was not arrived at by conjecture; it was a divine decree which cannot be averted. Ibn Kathir reports here, through ath-Thawri from ʿImarah bin al-Qaʿqaʿ from Ibrahim from ʿAbdullah bin Masʿud, that when Yusuf explained their dreams to them, the two men replied, *"We did not see anything at all"* — and it was then that he said this. Ibn Kathir draws the understanding: whoever claims that he saw a dream and was given its interpretation will be tied to that interpretation, "and Allah has the best knowledge." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the same from the commentators who held the dreams were made up: whether you saw it or not, the event will now come to be as described — as the punishment for the sin of inventing a false dream.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir cites an honourable hadith collected by Imam Ahmad from Muʿawiyah bin Haydah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: *"The dream is tied to a bird's leg, as long as it is not interpreted. If it is interpreted, it becomes a reality."* Which is exactly why the earlier rule matters: be careful whom you hand your dreams to.

And then Yusuf makes his one request. **اذْكُرْنِي عِندَ رَبِّكَ** — "mention me to your master." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān spells it out: when you are released from the prison, mention me before your master as the innocent person who is still languishing here. Ibn Kathir notes that Yusuf said this discreetly, so that the other man's suspicion that he would be crucified would not intensify. Even in asking for help, he shapes the asking around someone else's dread.

**فَأَنسَاهُ الشَّيْطَانُ ذِكْرَ رَبِّهِ** — Ibn Kathir states that the correct meaning is that this refers to the man who was saved: he forgot Yusuf's request and did not mention his story to the king, as Mujahid, Muhammad bin Ishaq and several others said. Ibn Kathir calls it a plot from the devil, so that Allah's Prophet (peace be upon him) would not leave the prison.

**بِضْعَ سِنِينَ** — "a few years." According to Mujahid and Qatadah, *biḍʿ* means between three and nine. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that some commentators said he had to live in the prison seven more years, and Ibn Kathir cites Wahb bin Munabbih: Ayyub suffered his illness for seven years, Yusuf remained in prison for seven years, and Bukhtanassar (Nebuchadnezzar, the Chaldean king of Babylon) was tormented for seven years.

**Two readings, both preserved.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives them side by side. On the first, Yusuf's asking the acquitted prisoner to mention him before his master tells us that making someone a medium of effort in order to get out of some difficulty is not against the principle of *tawakkul*, trust in Allah. On the second, Allah does not like His great prophets making efforts to achieve everything permissible and going on to make a human being the medium of their release — because it is the absence of any medium between them and Allah that spells out the true identity of prophets; and perhaps that was why this prisoner forgot the message, which made Yusuf stay in prison for many more years. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that in a hadith too the Prophet ﷺ has pointed in this direction, but gives neither the wording nor the collection, so nothing further can be said of it here.

## Living it: the method of calling to Allah

Out of this one scene Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a manual for anyone who wants to do good among people.

**Draw people in; never recoil from them.** Yusuf was confined in a prison, the notorious turf of criminals and bad characters — and he treated even them with his characteristic good morals and social graces, until all of them became enamoured with him. This tells us it is the duty of reformers to deal with sinners and criminals with compassion and concern, so as to bring them closer and let them become familiar, connected and reliant; and that they must not betray any attitude of hatred or distaste for them at any step.

**Earn trust before you ask for change.** The first duty of those who carry the call of truth is to bring people to put their trust in them through their good morals and conduct and their intellectual and practical excellences — even if that means unfolding some of those excellences, as Yusuf did here when he mentioned both his miracle and his membership of the House of Prophets. Citing Tafsir Mazhari, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that such a statement of personal excellence — if it is based on the intention to help people become better, and not to prove one's own rank — is not the self-praise prohibited in **فَلَا تُزَكُّوا أَنفُسَكُمْ**, "do not talk about the purity of your own self."

**Never let the errand displace the mission.** The carrier of a call must keep his mission first in all he does: if someone comes to him for something, he should not forget his real work — as Yusuf did not, giving these prisoners the gift of right guidance before answering their request. And note where this happened. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is direct about it: do not take daʿwah as something that takes place only in a conference, or on a pulpit or stage. This job is done far more effectively through personal contacts and private exchanges.

**Speak with wisdom, so it reaches the heart.** Whatever is said should be said with the strategy of wisdom, in a way that goes into the heart of the listener. Yusuf succeeded in showing them that the excellences they admired in him were the direct outcome of his disengagement from disbelief and his adoption of faith. Only after that did he describe the drawbacks of kufr and shirk — and he did it in a soft manner, one that appeals to the heart.

Two men brought Yusuf a question about wine and bread. He answered it — but first he gave them the one piece of knowledge that would still matter long after the wine and the bread were forgotten.

passages.title: The King's dream and Joseph's plan for the famine years
passages.tafsir:
**In brief.** A troubled king of Egypt dreams of seven fat cows swallowed by seven lean ones, and seven green ears of grain standing beside seven withered ones. His court experts cannot read it. The one man who can is sitting, forgotten, in a prison cell. These seven ayat trace a single unbroken movement: a dream is told (43), the experts fail (44), a buried memory stirs (45), a question is carried into a prison (46), and out of that cell comes not only the meaning of the dream but a plan that will carry a nation through famine (47–49).

## Allah's arrangement from behind the curtain

Ibn Kathir opens by naming what is really happening: the King of Egypt had a dream that Allah the Exalted made a reason for Yusuf's release from prison, with his honour and reputation preserved. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same in its own words: through the workings of the unseen (*al-ghayb*), Allah created a particular way out for the release of Yusuf (peace be upon him).

Look at how indirect that way out is. Yusuf had asked his fellow prisoner to mention him before his master as an innocent man still languishing in prison. That request seemed to come to nothing — the man forgot. What actually opened the door was a dream that came to a king who could not read it, and that left a whole assembly of professional interpreters with nothing to say. Allah did not answer Yusuf's request by the route Yusuf had chosen; He answered it by a route Yusuf could not possibly have engineered — and by that route Yusuf comes out of prison, in Ibn Kathir's phrase, with his honour and reputation preserved.

And it took years. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that because of that forgetting his freedom was further delayed, and the Qur'an describes the extra time with the phrase *biḍʿa sinīn* — "a few years" — a word that holds good for any figure between three and nine; some commentators have said he remained there seven more years. Allah's help was certain, but it was not quick, and the waiting was not wasted time.

## "A mishmash of dreams" — the experts bow out (ayah 44)

The king was astonished and fearful at what he saw, says Ibn Kathir, and gathered the priests, the chiefs of his state and the princes, telling them the dream and asking them to interpret it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that these were the known dream interpreters and soothsayers of his state — and that not one of them could understand the dream. Their answer in ayah 44 is: *aḍghāth aḥlām wa mā naḥnu bi-taʼwīl al-aḥlām bi-ʿālimīn.*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the key word. *Aḍghāth* is the plural of *ḍighth*, which literally refers to a bundle of chaff or husk separated from the grain while threshing — a collection of different kinds of waste material. So their verdict was: what you saw is somewhat muddled and confused, an admixture of many thoughts and things, and we do not know how to interpret dreams of that kind. Had it been a regular dream, they say, they would have interpreted it.

There is a bitter irony in the image they chose. The word names exactly what is separated off and discarded when grain is threshed — and the dream they threw away as waste was about grain, and about the harvest that would keep Egypt alive. Ibn Kathir reads their reply as an excuse covering their ignorance: they were saying, in effect, that even had it been a true vision rather than a mixed-up false dream, they would not have known its meaning. Interpretation is not simply a professional skill a court can hire; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Tafsīr Mazharī, says that Allah had blessed Yusuf with perfection in this art.

## The man who finally remembered (ayah 45)

Ayah 45 introduces "the one of the two who had been saved" — one of Yusuf's two companions in prison. Ibn Kathir states plainly that Shaytan had plotted to make him forget Yusuf's request that his story be mentioned to the king. Now, years later, he remembered after forgetfulness. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pictures the moment: while watching the proceedings of this event, the released prisoner recollected the message Yusuf had given him, though a long time had passed in between. He stepped forward and said he could tell them the interpretation.

Two things are worth sitting with. First, Shaytan's interference does not derail Allah's decree; it only sets its timing. The forgetting delayed Yusuf, it did not defeat him. Second, the memory returns at precisely the moment it is useful — not while the man was celebrating his freedom, but while he stood watching a court that had run out of answers.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that in asking to be allowed to meet Yusuf in prison, the man mentioned Yusuf's spiritual excellence, his expertise in dream interpretation, and his detention despite his innocence. The king arranged it for him, and he went.

## *Fa arsilūn* — a whole journey in one word

For that entire episode — the introduction of Yusuf to the court, the official permission to see him, and the final arrival at the prison — the Qur'an uses a single word: **فَأَرْسِلُونِ**, "so send me." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to this deliberately: those are parts of the event which can be understood from the context, and so they were not described specifically. The story simply moves straight into the prison scene, cutting from a helpless throne room to the face of a prisoner.

## "O Yusuf, the man of truth" (ayah 46)

The visitor's first words are not the dream but a title: **يُوسُفُ أَيُّهَا ٱلصِّدِّيقُ** — "Yusuf, O truthful one!" Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads this as a confession before it is a request: the man first confessed to Yusuf's truthfulness in word and deed, and only then requested the interpretation. That confession carries weight because of who is making it — a man who had been Yusuf's companion in the same prison, as Ibn Kathir notes, and had watched him under conditions where pretence does not survive.

He then asks, *laʿallī arjiʿu ilā al-nās laʿallahum yaʿlamūn* — "so that I may return to the people, that they may know." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the sense: if you tell me the interpretation, then when I go back and report it to the people, it is likely that in this way they will come to know your excellence and your expertise. The forgotten man is trying, belatedly, to repay a debt.

## Yusuf's response: no rebuke, no bargaining

Here Ibn Kathir pauses on something easy to read past. Yusuf gave the interpretation **without criticizing the man for forgetting** the request he had made of him, and **neither did he make it a precondition that he be released** before explaining the meaning. He had every worldly reason to do both. He had been wronged twice over — held in prison though innocent, then forgotten by the one man who could have spoken for him — and he was now holding the only piece of knowledge the kingdom wanted. Instead of leveraging it or settling scores, he simply answered: *"For seven consecutive years, you shall sow as usual…"*

That is what the title the visitor had just used — *al-ṣiddīq*, the man of truth — looks like in practice. Knowledge that Allah has given is not a bargaining chip, and a grievance you are entitled to press is not always a grievance worth pressing.

## How Yusuf read the dream

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Tafsīr Mazharī, offers an explanation of how dream interpretation works at all: what one sees in dreams is the format of events present in the world of autonomous images, and in that world those images carry particular meanings; the whole edifice of the art of interpretation depends on knowing what a given image means there. Allah had blessed Yusuf with perfection in this art. So as soon as he heard the dream related, he knew.

The reading itself is elegant. **Cows stand for years.** Ibn Kathir explains why: he interpreted the cows to be years because cows till the land that produces fruits and vegetables — which are represented by the green ears of corn in the same dream. Mazharī makes the same connection: seven fat cows and seven green ears denote seven years in which crops will grow well as usual, because animal-driven ploughing has a distinct role in levelling land and growing grain. The seven lean cows and seven dry ears mean that after those first seven will come seven years of severe famine. And the lean cows *eating* the fat ones means the grain stored during the first seven years will all be eaten up in the years of famine — with some grain remaining that is needed for sowing.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses over that eating in ayah 48 — *sabʿun shidādun yaʼkulna mā qaddamtum lahunna*, "seven hard years which shall eat up what you have stored for them." A year, it notes, is not something edible. The image is carried over from the dream itself, where lean cows ate the fat ones; the sense is that people and animals will eat up, during the time of famine, whatever grain was stored up during the past years.

## Ayah 47–48: interpretation turns into policy

Ibn Kathir's paraphrase of ayah 47 is direct: for seven consecutive years you will receive the usual amount of rain and fertility.

Then comes the instruction that is not in the dream at all: *fa-mā ḥaṣadtum fa-dharūhu fī sunbulih* — "whatever you harvest, leave it in its ear." Ibn Kathir explains the reasoning: leaving the harvest in the ears preserves it better and helps it stay healthy longer. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the same counsel in practical terms — keep the extra produce of the first seven years within the ears so that it is not affected by bacteria as it ages, and adds that it is borne out by experience that grain while in the ears is not affected by bacteria. This is a prophet giving a nation a storage technique.

The exception is as important as the rule: *illā qalīlan mimmā taʼkulūn* — "except a little of it which you may eat." Ibn Kathir's gloss is plain: eat the amount you need, which should not be substantial, and stay away from extravagance, so that what remains will carry you through the seven years of drought that follow. Prosperity is not a licence to consume; it is a window in which to prepare.

Ayah 48 ends with a second exception — *illā qalīlan mimmā tuḥṣinūn*, "except a little of that which you have guarded." Ibn Kathir renders *tuḥṣinūn* as what you have guarded and stored, and says of those years that the remaining ears will not produce anything and whatever they try to plant will not produce any harvest. Mazharī, as quoted in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, understands the small remainder as the grain needed for sowing. Both readings agree on the picture: everything will be eaten except a carefully protected margin.

## Ayah 49: more than the dream contained

The dream itself, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out, had told the king only of seven years of good crops followed by seven years of famine. Yusuf added something the dream had not carried: **ثُمَّ يَأۡتِي مِنۢ بَعۡدِ ذَٰلِكَ عَامٞ فِيهِ يُغَاثُ ٱلنَّاسُ وَفِيهِ يَعۡصِرُونَ**, "then thereafter will come a year in which people will have abundant rain and in which they will press." Ibn Kathir calls this exactly what it is — good news he delivered to them: after the consecutive years of drought there will come a fertile year, during which people will receive rain and the land will produce in abundance, and they will press wine and oil as usual.

Where did Yusuf get this extra year? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records two explanations and does not force a choice. Either he came to know it because the years of famine were no more than seven, so that by the customary practice of Allah the eighth year would be one of rains and crops. Or, as the early commentator **Qatādah** held, Allah made it known to him through a revelation, so that what they received would be over and above what the dream itself contained — and so that Yusuf's spiritual excellence would be all the more evident and become the cause of his release.

Notice what kind of statement that last year is. The storage plan is something a nation can act on; rain is not. Yusuf hands them work for fourteen years and, at the end of it, news of a mercy no granary can manufacture.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then makes the larger point: Yusuf did not consider it sufficient to limit himself to the technical interpretation of the dream. He also gave them good counsel based on wisdom and fellow-feeling — the storage plan, the warning against waste, and finally the hope at the end. That is the difference between an expert and a guide.

The passage stops there. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that the context of the story shows what happened next — the man returned to the king with the interpretation, and the king was pleased with it and convinced of Yusuf's intellectual and spiritual excellence — but the Qur'an has not considered it necessary to mention these things, because they are self-explanatory.

## Living it

**Do the work of the good years in the good years.** The whole plan in ayat 47–48 rests on acting during abundance for a hardship that has not yet arrived. Ease is not the reward; it is the opportunity.

**Eat a little, guard a lot.** "Except a little of it which you may eat" is a discipline, not a hardship — Ibn Kathir turns it straight into a warning against extravagance.

**Answer well, even when you have been wronged.** Yusuf neither reproached the man who forgot him nor made his own release a condition for giving the interpretation. Give people the good you have; let Allah handle the account.

**Trust the arrangement you cannot see.** A dream in a palace, a memory that returns after years, a prisoner nobody had thought about — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls it a way out created through the workings of the unseen. Allah's help arrives through doors you did not build and could not have found.

passages.tafsir:
# Yusuf clears his name: sūrah 12, ayat 50–53

The king has heard Yusuf's interpretation of his dream and sends for the man who gave it. What follows is not a release scene but an **investigation** scene — and it ends not in triumph but in a confession about the human self.

One concern holds these four ayat together: **that Yusuf leave prison not merely free, but innocent in the eyes of everyone who had doubted him.**

## A door opens, and he does not walk through it

When the king was conveyed the interpretation of his dream, Ibn Kathir writes, "he liked Yusuf's interpretation and felt sure that it was true. He realized the virtue of Prophet Yusuf, recognized his knowledge in the interpretation of dreams and valued his good conduct with his subjects in his country." So he commanded: **ائْتُونِي بِهِ** — *"Bring him to me"* — which Ibn Kathir unpacks as: "Release him from prison and bring him to me."

The emissary arrives with the news every prisoner longs for — and Yusuf does not move. Ibn Kathir: "Yusuf refused to leave the prison until the king and his subjects declare his innocence and the integrity of his honor, denouncing the false accusation that the wife of the 'Aziz made against him. He wanted them to know that sending him to prison was an act of injustice and aggression."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lingers on how unnatural this is: "He had been in the prison for a long time, restricted and helpless. He wished to be released." Yet he stayed — because "Allah Taʿālā bestows upon His Messengers a very high moral station which other people just cannot comprehend."

**"Return to your lord."** His reply begins *ارْجِعْ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ*, which Ibn Kathir glosses "Return to your lord (i.e. king)..." A few words later Yusuf uses the same word of Allah: *إِنَّ رَبِّي بِكَيْدِهِنَّ عَلِيمٌ*, which Ibn Kathir renders "Surely, my Lord (Allah) is Well-Aware of their plot," and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders "Surely, my Lord knows their guile well." One word, two masters: the messenger has a lord who can open a prison door, and Yusuf has a Lord who knows what really happened behind closed doors — which is exactly why the door can wait.

**Why he asked for an inquiry at all.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that Allah gives His prophets, along with perfect faith, "matching intelligence and insight into matters and conditions they have to face." From the tenor of the royal message, Yusuf deduced that the king intended to confer some honour on him. Wisdom then demanded that the charge be cleared up first. Otherwise "people would stop talking for a while because of the royal honour bestowed on him, but these doubts would keep ticking in their hearts making them think that he was the person who had violated the honour of his master."

## The names he deliberately did not say

Notice whom Yusuf names in his message: **"the women who cut their hands."** Not the wife of the ʿAzīz, who was, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, "the main cause of what had happened." Quoting Qurtubi, Maʿārif sees in this "consideration for the right of his master's house where he lived and where he was brought up, something elementally respected by a person of natural gentleness in him."

There was a shrewd mercy in it as well. Proof "could have come from those women as well," and it "would have not brought much of a disgrace on them" — had they confessed the truth, "they would have been, at the most, charged for having given false advice only." Making the wife of the ʿAzīz the target "would have proved far more disgraceful for her."

And of his closing line — *"Surely, my Lord knows their guile well"* — Maʿārif says: "He said this so that the king too will get to know the truth of the matter - which is a delicate approach to register his innocence in it."

## How the Sunnah praised him — and why it steers us differently
