Ibn Kathir cites a narration recorded in **the Musnad and the Two Sahihs** from Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"We are more liable to be in doubt than Ibrahim when he said, 'My Lord! Show me how You give life to the dead...' And may Allah send His mercy on Lut! He wished to have powerful support! If I were to stay in prison for such a long time as Yusuf did, I would have accepted the offer."*

Ibn Kathir adds **another narration collected by Ahmad** from Abu Hurayrah, in which the Prophet ﷺ said of Yusuf's message to the king: *"If it was me, I would have accepted the offer rather than await my exoneration first."*

**How to understand this.** The purpose of the hadith, Maʿārif stresses, "is to praise the patience, forbearance and the many noble traits of the character of Sayyidna Yusuf." But does it place the Prophet ﷺ below him? Maʿārif's first answer: he is "no doubt, the foremost among prophets, but the precedence of some other prophet in a certain part of his conduct would not be considered contrary to it."

The second answer, from Tafsir al-Qurtubi, is the one that touches our own lives. Yusuf's course is "highly commendable at its place." But "the pragmatic method of doing things which the Holy Prophet attributed to himself was particularly appropriate to and better for educating his community and offering to its teeming masses the best course of action likely to bring nothing but good to them." The reason: "the temperament of kings changes. On an occasion such as this, putting conditions or delaying the process is not the appropriate thing to do for common people." Yusuf was a prophet; he "could have been given to understand by Allah Taʿālā that the delay he would cause would not go against his interest in any way," and others do not enjoy that degree of closeness.

So this passage is not laying down a rule that you must refuse relief until your name is cleared. It is a window onto a station of patience — while the guidance the commentators draw for ordinary people is gentler: when the door opens, take it.

## The question that already knows its answer

Ibn Kathir: the king "gathered those women who cut their hands, while being hosted at the house of the wife of the 'Aziz. He asked them all, even though he was directing his speech at the wife of his minister, the 'Aziz in particular."

**مَا خَطْبُكُنَّ** — *"What was your affair..."* — which Ibn Kathir glosses, "what was your story with regards to... when you did seek to seduce Yusuf?... on the day of the banquet?" Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out what is easy to miss: "This question of the king tells us that he, on his part, had become certain that the party at fault was not Sayyidna Yusuf. He took those women to be at fault, therefore, he said: 'when you seduced Yusuf.'"

The women's reply: **حَاشَ لِلَّهِ مَا عَلِمْنَا عَلَيْهِ مِن سُوءٍ** — *"Allah forbid! No evil know we against him!"* Ibn Kathir renders their meaning: "Allah forbid that Yusuf be guilty of this, for by Allah, we never knew him to do evil."

Then the wife of the ʿAzīz speaks, and the passage turns on a single verb: **الْآنَ حَصْحَصَ الْحَقُّ**. Ibn Kathir reports, "according to Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others," that it means "the truth is manifest to all." Maʿārif renders her words: "Now, the truth has come to light. I did seduce him, and he is of the truthful." Her testimony confirms, as Ibn Kathir notes, precisely what Yusuf had said years earlier: *"It was she that sought to seduce me."*

Maʿārif draws the lesson that ties this back to the prison door: Yusuf never named her. "But that is how things happen when Allah jalla thanaʼuh decides to honour someone - people would rise and speak up, come forward and tell the truth, without let or hindrance or demur. So it was on this occasion. The wife of the governor found the courage."

## Whose voice ends the passage? Two readings

Ayat 52–53 are the hinge of the passage, and here the scholars genuinely differ — not over doctrine, but over who is speaking.

**View one — the wife of the ʿAzīz is still speaking.** On this reading she continues: *"in order that he may know that I betrayed him not in (his) absence."* Ibn Kathir gives her sense: "I admit this against myself so that my husband knows that I did not betray him in his absence and that adultery did not occur. I tried to seduce this young man and he refused, and I am admitting this so that he knows I am innocent." And *"And I free not myself (from the blame)"* becomes her own self-accusation: "I do not exonerate myself from blame, because the soul wishes and lusts, and this is what made me seduce him." Ibn Kathir calls this "the most viable and suitable understanding for the continuity of the story and the meanings of Arabic speech," notes that **Al-Mawardi** mentioned it in his Tafsir, and that **Imam Abu Al-ʿAbbas Ibn Taymiyyah** preferred it and "wrote about it in detail in a separate work." His decisive argument is a matter of staging: "Yusuf was not present at all during this time, for he was released later on and brought to the king by his order."

**View two — Yusuf is speaking**, explaining from the prison why he sent the emissary back: "I sent back the emissary, so that the king would investigate my innocence and the 'Aziz be certain that... I betrayed him not... in (his) absence." Ibn Kathir reports this as "the only explanation presented by **Ibn Jarir At-Tabari** and **Ibn Abi Hatim**."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān follows this second reading, and draws two reasons from Yusuf's own words.

**First:** *"I delayed my release so that the ʿAziz of Misr comes to know for sure that I did not betray him in any way during his absence."* It would be terrible, Maʿārif explains, if the ʿAzīz went on harbouring doubts and then had to watch royal honour conferred on the man he suspected: "he would be displeased with the honour given to him and far more painful would be the silence he would have to maintain." His pain "was too much to bear for Sayyidna Yusuf, intrinsically gentle as he was."

**Second:** *"and that Allah does not guide the plot of the betrayers."* Maʿārif offers two senses. An open investigation exposes betrayal, so "people would stand warned that betrayers are finally disgraced leaving a lesson for others to stay away from doing things like that in the future." And had Yusuf received royal honours while the cloud still hung over him, "it may have occured to all watchers that it was not impossible to betray and be honoured at the same time. This would have distorted their faith in fidelity and would have driven away the distaste for betrayal from their hearts."

## "And I free not myself"

**وَمَا أُبَرِّئُ نَفْسِي** — *"And I free not myself (from the blame)."*

Read as the wife's words, this is a guilty woman refusing to excuse herself. Read as Yusuf's — the reading Maʿārif ul Qurʼān develops — it is an innocent man refusing to take credit for his own innocence. Maʿārif places it under a heading worth memorising: *Claiming Purity for one's own Self is not proper except under special Conditions.*

Yusuf had just been compelled, by "an inevitable necessity," to press for a public declaration of his innocence — which "outwardly gave the impression of a pronouncement of personal integrity and purity." And that is exactly what Allah has censured: **"Have you not seen those who claim sanctity for themselves? In fact, Allah sanctifies whomsoever He wills"** (4:49), and **"Do not claim sanctity for your selves; He knows best who it is that guards against evil"** (53:32).

In Maʿārif's words, the substance of what he said was: "In a trial of such magnitude, my remaining safe from sin was no personal achievement of mine. In fact, this was a result of the mercy and help of Allah Taʿālā alone. Had He not removed evil desires from my heart, I would have become like the rest of human beings who would be prone to surrender before their desires."

Maʿārif also notes that "according to some narrations," he said this because "a kind of 'thought' did, after all, emerge in his heart - though, limited to a non-voluntary scruple" — one he considered beneath "the elegant station of prophethood with which he was blessed," so he "expressly confessed that he did not totally absolve his inner self from blame."

Whichever voice you hear in the ayah, the theology is the same: the vindication Yusuf worked so carefully to secure is handed straight back to Allah.

## The three states of the self

**إِنَّ النَّفْسَ لَأَمَّارَةٌ بِالسُّوءِ** — Ibn Kathir renders it: *"Verily, the (human) self is inclined to evil, except when my Lord bestows His mercy (upon whom He wills)"* — that is, upon "whom Allah the Exalted wills to grant them immunity."

Maʿārif brings two prophetic sayings here — the source names no collection for either, attributing the first to Qurtubi. In the first, the Prophet ﷺ asked the Companions what they thought of a companion who, if you treat him nicely, feed him and clothe him, would still throw you into all sorts of trouble, and who, if you insult him and keep him hungry and naked, would do you good. They said there could not be a worse companion in the whole world. He said: "By Him in whose hands rests my life, yourself inside you is such a companion." In the second, your greatest enemy is your own self, which disgraces you by involving you in evil deeds.

But the Qur'an does not leave the self there. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets out three states:

- **Nafs ammārah** — the self left "on its own," inciting to evil deeds. This is the state named in our ayah.
- **Nafs lawwāmah** — the reproaching self. "When one does not follow its dictates because of the fear of Allah and 'Akhirah," the self comes to hate its evil deeds, repent from them and seek forgiveness — "as is true in the case of the righteous people of the Muslim Ummah at large." Allah honours it by swearing by it: **"I do swear by the reproaching self"** (75:2).
- **Nafs muṭmaʼinnah** — the self at peace, reached when "someone keeps striving hard against his or her self, and brings it to a state where the very urge to turn to evil deeds does not remain there anymore." To it comes the call: **"O self at peace, come back to your Lord"** (89:27–28).

Two cautions follow. Righteous people can arrive at the third state "through spiritual strivings. Still, there is no certainty that this state will continue forever." And the prophets "are Divinely blessed with such self at peace without any previous striving - and it always remains constant at that state." Which is precisely Yusuf's point: his purity under that trial was a gift, not a trophy.

**The two names that close the passage.** *"Verily, my Lord is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful."* Maʿārif finds a hint in each. In **al-Ghafūr**: "When the self that incites to evil deeds ('Ammarah) is ashamed of its doings, repents, corrects and becomes the reproaching self (Lawwamah), then, certainly great is the forgiveness of Allah - He will forgive." In **al-Raḥīm**: that anyone is blessed with a self at peace "is nothing but a result of the mercy of Allah."

## Living it

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws practical rulings from this stretch of the story.

**Guard your reputation, especially if people rely on you.** A scholar "whose guidance is relied upon by Muslims should also watch out that he is not suspected by people - even though such a suspicion be totally unfounded," because suspicion "does interfere with the work of da'wah and teaching they carry out, and goes on to lighten the effect of what is said." The Prophet ﷺ said — the source quotes him here without naming a collection — *stay away even from places and occasions of blame.* Maʿārif recalls the example: once, walking with one of his blessed wives through a side-street of Madinah, he ﷺ saw a Companion approaching and, while the man was still at a distance, told him which of his wives was with him — so that the onlooker would not fall into doubt.

**Honour someone's rights even while acting against their interest.** Yusuf named neither the ʿAzīz nor his wife. Where circumstances force action against a person who has rights over you, "giving due consideration to the right and respect of that person, to the best of one's ability, is the duty of a thorough gentleman."

**Do not settle scores.** He had "suffered the loss of his freedom for seven or twelve years in the prison but, when he was released, the taking of revenge was a far cry, he did not even bear by the idea that someone would be put to the least inconvenience on his account." And when the released fellow-prisoner reappeared, Yusuf, acting "in accord with his prophetic morals," did "not to say much about an admonition, did not even mention the episode itself."

**Trust Allah's arrangement rather than people's favours.** Maʿārif's ninth ruling, drawing on Ibn Kathir: Allah "Himself manages things for His favoured servants by releasing unseen arrangements which help them achieve their objectives - for He does not like them to become indebted to anyone else created by Him." That is why the message entrusted to the fellow-prisoner was made to be forgotten, and why "the king of Egypt was made to see a disturbing dream, the interpretation of which proved to be beyond the abilities of the experts he had at his court."

He walked out of that prison owing his freedom to no one but Allah — and with his name cleared. And the last word he leaves us with is not *look what I withstood*, but *"I free not myself."*

passages.title: Given charge of Egypt's storehouses
passages.tafsir:
**The turn of the story.** In these four ayat Yusuf (peace be upon him) walks out of a prison cell and into the highest office in Egypt. Ayah 54 brings him before the king; ayah 55 records the single request he makes; ayah 56 tells us Whose hand actually placed him there; ayah 57 lifts our eyes past Egypt altogether. What binds them into one unit is that movement — a man wronged, held in the disgrace of slavery and imprisoned is raised high — and the refusal of the Qur'an to let us read the rise as a political success story. The verb in ayah 56 is not "he rose"; it is "**We** established Yusuf in the land."

## From the prison door to the throne room

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in what happens between ayah 53 and ayah 54. When the king investigated the affair — the investigation Yusuf himself had asked for — Zulaikha and all the women concerned confessed the truth. Only then did the king order Yusuf brought to him, not merely as a prisoner whose name had been cleared, but as a man he intended to make his personal adviser; and on that royal order he was brought from the prison to the court with full honours.

Imam al-Baghawi reports the manner of his going. When the king's emissary reached the prison the second time, Yusuf first made duʿā for all the inmates he was leaving behind, then took a ritual bath and put on new clothing. The duʿā he made on reaching the royal court was:

> For me sufficient is my Lord against my world and, for me, sufficient is my Lord against the whole creation. Mighty is he who comes under His protection; and most sublime is His praise; and there is no deity worthy of worship other than Him.

Notice where he places himself as he steps into the most powerful room in Egypt: under Allah's protection, not the king's.

Inside the court he turned to Allah again in the same spirit. He greeted the assembly in Arabic — *as-salāmu ʿalaykum wa raḥmatullāh* — and made his duʿā for the king in Hebrew. The king knew many languages, but not those two, and it was Yusuf who told him what each had been. It also appears in a narration that the king addressed him in language after language, and Yusuf answered each in the language spoken to him, with Arabic and Hebrew on top of those. This episode, Maʿārif notes, greatly increased the king's respect for him.

Then the king asked to hear his dream interpreted from Yusuf's own mouth. Yusuf first described details of the dream that the king had told no one, and only then gave the interpretation. What astonished the king was not so much the interpretation itself — it was how this man could know those details at all.

So the king asked him what to do next, and Yusuf laid out a plan. Through the seven years of heavy rain, give the people every incentive to bring the maximum land under cultivation and make the crops as plentiful as possible, and let them keep one fifth of their own produce stored with them — so Egypt's people would carry themselves through the lean years and the state need not worry on their account. Whatever grain reached the government through fixed taxes and state lands should be stored separately for those coming from outside the country, because this famine would be widespread and neighbouring lands would need Egypt's help; even at an ordinary price the treasury would gather wealth it had never held. The king was immensely pleased — and immediately ran into the obvious problem. A plan of that size needed a manager. Who?

Ayah 55 is Yusuf's answer.

## "This day you are with us high in rank and fully trusted" (54)

Ibn Kathir explains the king's words *astakhliṣhu li-nafsī* — "that I may attach him to my person" — as meaning: *that I may make him one of my close aides and associates.* Then comes the phrase *fa-lammā kallamahu*, "then, when he spoke to him." The appointment did not come from a report or a reputation; it came from a conversation. Speaking with Yusuf, the king recognised, in Ibn Kathir's words, his virtues, great ability, brilliance, good conduct and perfect mannerism — and told him: **makīn amīn**.

Two things are named in that one sentence, and the commentators keep them distinct. *Makīn*: "You have assumed an exalted status with us," is how Ibn Kathir renders it; Maʿārif puts it as "firmly accommodated." *Amīn*: "and are indeed fully trusted." Maʿārif marks the moment precisely — it was when the king "got an idea of his full potential by talking to him" that he said this. Rank and trust, both handed over in a single breath, to a man the king had just met.

## "Set me over the storehouses of the land" (55)

*Ijʿalnī ʿalā khazā'ini'l-arḍ, innī ḥafīẓun ʿalīm.* Qurtubi and Mazhari, as cited in Maʿārif, note that "the treasures of the land" here takes in the produce of the land, and read the request as: *appoint me over them, for I am a knowledgeable keeper — fully capable of conserving and guarding it, and aware of where to spend and how much to spend.* Ibn Kathir glosses the two words simply: **ḥafīẓ**, an honest guard; **ʿalīm**, one having knowledge and wisdom about the job he is to be entrusted with. In practical terms, Ibn Kathir says, he was asking to be made minister of finance, responsible for the storehouses in which produce would be gathered for the drought years he had foretold.

Maʿārif draws out how much work those two words are doing. The chief trustee of a national treasury has two distinct duties, and each word guarantees one of them:

- **Ḥafīẓ** covers the guarding side: public property must not be wasted; it must be collected, conserved and fully protected; and it must not be spent on undeserving people or on false heads of expenditure.
- **ʿAlīm** covers the spending side: he must not fall short in spending what has to be spent, where it has to be spent — and equally must not spend beyond the actual need.

Between them, Maʿārif comments, Yusuf has combined in two words every functional virtue a genuine finance minister needs. And the motive behind the request is not ambition. Ibn Kathir states it directly: he wanted to be the guard **so that he could dispense the harvest in the wisest, best and most beneficial way**. The king accepted at once, eager as he was to draw Yusuf close and to honour him.

One quiet detail from Maʿārif: the king did not hand over the ministry that day. Attached as he was to Yusuf, he kept him a year as his honoured guest — perhaps, Maʿārif suggests, because giving so great an office without first knowing a man's manners, morals and habits at close quarters did not seem right to him. Only after that year did he appoint him finance minister, and entrust him with the rest of the state's affairs besides.

## May a believer ask for office?

Ayah 55 raises a real difficulty, and the scholars meet it head-on. Two hadiths of *Sahih Muslim* are cited in Maʿārif. In the first, the Prophet ﷺ said to Sayyidnā ʿAbd-ur-Raḥmān ibn Samurah (may Allah be pleased with him): never seek an office of authority, because if you are given it for the asking, the support of Allah — by which you would have been kept safe from slips and errors — will not be with you; and if you are given it without asking, that help and support will be there, and through it you will be able to fulfil the rights of that office as they are due. In the second, a man asked to be appointed to a certain office, and the Prophet ﷺ replied: *"We would not give our office to a person who asks for it."* As a rule, Maʿārif notes, the Prophet ﷺ did not give an office to anyone who requested it for himself.

So why is Yusuf's request praiseworthy? Maʿārif answers by looking at what he faced. The king of Egypt was a disbeliever, and his staff likewise. A famine was coming, and when it came, selfish men would have no mercy on the creation of Allah and millions could die of hunger. He could see no one who would be relied upon to do justice to the rights of ordinary people. That is why he asked — and why he had to point to his own competence, as a matter of necessity, so the king would be satisfied and entrust the office to him.

From this the scholars derive a narrow permission. Seeking office becomes permissible — Qurtubi, as quoted in Maʿārif, goes so far as to say **obligatory (wājib)** — when no one else is available who would discharge that responsibility as it must be discharged, when an honest self-assessment tells a person that he can, and when there is no danger of being dragged into sin by it. The condition is absolute: the motive must not be love of recognition, power or wealth, but genuine service to Allah's creation and delivering people their rights with justice and equity — an intention lying in the heart, fully open before Allah. Where those conditions do not hold, the prohibition in the hadiths stands.

Maʿārif applies the same principle to the rightly-guided Khulafā' (may Allah be pleased with them all) — the successors who led the Muslim community after the Prophet ﷺ. They took on the Khilāfah, that office of leadership, because they knew no one else could carry it as it needed carrying then. The differences attributed to Sayyidnā ʿAlī, Sayyidnā Muʿāwiyah, Sayyidnā Ḥusayn and Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh ibn Zubayr (may Allah be pleased with them) rested on the same conviction — each held that he would discharge that responsibility with more wisdom and strength than others. None of them, Maʿārif insists, was moved by a desire for recognition, power or wealth.

## Serving under a ruler who does not share your faith

The second difficulty is sharper: Yusuf took office under a disbelieving king. Maʿārif reports a genuine disagreement here rather than flattening it.

Imām al-Jaṣṣāṣ, commenting on *"never shall I be a help to those who sin"* (28:17), held that it is not permissible to assist the unjust and the disbelieving, and that taking office in such a government amounts to becoming part of its working and helping it — help the Qur'an forbids in many places.

As for Yusuf's own case, **Mujahid** held that the king of Egypt had by then become a believer. Maʿārif observes that no proof in the Qur'an and Sunnah establishes that, so the majority of commentators explain his action differently: Yusuf had already ascertained that the king would not interfere in the discharge of his duties, would not compel him to enforce anything contrary to his faith, and would leave him full liberty to act by his own discretion and in line with the law of truth. Where a person has that liberty — where he is never compelled to act against his Sharīʿah — it is possible for him to serve under an unjust or disbelieving ruler, though the repugnance of cooperating with such a person remains exactly what it was. And there are circumstances in which such a ruler simply cannot be removed, while refusing office would mean the rights of many of Allah's servants are wasted or that they are oppressed. That is a situation of compulsion, and this much room for cooperation exists in it: the man is not himself made to do what the Sharīʿah forbids, so he helps the ruler in his sin only as a remote cause, and remote causes have room in the Sharīʿah under stated conditions. Maʿārif notes that many righteous elders among the Ṣaḥābah and Tābiʿīn faced such conditions, and it stands proved that they accepted posts under oppressive rulers.

ʿAllāma al-Māwardī, in his work on the political implications of religious law, records both positions: some commentators, on the basis of what Yusuf did, ruled office under disbelieving or unjust rulers permissible provided nothing against the Sharīʿah is required; others ruled it impermissible even with that condition, since it still supports the oppressor, and held Yusuf's conduct particular to him or to his Sharīʿah. **The majority of Muslim scholars and jurists went with the first position.** *Tafsir al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ* adds that where the refusal of learned and righteous people would mean rights are wasted and justice undone, accepting such office is not merely permissible but an act of reward (*thawāb*) — again, on condition that one is not compelled to act against the Sharīʿah.

**On praising oneself.** Ibn Kathir notes that Yusuf praised himself here, and that this is allowed when one's abilities are unknown and there is need to do so. Maʿārif states the ruling in the same terms: mentioning one's own qualities or expertise at a point of genuine need does not fall under the self-sanctification the Qur'an forbids — provided it is not prompted by pride, arrogance or boastfulness.

## "Thus did We establish Yusuf in the land" (56)

Now the Qur'an takes the story back from the king. Ibn Kathir explains *makkannā li-Yūsufa fi'l-arḍ* as full authority given to him in Egypt. On *yatabawwa'u minhā ḥaythu yashā'* — "to settle therein wherever he wills" — As-Suddī and ʿAbd-ur-Raḥmān bin Zayd bin Aslam said it means: *to do whatever he wants therein.* Ibn Jarīr aṭ-Ṭabarī read it against what came before: **he used to move about freely in the land after being imprisoned, suffering from hardship and the disgrace of slavery.**

Sit with Ṭabarī's contrast. A man who had known the inside of a prison, hardship, and the disgrace of slavery now moves through that same land wherever he wishes. Ibn Kathir adds a detail with a sting of its own: Yusuf was appointed minister of finance by Ar-Rayyān bin al-Walīd, the king of Egypt at that time, **in place of the ʿAzīz** who had bought him and whose wife had tried to seduce him.

Maʿārif describes the day itself: after the year of testing, the king convened a special assembly of all the officials and dignitaries of the state, and Yusuf was brought in with a crown on his head. He was given not merely the treasury but charge of virtually the whole state, and the king withdrew from active involvement in its affairs. Yusuf then governed so ably that no one had cause to complain; the whole country loved him; peace and prosperity prevailed, and he himself faced no distress in carrying the many responsibilities of government.

And Mujahid names the thing that never changed underneath the crown: beneath the outward grandeur of his rule Yusuf aimed at nothing except that the command of Allah be carried out in that land and that the faith Allah gave be firmly established. He never lost sight of his basic objective — calling the king of Egypt to faith — and in time, by Allah's grace, those efforts bore fruit and the king became a believing Muslim. Ibn Kathir reports the same from Mujahid: the king embraced Islam at Yusuf's hands.

Then the ayah widens: *"We bestow of Our mercy on whom We will, and We do not let the reward of the doers of good be lost."* Ibn Kathir reads this as Allah's own commentary on everything Yusuf endured: We did not let his patience — under the harm his brothers did him, and under imprisonment because of the wife of the ʿAzīz — go to waste; instead Allah rewarded him with His aid and victory. Nothing of those years was spent for nothing.

## "And the reward of the Hereafter is better" (57)

And then, having described a throne, the Qur'an points past it. Ibn Kathir: what Allah has prepared for His Prophet Yusuf in the Hereafter is much greater, more substantial and more honoured than the authority He gave him in this life. He draws the parallel with Sulaymān (peace be upon him), to whom Allah said, *"This is Our gift, so spend or withhold, no account will be asked of you"* — and then added, *"And verily, for him is a near access to Us, and a good final return"* (38:39–40). In both cases the kingdom is named, and then the eye is turned to what is waiting with Allah.

Maʿārif reads ayah 57 the same way: Allah had already blessed Yusuf with temporal power, wealth and an ideal state — and the high ranks of the Hereafter were waiting for him as well. Then it notes the two conditions the ayah attaches — *those who believed and had Taqwā*, that is, those who elect to believe, to keep away from evil, and to keep fearing Allah — and the door this leaves open: these ranks were never reserved for Yusuf. The ayah is an open invitation to everyone who meets those terms.

## What it looked like in practice

Maʿārif closes with the detail that shows what the two words of ayah 55 actually cost him. During his rule Yusuf carried out great projects for the peace and comfort of the people, projects whose parallel would be hard to find. When the seven good years passed and the famine set in exactly as he had interpreted, he stopped eating his fill. People said to him: the treasures of Egypt are in your hands, and you go hungry? He answered: **I do this so that the feeling for the hunger of my common people does not disappear from my heart.** He even made it policy — the royal cooks were ordered to prepare only one meal a day, at lunch, so that the residents of the palace too would share something of the hunger of their people.

That is the whole passage in one man's habit. Office was never the point; it was a trust to be guarded (*ḥafīẓ*) and spent rightly (*ʿalīm*), held by someone who kept his own hunger close to the hunger of the people he answered for — and who knew all along, as ayah 57 says, that the greater reward lay elsewhere.

passages.title: The brothers arrive and are told to bring Benjamin
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is.** The seven years of plenty are over, the famine has arrived exactly as the king's dream had been interpreted, and ten men from Canaan walk into the court of the man who now rules Egypt — not knowing that he is the brother they sold, years earlier, to a passing caravan. Ayat 58–62 are a single scene held together by one thing: a recognition that runs only in one direction. Yusuf knows them; they do not know him. Everything he does in these ayat — the questioning, the generous measure, the hard condition, the money quietly returned into their packs — is one carefully built arrangement to make them come back, and to bring his younger brother with them.

## Why they came at all

Ibn Kathir reports from As-Suddi, Muhammad bin Ishaq and others that once Yusuf became minister of Egypt, the seven years of abundance passed, and then came the seven years of drought that struck all the areas of Egypt. It did not stop at Egypt's borders. It reached Kana'an (Canaan), where Prophet Ya'qub (peace be upon him) and his children lived — the land Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies as part of Palestine, one of its cities still surviving by the name Khalil, known for the resting places of Ibrahim, Ishaq, Ya'qub and Yusuf (peace be upon them all).

Ibn Kathir says he efficiently guarded the people's harvest and collected it, and that what he collected became a great fortune for the people. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that because he knew in advance the famine would run seven years without any break, he arranged for the grain already in the country to be stored very carefully during the first year of the famine and kept fully preserved and protected. Then he rationed: Ibn Kathir says he would not give a family man more than whatever a camel could carry, as annual provisions for them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes from al-Qurtubi that the quantity of this camel-load was one *wasaq*, that is sixty *ṣāʿ* (*wasaq* and *ṣāʿ* being measures of quantity in use at the time). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also records a standing rule of procedure: no more than one camel-load to one person at one time, but once that had been consumed as calculated, he would allow it to be given a second time.

And he held himself to a harder standard than he held the people. Ibn Kathir records that Yusuf did not fill his stomach from this food, and that neither the king nor his aides ate more than one meal a day — and that by doing so, the people could sustain themselves with what they had for the remainder of the seven years. Ibn Kathir's verdict on the whole arrangement is a sentence worth carrying: Yusuf was a mercy from Allah sent to the people of Egypt. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that such was his concern for this responsibility that he himself used to oversee the sale of the grain — not a policy he set down and left to others.

Word of this reached Canaan. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says news had gone around that Egypt was the place where grain could be procured on payment, and Ya'qub had come to know that the king of Egypt was a man of mercy who would let those in need have it, so he told his sons to go and get some. Ibn Kathir says they knew that the *'Azīz* of Egypt — *'Azīz* is the title of the high office Yusuf now held, the one Ibn Kathir elsewhere calls minister of Egypt and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls master of the land — was selling food to people who needed it for a low price, so they took some merchandise from their land with them to exchange for it. Because no one person was given more than a camel-load, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says it was decided to send all the sons — which is why they arrive as a delegation of ten rather than one or two. All except Benyamin. Ibn Kathir explains that Ya'qub kept him back: he was the dearest of his sons to him after Yusuf; and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the father had become very attached to him since Yusuf's disappearance and held him back for his own comfort and care.

## "He recognized them, but they did not recognize him" (ayah 58)

The whole surah turns on this half-line. Ibn Kathir explains the asymmetry plainly: when they entered upon him in his court and the centre of his authority, he knew them the minute he saw them — but they got rid of him while he was still young and sold him to a caravan of travellers without even knowing the caravan's destination, and they could not have imagined that Yusuf would end up being a minister. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says he had been a seven-year-old child when they sold him to the people of the caravan, and reports from Sayyidna Abdullah ibn Abbas — citing Qurtubi and Mazhari — that forty years had now passed over that event. It is obvious, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, that the passage of such a long time would cause great changes in a person's looks, and it could never have occurred to them that a child once sold as a slave could become the king or minister of some country. Add to four decades the royal robe in which he now appeared before them, and their failure is not stupidity — it is the ordinary blindness of people who have already settled in their minds what became of someone.

The ayah does not say "they did not know him" with a simple negation; it calls them **munkirūn**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that in the Arabic language the real meaning of *inkār* is "to take as stranger," and so *munkirūn* here comes to mean "unable to recognize." They looked straight at him and took him for a stranger.

## The interrogation

Ibn Kathir reports from As-Suddi the exchange that followed. Yusuf opened the questioning: "What brought you to my land?" They answered, "O 'Azīz, we came to buy provisions." He pressed: "You might be spies." They said, "Allah forbid." He asked where they were from; they said the area of Kana'an, and that their father was Allah's Prophet Ya'qub. In Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's telling of the same report from Suddiyy, Yusuf interrogated them as one does with suspicious people, so that they would state the truth clearly: he opens by noting that they are not residents of Egypt and that they speak Hebrew, and asks how they got there. They answer that there is a great famine in their country and they have heard of him, so they have come for grain; he asks how he can know they are not enemy spies, and they reply that they could never do that — they are the sons of the Prophet of Allah Ya'qub, who lives in Canaan.

Then the question he actually wanted answered: does your father have any child other than you? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says this was precisely the purpose of Yusuf's questioning — to make his brothers open up and relate events fully. And out it came. "We were twelve brothers. Our youngest died in the desert" — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's version has "disappeared in the forest" — "and he used to be the dearest to his father. His full brother is alive and his father kept him, so that his closeness compensates him for losing our youngest brother."

Read that slowly. They are describing Yusuf's death to Yusuf. Forty years on, standing before the very man, the old account comes out unchanged, and they do not know whose face they are telling it to. Having heard it, Ibn Kathir says, Yusuf ordered that his brothers be honoured and allowed to remain; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says he gave orders that they be lodged as royal guests and given grain according to the set rules.

## "Bring me your brother" — the offer and the warning (ayat 59–60)

Ayah 59 comes at the moment their bags are being loaded: *when he had furnished them with their provisions*. Ibn Kathir notes that this was according to their needs and that he gave them what they wanted to buy — and only then made his request. A man dealing from fullness, not from scarcity.

Notice how Yusuf phrases it: **a brother of yours from your father** — rendered by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān as "your step brother from your father's side." Ibn Kathir gives both the wording and the stated reason: "Bring me your brother from your father's side *whom you mentioned*, so that I know that you have told me the truth." He asks for Benyamin inside their own account of themselves, never his own.

Then the two levers, one in each ayah.

The pull, at the end of ayah 59: *Do you not see that I give full measure, and that I am the best of hosts?* Ibn Kathir says this was to encourage them to return to him. And it was not an empty boast — they had just been measured out a full load and lodged as royal guests. He invites them back with evidence they can weigh in their hands.

The push, in ayah 60: *But if you do not bring him to me, there shall be no measure for you with me, nor shall you come near me.* Ibn Kathir explains the threat as it would have landed: if the next time they come without Benyamin, they will not be allowed to buy the food they need. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān supplies the logic Yusuf leaves implicit, rendering the ayah with the reasoning inside it — you deserve no measure from me, *because it will prove that you have lied to me*, and so you shall not come even close to me.

Ten hungry men now have exactly one route back to grain, and it runs through the one son their father will not let out of his sight.

## "We shall try to persuade his father" (ayah 61)

Their reply is measured. The verb **sanurāwidu** is rendered in the sources as "we shall try to get permission for him from his father" and "we will try to convince his father to let him come." Note what they do not say. Not "we will bring him" — they say they will *try*, they will work on him. Then they add *wa innā la-fāʿilūn*, "and verily, we shall do it." Ibn Kathir glosses this as: we will try our best to bring him with us, so that we spare no effort to prove to you that we are truthful in what we told you about ourselves.

There is a quiet irony the passage does not have to spell out. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān mentions, later in its commentary, that Ya'qub had come to realize his son was not eaten by a wolf at all but that it was some trick of his brothers. The men who once brought their father that story about a son who went out and did not come back are now bound to persuade him to let another son go out — and this time they will have to keep their word.

## The money in the saddlebags (ayah 62)

*And he said to his fityān: put their merchandise back into their packs, so that they may recognize it when they return to their people — perhaps they will come back.*

Ibn Kathir glosses **fityān** as his servants, or his slaves; **biḍāʿah** as their money — the merchandise they had brought with them to exchange for food; and **riḥāl** as their bags. And he adds the key detail: it was done while they were unaware. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pictures it exactly — Yusuf ordered his young workers to collect the cash, jewellery and other articles his brothers had paid as the cost of the grain and tie it up secretly with their supplies in the camel-packs, so that they would remain unaware of it while there and would find it only when they opened their packs after arriving home.

Why? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lists several possibilities described by Ibn Kathir:

1. **They may have had nothing left to bring.** It occurred to him that perhaps they had nothing other than the cash and jewellery they had brought — and if so, they would be unable to come for grain again. (Ibn Kathir's own comment on the ayah runs the same way: it was said that Yusuf did this because he feared his brothers might not have any more merchandise to exchange for food.)
2. **He could not bear to take payment from his father and brothers.** On this view he paid the amount due from his own pocket, had it deposited in the royal treasury, and returned their cash and jewellery to them — the public accounts untouched, his family fed at his own expense.
3. **He knew his father would insist on returning it.** When the goods turned up in their supplies at home and Ya'qub learned of it, he — being a prophet of Allah — would consider what had been found a trust of the Egyptian treasury and would certainly have it sent back. That made the brothers' return more assured.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums it up: Yusuf made all these arrangements so that his brothers could keep coming to him in the future, and so that he could also meet his younger real brother.

## A ruling drawn from the story

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a practical principle from this event: should the economic condition of a country worsen to the point where the government's failure to check the decline would leave people deprived of the basic necessities of life, the government is justified in taking over the regulation and control of such supplies, and may also fix an appropriate price for food grains. Muslim jurists, it notes, have explained this provision in detail.

## The hardest question in the passage

Under the heading "A Special Note," Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the thing an honest reader is already thinking. Ya'qub was so affected by the separation that constant weeping made him lose his eyesight. Yusuf was a prophet and messenger of Allah who naturally loved his father and knew his rights over him fully well. In forty years, how did it not occur to him even once to let his father know he was alive? Sending such information was not far out of reach even when he arrived in Egypt as a slave; in the home of the 'Azīz of Misr he had freedom, comfort and time; it could have been done from prison too — who does not know that messages from inside those walls can be delivered anywhere, near or far? And once Allah brought him out of prison with honour and authority over Egypt became his, presenting himself before his father should have been his primary task, or at the very least sending an emissary to comfort him, something ordinary given his status. Yet he is not reported even to have intended it — and when his brothers stood in front of him, he sent them back without telling them the real situation. These, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, are conditions one cannot imagine of an ordinary human being; how could an exalted messenger of Allah bear this?

Its answer is that the silence was not Yusuf's own choice. The author writes that the only answer that kept returning to him was that Allah, in His infinite wisdom, had stopped Yusuf from exposing himself — and that he then found this authentically clarified in Tafsir al-Qurtubi: Allah had, through *waḥy* (revelation), stopped Yusuf from sending any news about himself to his home.

Why? It is Allah alone who knows the workings of His infinite wisdom, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says plainly that to comprehend it all is humanly impossible. But once in a while there is something one may see through, and here, as it appears, the real consideration of wisdom was to complete the trial of Ya'qub. And it points to a matching detail at the other end of the story: at the very start, when Ya'qub had realized that his son was not eaten by a wolf but that this was some trick of his brothers, the natural demand of the situation was that he visit the place of the reported incident and make investigations — but, as Allah would have it, he was unable to think along those lines. Only after a long passage of time did he say, "Go and search for Yusuf and his brother." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's conclusion: when Allah wills to do something, this is the way He puts all its causes together.

## What to carry away

**Power is a trust, and one test of it is what the powerful eat.** Yusuf ran the grain of an empire and did not fill his stomach from it, and the king and his aides ate one meal a day — and by that restraint the people could sustain themselves through the rest of the seven years. Authority in these ayat looks like fixed rations, personal supervision of the sale, and the ruler holding himself to less.

**Justice and generosity together.** "I give full measure, and I am the best of hosts" — scrupulously fair in the transaction, open-handed beyond it. And with his own family he gave in a way they could not see: their payment was tied back into their packs while they were unaware, to be found only at home. On one of the explanations Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relays from Ibn Kathir, he simply could not bear to take the price of food from his father and brothers, and paid it into the treasury himself.

**People can stand in front of the truth and not see it.** Ten men looked at Yusuf and took him for a stranger — because forty years and a royal robe had changed everything about him, and because, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, it could never have occurred to them that a child sold as a slave could be ruling a country. Certainty about how someone's story ended is exactly what stops us reading the evidence in front of us.

**And the delay is not neglect.** Forty years of a father's weeping, and a son held back from speaking by Allah's own command. Ya'qub's blocked investigation, Yusuf's blocked message, the famine, the ration rule that put all ten sons on the road — these are not accidents strung together. They are, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, Allah putting together all the causes of what He wills. The believer's part in the middle of such a stretch is what Ya'qub's part was: to hold on through the trial without supposing that Allah has forgotten.

passages.title: Jacob's covenant over Benjamin
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** Yusuf's brothers come home from Egypt with grain and a condition attached: no further rations unless they bring their youngest brother with them next time. Ayat 63–66 are the negotiation that follows — the sons pressing their case, the father remembering what happened the last time he trusted them, and finally an old man letting his son go, not because he relied on the men standing in front of him, but because he had placed his trust in Allah. Running underneath these four ayat is one question: **who is the real guardian?** Twice the brothers promise that they will guard the boy (ayah 63, ayah 65). Their father answers by naming a different Guardian altogether (ayah 64).

## Where we are

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān places this as the closing segment of the same episode: the brothers reached Egypt, were given their measure, and were told by the ʿAzīz of Misr (Egypt) that future supplies of food-grain depended on bringing their younger brother. Now they are home, reporting to Yaʿqūb (peace be upon him) and asking him to let Benyamin accompany them, with the assurance that they would protect him and see to it that he faced no difficulty on the trip.

## Ayah 63 — the sentence they had said once before

*"Muniʿa minnā al-kayl"* — the measure has been withheld from us. Ibn Kathir fills in what they meant: no more grain **after this time** unless you send our brother Binyamin with us. He also notes that some scholars read this ayah in a way that means *"and he shall get his ration"* rather than *"we shall get our measure."* Either way, the boy's presence is now the condition on which food for the whole household depends.

Then they close with a promise: *wa innā lahu la-ḥāfiẓūn* — "and truly, we will guard him." Ibn Kathir points out the echo at once: this is what they had said to Yaʿqūb about their brother Yusuf — *"Send him with us tomorrow to enjoy himself and play, and verily, we will take care of him"* (12:12). Ibn Kathir glosses their intent here as: *do not fear for his safety, for he will be returned back to you.*

## Ayah 64 — the father's answer, in two halves

**First half: the wound speaks.** *"Hal āmanukum ʿalayhi illā kamā amintukum ʿalā akhīhi min qabl"* — "Can I entrust him to you except as I entrusted his brother to you before?" It is framed as a question, but it is not asking for information. Ibn Kathir renders the force of it: *'Will you do to him except what you did to his brother Yusuf before, when you took him away from me and separated me from him?'* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is blunt about what this reveals: "the drive of his remark makes it obvious that he did not trust their word. He had trusted them once, and suffered — for they had promised in the same words spoken earlier that they would guard him."

**Second half: the pivot.** Having said that much, Yaʿqūb (peace be upon him) does not stay in the wound. He had the need of the family in sight, and — as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it — he was blessed with the quality of trust in the Divine disposal of matters, so he spoke about the reality as he knew it: *fa'llāhu khayrun ḥāfiẓan* — "Allah is the best guardian."

Read the two halves together and the logic is complete. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān spells it out: he had already seen the outcome of their guardianship earlier, and now he was placing his trust in Allah alone as guardian. And it draws out the principle: man has no control over his gain or loss unless Allah Himself so wills, and when He wills it, it cannot be diverted or averted by anyone. Therefore it is incorrect to place one's trust in Allah's created beings in this matter — and equally inappropriate to keep depending on complaints against them to settle it.

**"And He is the Most Merciful of those who show mercy."** Ibn Kathir puts Yaʿqūb's meaning like this: *'Allah has the most mercy with me among all those who show mercy. He is compassionate with me for my old age, feebleness and eagerness for my son. I invoke Allah to return him to me, and to allow him and I to be together; for surely, He is the Most Merciful of those who show mercy.'* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it the same way — only from Him could he hope that He would look at his old age and the sorrows surrounding him and not let further shocks shake him.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums up the whole ayah in one line: Yaʿqūb (peace be upon him) did not rely on apparent conditions or on the pledges given by his sons; he agreed to send his youngest son **solely because he had now placed his trust in Allah**.

## Ayah 65 — the bags are opened

Ibn Kathir explains the fact behind the scene: Yusuf had ordered his servants to return the brothers' merchandise to their bags. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to the sequence — everything up to this point was talk about what had happened on the journey; the baggage had not yet been opened. When they opened it and saw the *entire* capital they had paid with sitting inside, they realised this had not been done by mistake. Hence their wording: *ruddat ilaynā*, "given back to us."

*"Mā nabghī"* carries two possible senses, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives both. Read as a question, it is: *what else do we want?* — the grain is here and what we paid for it has been returned too. Read with *mā* as a negation, it becomes: *we do not want anything from you* — just send our brother with us. Qatādah's comment reflects the first sense: "What more can we ask for, our merchandise was returned to us and the ʿAzīz has given us the sufficient load we wanted?"

Then comes their case, stacked argument on argument: *we shall bring food to our family, and we shall guard our brother, and we shall add the measure of one camel more.* Ibn Kathir explains what lies behind that last item: Yusuf (peace be upon him) was giving each man a camel's load of corn. And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the pressure behind the request — what they had brought back on this trip was much less than the family needed and was likely to be consumed soon.

Their closing line — *dhālika kaylun yasīr*, "that is an easy measure" — is, in Ibn Kathir's reading, persuasion: they said these words *to make their case more appealing*, arguing that taking their brother with them is worth this gain. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds their reassurance to their father: the way we have been treated shows that the ʿAzīz of Misr is kind to us, so we should have no apprehensions.

**A ruling that falls out of the returned money.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes a practical point of fiqh (Islamic jurisprudence) here. If property belonging to someone else is found in your baggage, and strong indications prove that he put it there with the specific intention of giving it to you, then keeping it and using it is permissible — as was the case with this capital, which is why Yaʿqūb (peace be upon him) gave no instruction that it be returned. But if there is a doubt that it may have come to you by oversight or forgetfulness, using it without making the necessary inquiries from the owner is **not** permissible.

## Ayah 66 — a pledge, with a door deliberately left open

*"Lan ursilahu maʿakum ḥattā tu'tūni mawthiqan mina'llāh"* — "I shall never send him with you until you give me a pledge in the name of Allah that you will bring him back to me." Ibn Kathir: until you swear by Allah **with the strongest oath**.

But look at what Yaʿqūb attaches to it: *illā an yuḥāṭa bikum*, "unless you are overpowered." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the reasoning. Could someone able to see reality ever miss the fact that man, however strong he may be, is dependent and helpless before the all-pervading power of Allah? On what basis, then, would anyone pledge to bring another person back safe? He does not have the absolute power and control to accomplish it. So the pledge is given with an exception built into it. Mujāhid, an early authority in tafsir, explains the exception as: *unless all of you are killed.* Qatādah, another early authority, says it means: *unless you become totally helpless and overpowered.* Ibn Kathir's gloss agrees: unless you were all overwhelmed and unable to rescue him.

And when they had sworn their solemn oath, he added one more sentence: *allāhu ʿalā mā naqūlu wakīl* — "Allah is the Witness to what we have said." Ibn Kathir notes that he said this to affirm the oath further. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the meaning: this giving and taking of solemn oaths is something that ultimately rests with Allah alone. It is only by His *tawfīq* — His granting of enabling help — that one person can keep another protected and so become able to fulfil a pledge. Otherwise man is helpless; he has nothing under his personal control.

Ibn Ishāq adds the human bottom line: "Yaʿqūb did that because he had no choice but to send them to bring necessary food supplies for their survival. So he sent Binyamin with them."

**A principle for oaths and pledges.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān derives from the exception clause that no one should be asked to give a pledge on oath whose fulfilment does not lie fully within his control — as Yaʿqūb (peace be upon him) exempted from his sons' oath the situation in which they might become totally helpless or find themselves in near-death circumstances. It cites as a parallel that when the Prophet ﷺ asked the noble Companions to give him a pledge of obedience, he himself added a restriction to it — the restriction of *ability* — so that the pledge ran: *we shall obey you fully, as far as it is within our ability and control.*

**A point of Islamic law.** Because the brothers were asked to pledge that they would bring Benyamin back, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes the passage as evidence for the permissibility of *kafālah bi'l-nafs* — a technical term of Islamic law meaning a personal bail or guarantee for the due appearance of someone involved in a case on its hearing date in court. Here the scholars genuinely differed: the view of Imam Mālik is that only a financial guarantee is allowed in the Sharīʿah, and he does not hold personal bail to be permissible.

## Living it

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws several lessons from this exchange, and they are unusually concrete.

**How a parent handles a child who has done something serious.** The brothers' earlier mistakes were not small; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lists them as sins, major and grave: they lied to their father and made him agree to send Yusuf (peace be upon him) out with them; they gave their father a pledge and then broke it; they treated their young and innocent brother cruelly; they caused their father extreme pain and did not care much about it; they conspired to kill an innocent human being; and they sold a free human being forcibly and unjustly. These were crimes severe enough to have demanded that Yaʿqūb (peace be upon him), once he understood what they had knowingly done, sever his relationship with them or turn them out of his house. He did neither. He let them keep living with him, sent them to Egypt to bring back food grains, and — as we see in these very ayat — yielded to them again and allowed them to take his young son. The lesson drawn: if one's children fall into sin or make mistakes, it is the father's responsibility to seek their correction through appropriate education and training, and as long as there is hope of betterment, not to sever the relationship. That is what Yaʿqūb (peace be upon him) did — and in the end all of them were ashamed of their wrongdoings, turned away from sins and lived a reformed life. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān does add the limit: should no hope of betterment remain, and the parents realise that maintaining the relationship poses a danger to the religious upbringing of others, then in that condition severing the relationship is more appropriate.

**Good dealings and good manners.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presents these as two great qualities of character, of which Yaʿqūb (peace be upon him) was a mirror. Despite such serious crimes committed by his sons, he kept dealing with them in a manner that left them facing no qualms of conscience when they came to him with a second request.

**Rebuke, then a fresh start.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads ayah 64 as a model of how to admonish a wrongdoer in the interest of his betterment: it amounts to telling him that his behaviour demanded that his plea be rejected, but then giving him the feeling that he is being given a fresh chance by forgoing what has gone before — so that his sense of shame returns to him later and he becomes totally repentant. That is precisely the shape of Yaʿqūb's reply: first the caustic reference to their past record — *"Shall I trust you about Benyamin as I had trusted you earlier about Yusuf?"* — and then, having warned them pointedly, he realised their penitence from their apparent condition, placed his trust in Allah and handed his young son into their custody.

**Where trust actually belongs.** This is the heart of the passage. Placing one's trust, in the real sense, in the promise or protection of a human being is wrong; the real trust should be in Allah. He alone is the real mover and maker of things and the causer of causes — to bring forth causes and to give them effect lies in His control alone. Hence *fa'llāhu khayrun ḥāfiẓan*. And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records a saying reported from Kaʿb al-Aḥbār: because Yaʿqūb (peace be upon him) this time did not simply trust the word of his sons but entrusted the matter to Allah, Allah said, *"By My honour, now I shall send both of your sons back to you."*

The passage ends with a father who has been hurt once, is exposed again, and has done everything a human being can reasonably do — taken the strongest oath, named the exception, called Allah as Witness over what was said — and then let go. He is not naive; ayah 64 proves that. He simply knows what Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states plainly at the end of this ayah: otherwise man is helpless, and has nothing under his personal control.

passages.title: Separate gates, and a word in secret to Benjamin
passages.tafsir:
**These three ayat sit at the hinge of the second journey to Egypt.** Ya'qub (peace be upon him) has finally let Benyamin go, and as the brothers set out he gives them one strange, precise instruction: do not all enter by a single gate. What binds the passage together is a single question, asked under the most testing circumstances a father could face — what is the relationship between taking precautions and trusting Allah? Ayah 67 gives the precaution and its disclaimer in one breath. Ayah 68 tells us exactly what the precaution did and did not achieve. Ayah 69 then shows Allah's decree already quietly at work inside the palace: while the brothers were busy at the gates, Yusuf (peace be upon him) was drawing his younger brother aside.

## Why this instruction, and why only now

Ibn Kathir states the scene plainly: Allah tells us that Ya'qub (peace be upon him) ordered his children — when he sent Binyamin with them to Egypt — to enter from different gates rather than all of them entering from one.

Maarif ul Qur'an fills in the picture. They were eleven; on reaching the outer wall of the city they were to disperse and come in by separate gates. And Maarif notices something easy to miss: **he had not said this on the first trip.** Why now?

Because the first time they had arrived as common travellers, in a broken-down condition. Nobody knew them; there was no danger that anyone would take special notice of them. But on that first visit the master of Egypt gave them an unusual welcome, and that welcome introduced them to state functionaries and to the people of the city. Now the danger was real — someone might cast an evil eye on them, or people might simply envy so imposing a group of visitors. And this time Benyamin was with them, which — as Maarif puts it — became the cause of the father's added attention.

## What he feared

Ibn Kathir gathers an unusually broad list of early authorities on the reason: Ibn 'Abbas, Muhammad bin Ka'b, Mujahid, Ad-Dahhak, Qatadah, As-Suddi and several others all said that **he feared the evil eye for them**, because they were handsome and looked beautiful and graceful. He feared that people might direct the evil eye at them — and, in Ibn Kathir's words, the evil eye truly harms, *by Allah's decree*, and brings down the mighty warrior-rider from his horse.

That qualifier — *by Allah's decree* — is the theological spine of the whole passage. Nothing in creation acts of itself.

Maarif adds a second concern running alongside the first: he was concerned lest people find out that these eleven were sons of the same father and brothers to one another; their coming in all together might make some people envy them, or even cause them some pain.

## The evil eye is real — and it is entirely under Allah's power

Maarif ul Qur'an is emphatic that this cannot be dismissed as ignorance, superstition or fancy, which is why a prophet of Allah took it seriously enough to plan around it. Maarif reports that the Prophet ﷺ confirmed its truth, citing a hadith — without naming the collection it comes from — in these words: *"The evil eye makes a human being enter the grave, and a camel enter a petty pot."* Maarif adds that among the things the Prophet ﷺ sought refuge from, and directed his Ummah to seek refuge from, is *min kulli 'aynin lammah* — "I seek refuge from the evil eye."

Maarif then relates the well-known event of the noble Companion Sahl ibn Hunayf, may Allah be pleased with him. He had taken off his shirt to get ready for a bath. 'Amir ibn Rabi'ah happened to cast a glance at the bright tint and healthy look of his body, and the spontaneous remark he made was: "Until this day, I have never seen a body as handsome as this!" No sooner had the words escaped his mouth than Sahl was seized by an instant high temperature. When the Prophet ﷺ was informed, the treatment he suggested was that 'Amir ibn Rabi'ah should make wudu', that the water from the wudu' be collected in a utensil, and that it be poured over Sahl's body. When it was done as ordered, the temperature dropped immediately; Sahl became fully fit and left on the expedition he was going on with the Prophet ﷺ. Following this event, the Prophet ﷺ also gave 'Amir ibn Rabi'ah a gentle warning, telling him:

> *"Why would someone kill his brother? (When you saw his body) you could have made Wudu' for barakah. It is true that the evil eye leaves its effect."*

Maarif draws two practical lessons straight from that hadith. First: should you notice something unusual about another person's body or property, **make wudu' for him**, so that Allah blesses him with barakah in it — and according to some narrations one should say *masha'Allahu la quwwata illa billah* ("whatever Allah wills — there is no power but with Him"), which removes the effect of the evil eye. Second: if someone has already been affected by another's evil eye, pouring over him the water that person used in washing his face, hands and feet in wudu' will help eliminate the effect. Al-Qurtubi, Maarif reports, has said that there is a consensus of all the scholars of the Muslim Ummah among Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah on the truth of the evil eye as affecting and causing harm.

But Maarif is equally careful to close the door on superstition. Its explanation is that the effect works as a kind of mesmerism — an induced state — comparable to a harmful food or medicine that makes a person sick, or excessive heat or cold that makes some diseases show up. These are *customary causes* through which effects become manifest; in truth they have no real effectiveness of their own. All universal causes operate under the perfect power, will and intention of Allah. No favourable measure taken against what has been Divinely destined can prove beneficial, nor can a harmful measure become effective against it.

## "And I cannot avail you against Allah at all" (ayah 67)

This is precisely why the ayah does not stop at the instruction. Ya'qub (peace be upon him) immediately says **وَمَا أُغْنِي عَنكُم مِّنَ اللَّهِ مِن شَيْءٍ** — "and I cannot avail you against Allah at all." Ibn Kathir: this precaution will not resist Allah's decision and appointed decree; whatever Allah wills cannot be resisted or stopped.

Then **إِنِ الْحُكْمُ إِلَّا لِلَّهِ** — "the decision rests only with Allah," rendered by Maarif as "Sovereignty belongs to none but Allah." And then the trust: **عَلَيْهِ تَوَكَّلْتُ وَعَلَيْهِ فَلْيَتَوَكَّلِ الْمُتَوَكِّلُونَ** — "In Him I put my trust, and let all those that trust put their trust in Him."

Notice the movement in that sentence. It begins as one man's private confession — *I* put my trust in Him — and ends as an instruction to every believer who ever reads it. A frightened father's inner state is turned into a rule for the Ummah.

Maarif paraphrases his meaning beautifully: *I know that the necessary precautions I have ordered cannot avert the will and intention of Allah; what works here is but the command of Allah. However, one has been asked to do what is physically possible, so I have given you this advice. But I place my trust not in these physical arrangements — in Allah alone. And it is imperative for everyone to trust in and rely on Him alone, never placing one's trust in physical and material means.*

## Ayah 68: what the plan achieved, and what it could not

"Then when they entered as their father had instructed them, it did not avail them in the least against Allah; **it was but a need of Ya'qub's inner self which he discharged**" — *illa hajatan fi nafsi Ya'quba qadaha*. Ibn Kathir explains that "need" as this very precaution against the evil eye. Maarif puts it warmly: the sons carried out their father's instructions and his desire stood fulfilled — and as for the paternal love and concern of Ya'qub (peace be upon him) for his sons, that he did demonstrate to his heart's content, even though the measure could not avert anything already destined by Allah.

Maarif then makes a precise and consoling distinction. The measure taken against the evil eye or envy **did** succeed: no such incident showed up during this trip. What failed was the essential objective his heart was really set on — the safe return of Benyamin. Benyamin was detained in Egypt, and Ya'qub (peace be upon him) received another severe shock. The blow came from a direction he had not noticed and could do nothing to counter, because it was what Divine destiny had in store.

And yet, Maarif observes, despite this visible failure it was the barakah of his tawakkul that this second shock turned out to be an antidote for the first, resulting in the happy reunion with both his sons, Yusuf and Benyamin, safely and honourably. The reader watching the story unfold learns something the actors inside it could not yet see — that a plan "failing" is not the same as Allah abandoning the one who trusted Him.

## "And verily he was endowed with knowledge because We had taught him"

Rather than criticising Ya'qub (peace be upon him) for planning, the ayah praises him — and the commentators read the praise in two complementary ways.

- **Qatadah and Ath-Thawri**, as Ibn Kathir reports, took it to mean he had knowledge *that he implemented* — knowledge acted upon, not merely held. Maarif notes that some commentators read the word "knowledge" here as acting in accordance with the dictate of knowledge, giving the rendering: "He was a man of action according to the knowledge We gave him" — and therefore he placed his trust not in material means but in Allah alone.
- **Ibn Jarir** read it as simply "he has knowledge that We taught him."

Maarif draws out the force of "because We had taught him": his knowledge was not acquired and did not come from books — it was directly a Divine gift. That is what made his balance possible: he employed physical means, something legally required and commendable, yet did not place his total trust in them.

And the closing clause, **وَلَٰكِنَّ أَكْثَرَ النَّاسِ لَا يَعْلَمُونَ** — "but most people do not know." Maarif applies it to exactly this point: most people do not know the reality behind it, and thus unaware they fall into doubts about Ya'qub (peace be upon him), thinking that the employment of these means did not match the station of a prophet. The ayah is, in part, a defence of him.

## Ayah 69: the word in secret

The scene shifts, and the tenderness of it is easy to rush past.

Ibn Kathir: when Yusuf's brothers went in before him along with his full brother Binyamin, he invited them to a place of honour as privileged guests, and granted them gifts and generous hospitality and kindness. Maarif reports from the tafsir authority **Qatadah** the small detail that unlocks the moment: the arrangement made by Yusuf (peace be upon him) was that two brothers were lodged in one room — which left Benyamin alone. So Benyamin was asked to stay with him.

**آوَىٰ إِلَيْهِ أَخَاهُ** — "he lodged his brother with himself," he took him to his own side. Alone with him, Yusuf (peace be upon him) disclosed his identity to his younger brother and told him the story of what had happened to him and that he was in fact his brother. **إِنِّي أَنَا أَخُوكَ** — "Behold, I am your brother." Then: **فَلَا تَبْتَئِسْ بِمَا كَانُوا يَعْمَلُونَ** — "so do not grieve for what they have been doing." Ibn Kathir glosses it as: nor feel sad for what they did to me. Maarif: he comforted him and asked him not to worry about what their brothers had been doing until that time.

Two brothers who had each lost the other, one of them for decades, and the first thing the 'Aziz of Egypt says is a request not to be grieved over.

Ibn Kathir adds the strategic half: Yusuf (peace be upon him) ordered Binyamin to hide the news from the others and to refrain from telling them that the 'Aziz was his brother Yusuf, and he plotted with him to keep him in Egypt enjoying honour and great hospitality. Benyamin, in other words, is inside the plan — not a victim of it.

## Why did Yusuf not send word to his father?

Maarif raises the question honestly: Yusuf (peace be upon him) made efforts to have his younger brother brought, even insisted on it, and when he came disclosed his identity to him — yet he neither thought of calling his father nor took any steps to inform him of his well-being, though there is no doubt he had many opportunities during those forty years.

Maarif's answer is that whatever happened in this matter was Divine decree communicated through the medium of wahy (revelation). Allah would not have given him permission to tell his father about himself, because Ya'qub (peace be upon him) was yet to be tested once again through his separation from his son Benyamin. It was to complete this Divine arrangement that all these situations were created. Yusuf's silence is not coldness; it is obedience.

## Living it

Maarif ul Qur'an draws these rulings and points of guidance from ayat 67–68:

1. **The effect of the evil eye is true**, and to try to stay safe from it is permissible in the Shari'ah and commendable — just as one tries to stay safe from harmful foods and actions.
2. **Concealing your special personal blessings and attributes** from people, so as not to be envied by them, is a correct thing to do.
3. **Employing physical and material means** to stay safe from harmful effects is neither against tawakkul (trust in Allah) nor against the status of prophets.
4. If you fear harm or hurt may come to another person, it is better to **let them know about the danger and suggest how to stay safe** from it — as Ya'qub (peace be upon him) did.
5. When you find some personal excellence or blessing in another person that strikes you as unusual, and there is a danger they may be affected by the evil eye, it becomes **obligatory (wajib) on the beholder** — the one who noticed — to say *barakallah* ("may Allah bless") or *masha'Allah* ("whatever Allah wills"), so that the other person remains safe from any possible harm.
6. Employing all possible means to stay safe from the evil eye is permissible, including seeking treatment through **du'a and ta'widh** (spoken or written words seeking the protection of Allah) — as the Prophet ﷺ did when, seeing the weakness of the two sons of Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, he allowed him to have them treated in this way.
7. The ideal approach of a wise Muslim: **place your real trust in Allah to begin with**, and at the same time do not ignore physical and material means — falling short in none of the permissible means you can assemble. This was the way of Ya'qub (peace be upon him), and, Maarif says, the blessed way of our Messenger ﷺ, expressed in the line Maarif quotes from the Sage Rumi: *"Tie the leg of your camel and trust in Allah."*

That is the passage in one sentence: **tie the camel, take the separate gates, speak the kind word in private — and then leave the outcome entirely with the One to whom the decision belongs.**

passages.title: The planted cup: accusation, search, and Benjamin's detention
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes how Yusuf (peace be upon him) arranged to have his own full brother, Benyamin, stay on with him in Egypt. Every brother was given grain according to the rules, each man's share loaded onto his camel separately and by name. Into the load prepared for Benyamin, a bowl was concealed. What follows is a staged accusation of theft, and a verdict the brothers pronounce themselves without realising they are sentencing their own. Ayat 70–79 are one unbroken scene, and at its centre Allah interrupts the narrative: **"Thus did We plan for Yusuf"** (76).

## The cup, and the pause before the cry (70–72)

The Qur'an names the object twice. In ayah 70 it is **as-siqāyah**, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains means a bowl used for drinking water. In ayah 72 the heralds call it **ṣuwāʿ al-malik**, "the king's *ṣuwāʿ*" — a similar utensil, but here tied to the king himself. Maʿārif notes that attributing it to the king signals that this bowl carried some special value or status.

What was it made of? The early authorities differ. Ibn Kathir says the majority of scholars hold that it was Yusuf's **silver** bowl; some said the king's bowl was gold. Shuʿbah said that Abu Bishr narrated from Saʿid bin Jubayr from Ibn ʿAbbas that it was made of silver and the king used it to drink with. Ibn Zayd added that the king drank from it and *later* measured food grains with it, since food had become scarce in that time — reported also from Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, Ad-Dahhak and ʿAbdur-Rahman bin Zayd. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that according to some narrations it was made of a precious stone similar to emerald. The common ground, as Maʿārif puts it: the bowl was fairly precious, and it had some special connection with the king of Egypt — whether he drank from it himself, or had it declared the official measure for grain.

**A detail easy to read past.** Ayah 70 does not say "and" a crier cried — it says **thumma**, "*then*". Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws real meaning from that word: the public announcement was not made instantly. A temporary delay was allowed for the caravan to leave, and the cry went up only after that, to offset the likelihood of anyone sensing foul play.

Ayah 71 catches the brothers' body language: *qālū wa-aqbalū ʿalayhim* — "they said, **turning towards them**". Ibn Kathir describes them looking at the man heralding this statement and asking him. Maʿārif reads the turn as protest — they wheel round on the announcer, as if objecting at being made into thieves, and ask him to say what it is he claims to have lost.

The answer in ayah 72 sets a bounty — **a camel-load** for whoever brings it back — sealed with **"wa anā bihi zaʿīm"**, "and I stand surety for it." Ibn Kathir explains this as assurance that the reward would be delivered. Two practical rulings are drawn from this half-verse in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, both citing al-Qurtubi:
