- A **public announcement of a reward** for a particular act is valid — much like the modern custom of announcing rewards for the arrest of absconding criminals or the return of lost property. This form of transaction does not fall under the jurists' definition of *ijārah* (hiring), yet this ayah establishes its justification.
- One person may become the **guarantor (surety)** of another's financial obligations. According to the majority of Muslim jurists, the creditor may recover from the debtor or from the guarantor, as he chooses; and if from the guarantor, the guarantor may then recover from the debtor whatever was taken from him.

## The oath — and the trap they walk into (73–75)

In ayah 73 the brothers swear: **"ta'Llāhi"** — "By Allah!" — *you know full well we did not come to make mischief in the land, and we are not thieves.* Ibn Kathir unpacks the appeal: ever since the Egyptians had known them, they had become certain of this from their good conduct. "Theft is not in our character, as you came to know." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it the same way — the responsible people of the state knew them, and knew they had never been thieves.

Then comes ayah 74: *"What then shall be the penalty, if you are liars?"* Yusuf's men do not impose a punishment. They **ask** the accused to name it — as Maʿārif puts it, the royal staff asked them what they themselves suggest the punishment for theft should be.

The brothers answer in ayah 75: *the one in whose bag it is found — he himself is the penalty. Thus we punish the wrongdoers.* Ibn Kathir identifies this as the law of Prophet Ibrahim (peace be upon him): the thief is given as a slave to the victim of the theft. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls it the Sharīʿah of Sayyidnā Yaʿqūb — the same ruling — and names the manoeuvre outright: the state functionaries got the brothers to state the punishment of a thief as it stood in Jacobian law, and thereby had them committed in advance to handing Benyamin over once the property was recovered from his baggage.

Ibn Kathir makes the legal logic explicit: Yusuf took Benyamin as a slave **"according to their judgement and the law which they believed in."**

## The search (76)

*"So he began with their bags before his brother's bag."* Ibn Kathir: he started with theirs first "to perfect the plot." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: to cover up the real plan, the officials searched every brother's baggage first, lest opening Benyamin's cause doubts. His was opened last of all, and the king's bowl was recovered from it. Maʿārif adds the human aftermath: at that sight all the brothers were put to shame, and they began chiding Benyamin for having disgraced them.

Then Allah says: **kadhālika kidnā li-Yūsuf** — "Thus did We plan for Yusuf." Ibn Kathir pauses over the word to say that this is a *good* plot, one Allah likes and prefers, because it seeks a certain benefit using wisdom, and the benefit of all.

The next clause explains why the arrangement was needed: **"He could not have taken his brother by the law of the king."** Ibn Kathir reports from Ad-Dahhak and several other scholars that taking him as a captive was not the law of the king of Egypt. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān specifies what Egyptian law did prescribe: corporal punishment for the thief, after which he was released on payment of twice the cost of the stolen property — which would never have kept Benyamin in Egypt. But Yusuf had already drawn out the law of theft operative in the Sharīʿah of Sayyidnā Yaʿqūb; under *that* law, detaining Benyamin was correct and valid. Ibn Kathir puts it from the other side: Allah allowed Yusuf to take his brother as a captive only after the brothers had agreed to this judgement beforehand, and he knew this was their law. And the ayah adds the decisive qualifier: **"except that Allah willed it."**

## The hardest question here — and Maʿārif's answer

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān confronts the difficulty head-on. **First**, why would Yusuf choose this device to detain Benyamin, when he knew that his own separation had already been a shock to his father — how could he bear to give that father a second shock? **Second — and far more important** — this involves accusing innocent brothers of theft and secretly concealing property in their baggage in order to disgrace them later. These are impermissible acts, and Yusuf was a prophet of Allah.

Maʿārif rejects the attempted answers one by one:

- *That Benyamin asked for it.* Some commentators, al-Qurtubi among them, have stated that once Benyamin recognised Yusuf and was at peace, he requested not to be sent back with his brothers but to be allowed to stay; Yusuf first objected that this would shock their father; and then no way remained of keeping him except to blame him of theft and arrest him for it — and Benyamin, so disgusted with the ways of his brothers, was ready to go through all this. Maʿārif's verdict: even taking this event as correct, the heartbreak caused to his father and the disgrace inflicted on all his brothers by dubbing them thieves cannot become permissible simply because of Benyamin's pleasure.
- *That the herald's accusation was made without Yusuf's knowledge or permission.* Maʿārif calls this "a claim without any proof and, given the anatomy of the event, incoherent too."
- *That they were called thieves because of something they had done earlier.* Maʿārif mentions this only to set it aside as "a long-drawn explanation."

**The correct answer**, Maʿārif states, is the one given by al-Qurtubi and Mazhari: whatever was done and said here was neither the outcome of Benyamin's wish nor of Yusuf's own initiative. All of it was the manifestation of the infinite wisdom of Allah alone, under whose command these things came to be what they were — and what was being completed through them was the trial and test of Sayyidnā Yaʿqūb (peace be upon him). The proof is inside the passage itself: ayah 76 says **"Thus did We plan for Yusuf,"** and in it Allah has very clearly attributed this plan to Himself. Once these things took shape as divinely commanded, calling them impermissible becomes meaningless.

Maʿārif offers a parallel: the dismantling of the boat and the killing of the boy in the event relating to Sayyidnā Musa and al-Khadir (peace be upon them both). Obviously these were sins — which is exactly why Musa registered his disapproval of them. But al-Khadir was doing all this with divine assent and permission, under particularly expedient considerations, and so was not committing any sin.

**One caution, drawn from the same ayah.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān derives from *"Thus did We plan for Yusuf"* that it is permissible, for a valid reason recognised by the Sharīʿah, to change the form of a transaction in a way that changes its legal status — what the jurists call *ḥīlah sharʿiyyah*, a lawful device to avoid a real hardship. But the condition is absolute: such an action must not cause the invalidation of the injunctions of the Sharīʿah. If it does, all such devices are Haram by the consensus of Muslim jurists — for example, finding an excuse to avoid paying Zakāh, or embarking on an unnecessary journey before or during Ramadan simply to manufacture an excuse not to fast. The hunt for such excuses and devices has brought divine punishment on some nations, and the Prophet ﷺ prohibited the use of such stratagems. Acting upon them does not make what is done permissible; what falls on the doer is a twofold sin — first, the original impermissible act; second, the impermissible device, which amounts in a way to cheating Allah and His Messenger. Maʿārif notes that Imam al-Bukhari established the impermissibility of all such *ḥiyal* in his *Kitāb al-Ḥiyal*.

## "And above every possessor of knowledge is one more knowing" (76)

**"We raise in degrees whom We will"** — Ibn Kathir sees here Allah's praise of Yusuf, and links it to His words elsewhere, *"Allah will exalt in degree those of you who believe"* (58:11). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it in context: in this very event, Yusuf's rank was elevated over his brothers'.

Then: **wa fawqa kulli dhī ʿilmin ʿalīm.** Al-Hasan said: "There is no knowledgeable person, but there is another person with more knowledge until it ends at Allah the Exalted and Most Honoured." Qatadah said much the same, adding: "Verily, knowledge started from Allah, and from Him the scholars learn, and to Him all knowledge returns."

ʿAbdur-Razzaq recorded that Saʿid bin Jubayr said: they were sitting with Ibn ʿAbbas when a man in the audience exclaimed, "All praise is to Allah! There is an all-knowing above every person endowed with knowledge." Ibn ʿAbbas responded: **"Allah is the All-Knowing, and His knowledge is above the knowledge of every knowledgeable person."** Simak narrated that ʿIkrimah said that Ibn ʿAbbas said of this ayah: "This person has more knowledge than that person, and Allah is above all knowledgeable persons." And ʿAbdullah bin Masʿud read the ayah as *"and above every scholar is the All-Knower (Allah)."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān holds both ends together: Allah has given precedence to some over others in knowledge, so that above the highest of the high in knowledge there is someone more knowledgeable still — and above the best of Allah's creation stands the ʿIlm of Allah, highest of all, forever.

## The old wound, reopened (77)

The bowl is out of the bag, and the brothers say: *"If he steals — a brother of his stole before."* Ibn Kathir: they were trying to show themselves as innocent of being like Benyamin, saying he did just as a brother of his had done before — meaning Yusuf (peace be upon him). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān catches what the phrasing was meant to convey: that Benyamin was not their real brother but their step-brother, and that he had a full brother who had stolen too. They said it, Maʿārif notes, in irritation, out of shame at what had just been recovered.

**What were they referring to?** Reports differ, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, which then relays the account as Ibn Kathir reports it from Muhammad ibn Ishaq and from the tafsir authority Mujahid. Benyamin was born soon after Yusuf, and his birth became the cause of their mother's death. Left without her, both boys were raised by their paternal aunt. Allah had blessed Yusuf from his very childhood with such an attractive person that whoever saw him became deeply attached to him, and his aunt was no exception. His father was no less fond of him, but a small child had to be kept in a woman's care. When Yusuf had learnt to walk, Yaʿqub thought of having him come to live with him. The aunt was reluctant; under compulsion she handed him over — but she made a plan to get him back. She owned a highly valued antique waist-band that had come to her as the legacy of Sayyidnā Ishaq (peace be upon him). She tied this band around the boy's waist underneath his dress, and after he had gone, spread word that her waist-band had been stolen. When a search was made, it turned out to be with young Yusuf. Under the Sharīʿah of Yaʿqub, the aunt now had the right to keep him as her slave; and Yaʿqub, seeing that she had become his owner on the authority of the religious law of the land, handed him over. Yusuf went on living with her as long as she was alive.

So even then, the truth came to light and he was found free of the least doubt of theft: it was his aunt's love that had contrived the whole thing. **And the brothers knew this truth all too well.** Maʿārif places the remark in ayah 77 as the last in the series of excesses his brothers inflicted on Yusuf.

**And Yusuf's response?** *fa-asarrahā Yūsuf fī nafsihi wa-lam yubdihā lahum* — "Yusuf kept it within himself and did not reveal it to them." Ibn Kathir explains that what he kept in himself was the very statement that follows: *"You are in an evil situation, and Allah is the Best Knower of that which you describe."* He said it to himself, intending to hide what he wanted to say even before he said it. Al-ʿAwfi reported the same from Ibn ʿAbbas. Maʿārif reads it as a man who heard a fresh slander and kept it in his heart, not letting his brothers know he had heard it or been affected by it — though it allows that the second sentence, *"Allah knows best of what you allege,"* may possibly have been said aloud in reply.

## "Allah forbid" (78–79)

Out of options, the brothers turn to pleading in ayah 78: *"O ʿAzīz! He has a father, aged and advanced in years — so take one of us in his place. Indeed, we see you as one of the doers of good."* Ibn Kathir fills in what they mean: a father who loves him very much and is comforted by his presence for the son that he lost. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that they began flattering the ʿAzīz of Misr — appealing to a generosity they felt in him, and which they had already tasted from him.

Yusuf's reply in ayah 79 begins **maʿādha 'Llāh** — "Allah forbid" — that we should take anyone but the one with whom we found our property. Ibn Kathir: this is *according to the judgement that you yourselves gave*; to take an innocent man instead of the guilty one would make us wrongdoers. Maʿārif puts it as a matter of the regulations followed in his country: he was not authorised to detain anyone he wished, and by their own *fatwā* and ruling, arresting someone other than the man from whose possession the property was recovered would be injustice.

## What to carry away

Yusuf could not lawfully hold his brother under the law of the king of Egypt. The law that held him was the one his own brothers stated aloud, certain of their innocence, before a single bag was opened. And ayah 76 tells us who was really arranging the scene.

**Legal form matters, and so does intention.** The same ayah that permits reshaping a transaction for a genuine, Sharīʿah-recognised need also condemns the device contrived to escape an obligation. The difference is not cleverness; it is whether the Sharīʿah's injunctions are served or invalidated.

**Guard your tongue when you are exposed.** Caught out and shamed, the brothers reached in irritation for an old accusation against an absent man they knew to be innocent. Humiliation is exactly when the tongue reaches for someone else's reputation.

**And swallow it, as Yusuf did.** He had every proof, every power, and the perfect moment. He kept it within himself and did not reveal it to them — leaving the verdict where it belongs: *"and Allah is the Best Knower of that which you describe."*

passages.title: The eldest brother stays behind in Egypt
passages.tafsir:
**The scene in one breath.** Ibn Kathir opens the passage by telling us where the brothers stand: they "were desperate because they could not secure the release of their brother Binyamin, even though they had given a promise and sworn to their father to bring him back." Ayat 80–82 are what happens in the moments afterwards: they pull aside where no one can overhear, and the eldest of them takes charge — refusing to go home at all, and dictating the message the others must carry back to their father.

What holds these three ayat together is that they are essentially **one man speaking**. He begins in ayah 80: first he indicts his brothers, then he announces that he is staying behind in Egypt. Ibn Kathir then says that "he next ordered them to narrate to their father what happened so that they could present their excuse about that happened to Binyamin and as claim their innocence before him" — and what follows in ayat 81 and 82 is the message he tells them to deliver, down to the corroborating witnesses they should offer.

## "When they lost all hope in him, they spoke privately" (80)

Ibn Kathir sets the emotional temperature: they had bound themselves by a promise and an oath to their father, and "they were unable to fulfill their promise to their father."

Two Arabic words carry the scene. **خَلَصُوا** (*khalaṣū*) Ibn Kathir glosses as "in private" — *away from people's eyes*. **نَجِيّٗا** (*najiyyan*) he glosses as "they consulted," among themselves. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the whole phrase plainly: "they went aside for consultation." So the picture is a huddle: men stepping out of sight and earshot to work out what on earth they will say at home.

Ibn Kathir adds one detail about the brother who now takes the lead: "He was the one among them who recommended throwing Yusuf into a well, rather than killing him." So the man about to name their old crime out loud is a man who was himself inside that old episode. And, as we will see, he is the one who now says it plainly.

## Who was "the eldest"?

The Qur'an says **كَبِيرُهُمْ**, rendered by Ibn Kathir as "the eldest among them" and by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān as "the oldest of them." The commentators differ over who exactly this was.

- **Ibn Kathir** reports his name "was Rubil, or Yahudha," and in the narration that follows he goes with Rubil.
- **Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** lays out three positions: some commentators identify him as **Yahuda (Judah)** — "though not the oldest in age, but... certainly the eldest in knowledge and merit"; others say **Ruebel (Rueben)**, who "is the oldest in age and he was the one who had suggested that Sayyidna Yusuf (peace be upon him) should not be killed"; and still others say it was **Shamʿun**, "who was known to be the eldest in power and rank."

The Qur'an itself does not settle it, and neither should we. What is worth noticing is how the commentators themselves reason: in their three answers, being "the eldest" is variously understood as seniority in age, in knowledge and merit, or in power and rank. Even among those who studied this word closely, it was not automatically a matter of birth order.

## The indictment: two failures, not one

His speech opens with a question that is really an accusation: *"Know you not that your father did take an oath from you in Allah's Name...?"*

The word is **مَّوْثِقٗا مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ** — an oath taken *in Allah's Name*, which Maʿārif renders as a pledge given "in the name of Allah." Ibn Kathir specifies what it was about: "that you will return Binyamin to him." And then comes the sentence that must have landed like a stone: "However, you were not able to fulfill this promise and, before you caused Yusuf to be lost from his father."

That is the shape of his argument. He is not merely saying *we have failed today*; he is saying *we failed once before, and this is the second time our father will lose a son on our watch*. Maʿārif puts the same charge in his mouth: "you had defaulted earlier in the case of Yusuf (peace be upon him)." The old sin is not buried. It is standing right there in the huddle, giving the present disaster its full weight — and, as ayah 82 will show, it is also the reason no one at home is going to believe a word they say.

## "I will never leave this land" (80)

**فَلَنۡ أَبۡرَحَ ٱلۡأَرۡضَ** — Ibn Kathir: "I will not leave Egypt." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it as an absolute refusal: "I shall **never** leave this land." He does not negotiate; he does not set a date. He pins himself to the ground.

He then allows himself exactly two ways out, and it is worth noticing how carefully chosen they are:

**1. "…until my father permits me."** Ibn Kathir explains this as: until he "allows me to go back to him **while he is pleased with me**." This is not merely waiting for travel clearance. He will not walk back into his father's house as a man his father has not forgiven. He would rather stay in a foreign country indefinitely than face Yaʿqub (peace be upon him) with an unaccepted excuse.

**2. "…or Allah decides my case."** On **أَوۡ يَحۡكُمَ ٱللَّهُ لِي**, Ibn Kathir reports two understandings: that Allah decides for him "by using the sword," or, as others said, "by allowing me to secure the release of my brother." The commentary as we have it here gives no more than that, so we leave it where it leaves it. What both readings share is that the second exit is not something he can manufacture. It is Allah's ruling, not his plan.

And then: **وَهُوَ خَيۡرُ ٱلۡحَٰكِمِينَ** — "and He is the Best of the judges." A man who has run out of moves, in a country not his own, with a brother detained and a father he cannot yet face, ends his vow by handing the case up to the only court that never errs. This is the believer's posture when every human avenue closes: not paralysis, and not despair, but staying put and letting Allah rule.

## The message he dictates (81)

Ibn Kathir explains the turn: "He next ordered them to narrate to their father what happened so that they could present their excuse about that happened to Binyamin and as claim their innocence before him." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives it in the eldest brother's own voice: *I am going to stay here. You all go back to your father and tell him that his son has committed a theft, and that whatever we are saying is what we have seen with our own eyes, and that the stolen property was recovered from his baggage before us.*

Notice how tightly he limits their claim. They are to say: **"we testify not except according to what we know"** — we report only what we witnessed — and then: **وَمَا كُنَّا لِلۡغَيۡبِ حَٰفِظِينَ**, "we could not know the Unseen" (Ibn Kathir), or "we could not guard against the unseen" (Maʿārif). *Al-ghayb* is what lies outside human perception: what is hidden from you, what you cannot see and cannot control.

The commentators read this key phrase in more than one way:

- **Qatadah and ʿIkrimah** (as reported by Ibn Kathir): it means *"we did not know that your son had committed theft."*
- **ʿAbdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam** (also in Ibn Kathir): it means *"we did not know that Binyamin stole something that belonged to the king, we only stated the punishment of the thief."*
- **Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** offers two complementary senses. First: the pledge they gave about Binyamin "was given in terms of outwardly visible circumstances. We did not know what we did not see and control — thus how could we know that he would steal and be arrested for it leaving us helpless in this matter." Second: "we did our best to keep Benyamin protected seeing that he does nothing which would put him in trouble. But, this effort of ours could be within the limits of our outwardly visible circumstances."

In other words, they are drawing the honest line between what a person guarantees and what is simply not his to guarantee.

## "Ask the town, ask the caravan" (82)

The last move is corroboration. **وَسۡـَٔلِ ٱلۡقَرۡيَةَ** reads literally "**ask the town**" — which is why the renderings supply the words in brackets: "ask (the people of) the town." Qatadah, as reported by Ibn Kathir, takes the town to be Egypt; Ibn Kathir adds "or another town." **وَٱلۡعِيرَ ٱلَّتِيٓ أَقۡبَلۡنَا فِيهَا** — "and the caravan in which we returned" — Ibn Kathir explains they are inviting inquiry "about our truthfulness, honesty, protection and sincere guardianship." And then the seal: **وَإِنَّا لَصَٰدِقُونَ**, "and indeed we are telling the truth" — Ibn Kathir: truthful "in what we have told you, that Binyamin stole and was taken as a captive as compensation for his theft."

Why would grown men need to offer witnesses to their own father? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is blunt about it: "Since the brothers of Yusuf (peace be upon him) had deceived their father earlier, and knew that their father would never be satisfied with their statement... and he would never believe in what they would tell him, therefore, for additional emphasis, they said: '(and if you do not believe us), you can check with the people of the town in which we have been (that is, the city in Egypt). And you can also check with the caravan which has come from Egypt to Canaan with us. And we are true in what we are saying.'"

This is the long tail of a lie. They had deceived this man once before, and now, telling the truth, they have to stack up witnesses — and they still expect not to be believed. A reputation for honesty is a form of wealth; once spent, it is very hard to earn back.

## Rulings the scholars drew from these ayat

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lists three principles under "Rules and Principles":

**1. Obligations run only as far as the visible.** From the words "and we do not testify except what we know," it is established that "human transactions and contracts are based on apparently known circumstances. They do not cover things which no one knows." The brothers' pledge to protect Binyamin "was related to things which were in their control." His being accused of theft and arrested for it "was a different matter which does not affect the pledge as such." Practically: a person is answerable for the diligence he owed, not for outcomes no one could foresee.

**2. Testimony rests on knowledge — however that knowledge was obtained.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites **Tafsir al-Qurtubi**: this sentence proves that testimony depends on knowledge, and "no matter how this knowledge is acquired, testimony can be given in accordance with it." Just as an event may be testified to because one saw it with one's own eyes, it may be testified to because one heard it "from someone reliable and worthy of trust" — subject to the condition that the witness "does not conceal the truth of the matter," but states plainly that he has not seen it personally and heard it from such-and-such a reliable person. It is on the basis of this principle, Qurtubi notes, that **Maliki jurists** have ruled the testimony of a blind person permissible.

**3. Clear the suspicion off yourself.** These ayat also prove that if a person is "true, right and proper," but the situation is such that others may suspect him to be otherwise, "he must remove that shadow of doubt so that those who see him do not fall into the sin of (unwarranted) suspicion." In this very incident, an occasion of accusation and doubt existed "because of a past event in the life of Sayyidna Yusuf (peace be upon him)" — so the testimony of the people of the city and of the caravan was presented in support.

**From the Sunnah.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Qurtubi, notes that the Prophet ﷺ affirmed this principle positively by his personal conduct. On his way back from his Masjid, going through an alley with Umm al-Muʼminin Safiyyah (may Allah be pleased with her), he noticed two persons appearing at the head of the alley. They were still at some distance, but he ﷺ told them that he was with Safiyyah bint Huyayy. They said: *Ya Rasul Allah, can anyone have any suspicion about you?* He said: Yes — the shayṭan keeps seeping through the human body; it may be that it drops a doubt in somebody's heart. (**Al-Bukhari and Muslim**)

The lesson is striking. The companions' own reaction — *can anyone have any suspicion about you?* — shows how unnecessary the precaution must have looked, and he ﷺ took it anyway. Not for his own sake, but so that no one else would be pushed into a sin of the heart. Protecting other people from thinking badly of you is an act of care towards *them*.

## The hard question: how could Yusuf do this?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the question here directly, because it presses hardest at exactly this point in the story: why would Yusuf (peace be upon him) bear such apparently heartless treatment of his father? As Maʿārif puts it, it was surprising that Yusuf (peace be upon him) "did not tell his father about himself, then detained his brother too, then his brothers made repeated visits to Egypt and he never told them about himself nor sent some message to his father."

The answer it quotes is from **Tafsir Mazhari**: *innahu ʿamila dhālika bi-amri-llāhi taʿālā li-yazīda fī balāʾi Yaʿqūb* — that Yusuf (peace be upon him) "did that with the command of Allah Ta'ala so that (the cycle of) the test and trial of Yaʿqub (peace be upon him) reaches its completion."

That single sentence reframes the whole passage. What looks from ground level like an eldest brother's improvised crisis management — a vow made in a huddle, an excuse rehearsed for a grieving father — is, from above, a trial being carried to its appointed end under Allah's own command. The brothers are scrambling. Allah is not.

## Living it

Three things this passage asks of a believer, all of them modelled by a man who had himself been inside the earlier wrong done to Yusuf (peace be upon him):

**Name your own past honestly.** The eldest brother's opening words were not an excuse but an accounting: the oath they had taken in Allah's Name, and — before that — "you did fail in your duty with Yusuf." Facing the truth about yourself is where any real repair begins.

**Do not promise beyond your reach — and do not accept blame beyond it either.** "We could not guard against the unseen" is the boundary of honest responsibility: own the diligence that was yours, and leave the unseen to the One who alone knows and controls it.

**When you have done all you can, stay and let Allah judge.** "I shall never leave this land... or Allah decides about me. And He is the best of all judges." Holding your post when you cannot see the outcome, with the case entrusted to the best of judges, is not passivity. In this story, it is part of a trial that Allah was already carrying to its completion.

passages.title: Jacob's grief, beautiful patience, and hope in Allah
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is.** Ayat 83–87 are Ya'qub's response, peace be upon him, to a second bereavement: his sons come back from Egypt without Binyamin and without Rubil, and the old wound of Yusuf tears open again. What holds the five ayat together is one arc — a father pushed to the limit of endurance, and the discipline he holds his grief with: patience that is *beautiful*, complaint addressed to Allah alone, and a hope that finally moves him to act and send his sons out to search.

## The news, and a father who cannot believe it (83)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene. After Binyamin's detention the brothers returned home and reported what had happened, urging their father that it could all be verified — from the people of Egypt, and from the caravan they had travelled with, who could confirm that Binyamin had been apprehended for theft and arrested. And this time they were telling the truth. But, Maʿārif notes, Ya'qub knew they had lied to him before over Yusuf, so he could not bring himself to believe them now.

Ibn Kathir puts it sharply: Ya'qub answered them with the very words he had used the first time, when they came with the false blood on Yusuf's shirt — *"Nay, but your own selves have beguiled you into something. So patience is most fitting."* Muhammad bin Ishaq said: "When they went back to Ya'qub and told him what happened, he did not believe them and thought that this was a repetition of what they did to Yusuf." Ibn Kathir also records a second explanation: because this new development came after what they had done before, the same verdict was extended to it.

Two further readings deserve attention.

**A prophet's ijtihad.** From this, al-Qurtubi (as reported in Maʿārif) deduces something delicate. Whatever a *mujtahid* — one exerting his own reasoned judgement — concludes by that reasoning may contain error; so much so that even a prophet, when he speaks on the basis of his own ijtihad, may be mistaken, though only initially, as happened here when he declared his sons' true report a lie. But prophets have a special standing and a personal exclusivity: by Allah's will they are alerted to the mistake and moved off it, and finally they find the truth.

**A different target.** Maʿārif offers another possibility: "your souls have contrived something for you" may point not at his sons but at what was contrived *in Egypt* — Binyamin held on a false charge engineered for a particular purpose, whose good result would only unfold later. The hint lies in the next clause, "Hopefully Allah will bring them all to me." Either way his refusal had something true in it: there had been no real theft, and the truth of the matter lay elsewhere — though what his sons said, as far as they knew it, was not wrong either.

## "So, beautiful patience" — and the du'a inside it (83)

*Fa-sabrun jamīl.* Notice where he turns in the same breath: *"'Asā Allāhu an ya'tiyanī bihim jamī'an"* — hopefully Allah will bring them **all** to me. Ibn Kathir reads "all" precisely: he was begging for three sons, not one — Yusuf, Binyamin, and Rubil, who had remained in Egypt awaiting Allah's decision about his case, either his father's permission ordering him home, or a way to secure his brother's release in confidence. Maʿārif reports the separation from Yusuf as forty years in some narrations and eighty in others; and the du'a, as Ibn Kathir reads it, still asks for him.

Then the two names. Ibn Kathir: *"Truly He, only He is al-'Alīm"* — the All-Knowing — of my distress; *"al-Hakīm"* — the All-Wise — in His decisions and in the decree and preordainment He appoints. That is the load-bearing wall under the patience: nothing in his pain is hidden from Allah, and nothing in the decree is without wisdom.

## The turning away, and the white eyes (84)

After this second shock, says Maʿārif, he closed the chapter of discussing the matter with his sons and turned to his Lord with his plaint. Ibn Kathir: he turned away from his children, and the new grief over Binyamin and Rubil renewed the old sadness he had been keeping to himself — *"Yā asafā 'alā Yūsuf!"*

*"And his eyes turned white from grief."* Maʿārif: constant weeping at the separation caused his eyes to turn white — meaning he lost his sight, or it became very weak. The tafsir authority Muqatil said this state lasted six years, by the end of which his eyesight had nearly gone. Of the separation from Yusuf as a whole, Maʿārif reports forty years in some narrations, eighty in others, through which he wept continuously until his sight was gone.

**"Fa-huwa kazīm."** This word repays slowing down for. Maʿārif: *kazīm* is from *kazm*, meaning to be choked up, or filled. The picture is a heart filled to the brim with sorrow and a tongue tied — silent, unable to share his pain with anyone. The same root is used of suppressing anger: the heart full of it, yet the anger never becomes the motivating factor of doing something, by word of mouth or movement of hand, as the anger demands. Maʿārif cites a hadith to that effect — whoever suppresses his anger when he is able to act on it, Allah will reward him — and another that on the Day of Resurrection (*al-Hashr*) Allah will bring such people before the whole multitude of people and give them the option to take whichever of the blessings of Paradise they like. (Maʿārif reports both without naming a collection, so no collection is named here either.)

So *kazīm* is not numbness, and it is not stoicism in the cold sense. Ad-Dahhak said simply, "Ya'qub was aggrieved, sorrowful and sad." Qatadah and other scholars said he suppressed his sorrow and did not complain to a created being. The grief was total and the containment was total, and both are true at once.

## The word he was not given

Ibn Kathir carries a striking observation: 'Abdur-Razzaq narrated from Ath-Thawri, from Sufyan al-'Usfuri, from Sa'id bin Jubayr, that only this nation — the following of Prophet Muhammad ﷺ — were given *al-Istirjā'*: "Innā lillāhi wa innā ilayhi rāji'ūn," *to Allah we belong and to Him we return*. His evidence was this very ayah: "Have you not heard the statement of Ya'qub, peace be upon him — *Yā asafā 'alā Yūsuf*?" Maʿārif reports the same from a hadith recorded by Imam Ibn Jarir, and by al-Baihaqi in his *Shu'ab al-Imān* from a narration of Ibn 'Abbas: reciting it at a time of distress, or prompting another to recite it, is a distinguishing characteristic of this Ummah, and this kalimah is highly effective in delivering a person from the suffering of sorrow.

Let that land. The sentence a Muslim says almost reflexively at bad news was not, on this report, given to earlier nations. It is a gift. Use it like one.

## The sons' worry (85)

Their words are not a rebuke. Ibn Kathir says they spoke feeling sorrow and compassion: *"By Allah, you will never cease remembering Yusuf until you become weak with old age"* — *haradan*, that is, until your strength leaves you — *"or until you be of the dead"*: if you go on like this, we fear you might die of grief. Maʿārif adds their reasoning: every shock ends eventually and every sorrow fades as the days pass, yet he stood exactly where he had stood, his sorrow as fresh as the hour it came.

## "I complain of my anguish and my grief only to Allah" (86)

This is the heart of the passage, and it separates two things people constantly confuse. Ya'qub does not deny that he is complaining. He names its address. Ibn Kathir: *"I complain of my grief and sorrow"* — for the afflictions that struck me — *"to Allah,"* alone. Maʿārif renders the force of it: not to you, nor to anyone else, but to Allah Himself; therefore leave me alone as I am.

Complaint made to Allah is not a breach of patience; it is what patience looks like when it has somewhere to go. Weeping is not the failure — broadcasting is. Maʿārif places beside this ayah a saying of the Prophet ﷺ reported from Abu Hurayrah: *man baththa lam yasbir*, one who goes about narrating his distress before everyone has not observed sabr. (Maʿārif does not name a collection for it.) The word Ya'qub uses of his own anguish, *bathth*, is that same word: he does spread his pain out — before Allah.

**"And I know from Allah what you do not know."** Ibn Kathir: 'I anticipate from Allah each and every type of goodness.' Ibn 'Abbas explained it as: the vision that Yusuf saw is truthful, and Allah will certainly make it come true. Maʿārif adds that he was indicating his remembering would not go to waste — he had been promised by Allah that He would bring them all together with him. His grief was never despair, because underneath it sat a promise.

## "Go and search… and do not despair" (87)

Then the turn. Maʿārif notes the timing: after the passage of such a long time, this is the first time Ya'qub tells his sons to go and search for Yusuf and his brother — before this he had never given an order of this nature. All these things were subservient to the divine destiny; meeting earlier was not so destined, so no such action was taken. Now the time to meet had arrived, and Allah put into his heart the way out appropriate to it. Notice the direction, too: Egypt — known and definite in Binyamin's case, but with no obvious outward reason to look for Yusuf there. When Allah intends to do something, He arranges to put together the appropriate causes for it. Some commentators, Maʿārif reports, say a clue had been working on him — the 'Aziz of Misr had treated them unusually the first time, returning their capital by putting it inside their baggage, a nobility and generosity that made him wonder whether this 'Aziz might be Yusuf himself.

Ibn Kathir on the instruction itself: he ordered them to go back and inquire about the news of Yusuf and his brother *in a good manner, not as spies.* He encouraged them, delivered good news to them, and ordered them not to despair of Allah's mercy — never to give up hope in Allah, nor ever to discontinue trusting Him for what they seek to accomplish — for only the disbelieving people despair of Allah's mercy.

That last clause is the passage's hardest edge and its greatest comfort. Despair is not filed under weakness; it is placed on the side of disbelief. Ya'qub is blind, decades into a grief that never faded, holding a report he never accepted, and he sends his sons back to a foreign court on the strength of a hope. That is what "never give up hope of Allah's mercy" looks like in a human body.

## Why was he tried like this?

Maʿārif raises the difficulty honestly: how could a prophet be so consumed by love for a son, when the Qur'an says your wealth and children are a *fitnah*, a trial (64:15), and that Allah made the prophets special to specialize in the remembrance of the Home of the Hereafter (38:46) — which Malik ibn Dinar explained as: He took the love of the world out of their hearts and filled them instead with nothing but the love of the Akhirah, so that the Akhirah is their only criterion in taking or leaving anything.

The answer Maʿārif reports from Qadi Thana'ullah Panipati's *Tafsir Mazhari*, from a special research of Mujaddid Alf Thani: love of the world and its enjoyment is indeed blameworthy, as categorical statements of Qur'an and Hadith prove; but love of those worldly things that relate to the Hereafter is in reality included under love of the Hereafter. Yusuf's excellences were not limited to his physical beauty alone — there was also his prophetic chastity and his high morals. Taken as a whole, loving him was not love of what worldly life has to offer. And yet, Maʿārif observes, because that love still had a certain worldly touch, it became the source of the trial and test of Ya'qub, for which he had to undergo the shock of a forty-year separation.

Maʿārif also observes how the events kept taking shape as Allah determined, so that the shock stretched longer and longer. A father who loved his son that intensely would otherwise not have simply listened to his other sons and stayed home; had he gone to the site of the incident at the outset and made inquiries, he would have known the truth on the spot — but things happened as Allah would have them, and it simply did not occur to him. Yusuf, for his part, was stopped through revelation from sending his father any news about himself, even after his ascension to power in Egypt, even through his brothers' repeated visits; instead he detained yet another brother through a secret plan. Actions like these could not issue from a great prophet unless he had been prohibited from doing otherwise through the medium of *wahy* (revelation); so al-Qurtubi and other commentators declared this entire range of Yusuf's actions to be directly prompted by divine revelation, with the Qur'an's own words indicating in that direction: "This is how We planned for Yusuf" (12:76). And Allah knows best.

Al-Qurtubi further gives a reason for the severity of the trial, as it appears in some narrations: that one day Ya'qub was performing his Tahajjud prayer with Yusuf asleep before him, and the sound of the boy's snoring caused his attention to be diverted to him — this happened twice, and thrice; and Allah said to His angels: Look, this is My friend and My favoured servant, see how, in the middle of his address and approach to Me, he turns his attention to someone other than Me; by My honour and power, I shall take out these two eyes of his with which he turned his attention to another, and the one to whom he turned his attention I shall separate from him for a long time. Maʿārif attaches to this a hadith of Al-Bukhari narrated by 'A'ishah, who asked the Prophet ﷺ how it is to look elsewhere during Salah, and he replied that through it the shaytan snatches away the Salah of a servant of Allah.

## Living it

Maʿārif gathers the practical lessons under "Points of Guidance":

**Patience is obligatory, not optional.** Al-Qurtubi: this episode proves it is *wājib* on every Muslim, when faced with distress or pain in the case of his person, children, family or property, to seek redress from it by resorting to patience at its best and by becoming resigned to and content with the decree of Allah — following the example of Ya'qub and the other blessed prophets.

**Two swallowings.** Al-Hasan al-Basri: out of what one swallows, two are the best in the sight of Allah — patience over pain or distress, and swallowed anger.

**Choose your listener.** Complain upward, not sideways. Grief poured out to Allah is worship; grief toured around the gathering is, in the words reported from Abu Hurayrah, the loss of sabr itself.

**The reward is enormous.** Ibn 'Abbas said Allah conferred on Ya'qub the reward of the *shuhadā'*, the martyrs, for this patience — and that in this Ummah too, whoever observes patience while in distress shall receive a similar reward.

**Never close the file.** Say *'asā Allāh* — hopefully Allah — about the very thing you have given up on. Ya'qub's du'a for "all of them" included, as Ibn Kathir explains, the son who had been gone the longest.

passages.title: "I am Joseph" — the brothers recognize him
passages.tafsir:
Famine has driven the sons of Yaʿqub (peace be upon him) back to Egypt a third time, and they come with almost nothing worth trading, to plead before the ruler of the land — a man they do not recognise. These five ayat carry the sūrah over its crest: the disguise falls, the wrong is named aloud, and instead of the reckoning everyone expects, Yusuf (peace be upon him) gives them pardon and a prayer.

## The third journey

Ibn Kathir places these words immediately after ayah 87, where Yaʿqub (peace be upon him) ordered his sons to go back and inquire about Yusuf (peace be upon him) and his brother — and, Ibn Kathir stresses, in a good manner, not as spies. He encouraged them, delivered the good news, and ordered them never to despair of Allah's mercy nor to discontinue trusting in Him, because only the disbelieving people despair of Allah's mercy.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out what the brothers themselves could not see. They set out for Egypt for practical reasons: they knew Binyamin was there and had to try to get him released first; they needed food grains; and their request for grain gave them a pretext to appear before the ʿAzīz and put forward their plea for their brother. That Yusuf (peace be upon him) was in Egypt at all was not known to them. Yet, as Maʿārif puts it, when the time comes for something to happen, human plans too start falling into place, unconsciously and without any intentional effort — and it cites a hadith to the effect that when Allah intends to do something, He makes its causes get together automatically. (The source quotes this teaching without naming the collection it comes from, so no collection is named here either.) They thought they were going to buy food. They were walking into the answer to their father's long grief.

## Nothing left to bargain with

They address him by his office, not by any name they know — *yā ayyuhā al-ʿAzīz*. Maʿārif describes their manner: they talked to him in a flattering tone, presenting their need and helplessness.

**"Hardship has touched us and our family."** Ibn Kathir explains this as being because of severe droughts and the scarcity of food. Maʿārif says the same: they did not have even adequate funds to purchase food grains.

**"And we have come with a *biḍāʿa muzjāt*" — poor capital.** Mujahid, al-Ḥasan and several others explain the phrase, Ibn Kathir reports, as meaning: we brought money for the food we want to buy, but it is not substantial. Maʿārif renders *muzjāt* "capital of very little worth": the word really means something which does not move on its own, but has to be moved by someone else forcefully. As for what exactly it was, Maʿārif is careful: the Qur'an and hadith have not clarified it, and the sayings of the commentators differ. Some say bad dirhams which were not acceptable in the open market; others say household articles.

**"So give us the full measure, and be charitable to us."** Ibn Kathir renders the sense: in return for the little money we brought, give us the full measure that you gave us before. He also records that Ibn Masʿūd read this ayah in a way that means, "So give the full load on our animals and be charitable with us," and that Ibn Jurayj commented, "So be charitable to us by returning our brother to us." Maʿārif adds that this was not their right: they were asking a generous man to accept whatever they had and still give them the full measure of grain usually given for goods of good value, pleading that it be given as if in charity.

They stand before the most powerful man in Egypt holding goods that cannot cover what they are asking for — and the man they are begging from is the brother who, as Maʿārif notes, had undergone hardship for a long time due to the actions of these very brothers.

## Was it lawful for them to ask for charity?

Maʿārif treats this as a real question: how could *ṣadaqa* be lawful for the brothers of Yusuf (peace be upon him), who are the progeny of prophets — and even if it were lawful, how could asking for it be lawful? And Yusuf himself was certainly a prophet: why did he not warn them against this error?

First, the word *ṣadaqa* used here does not mean real charity. They never asked for a free supply of grain; they offered capital, poor as it was, and their request was that this capital of very little worth be accepted in the spirit of remission given in such hard circumstances. It is that concession in the transaction which has been given the name of charity. Second, Maʿārif adds that it is also possible that the unlawfulness of charity for the progeny of prophets is exclusive to the Ummah of the Prophet ﷺ — a view it attributes to Mujahid, citing *Bayān al-Qurʼān*.

Ibn Kathir records that when Sufyān bin ʿUyaynah was asked whether charity was prohibited for any Prophet before our Prophet ﷺ, he answered by asking, "Have you not heard the ayah, *so pay us full measure and be charitable to us. Truly, Allah does reward the charitable*?" Ibn Jarīr aṭ-Ṭabarī collected this statement.

## Why they said "Allah rewards the charitable" and not "Allah will reward you"

The last words of ayah 88 look like a stock phrase. Maʿārif, citing *Bayān al-Qurʼān*, shows they are a carefully chosen one. Allah's return for what is spent in charity comes in two kinds: a general return, received by everyone, believer or disbeliever, in the present world, in the form of the removal of disasters and hardships; and a return particularly attached to the Hereafter, that is, Paradise — and that is for the believers only.

The man they were addressing was the ʿAzīz of Misr, and they did not know whether or not he was a believer. So they opted for a sentence which was general, covering the return of this world as well as that of the Hereafter, rather than promising him anything in particular. Qurṭubī, cited here, makes the same point from the side of style: the occasion demanded a direct address — "Allah will give you the best of return" — but because his being a believer was not known, the form of address used was general, and no special reward was mentioned for him. A small swerve in wording that keeps their speech honest: they would flatter him, but they would not pronounce on what they did not know.

## The letter that broke him

Maʿārif, on the basis of a narration of Ibn ʿAbbās reported in *Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī* and *Mazharī*, says that Yaʿqub (peace be upon him) had sent a letter addressed to the ʿAzīz of Misr:

> "From Yaʿqub Ṣafī Allah Ibn Isḥāq Dhabīḥ Allah Ibn Ibrāhīm Khalīl Allah to the ʿAzīz of Misr. After offering praise to Allah: Our entire family is known for hardships and trials. My grandfather, Ibrāhīm Khalīl Allah was tested through the fire of Nimrūd. Then, my father, Isḥāq was put to a hard test. Then, I was tested through a son of mine whom I held very dear — to the limit that I lost my eyesight when separated from him. After that, there was his younger brother, a source of comfort for me in my grief, whom you arrested on a charge of theft. And let me tell you that we are the progeny of prophets. Never have we committed a theft, nor has there ever been a thief among our children. And peace on you!"

An old man who has lost his sight, writing to the stranger who holds his son, reading his family's history as a chain of trials. He does not know that the stranger receiving the letter is that son. When Yusuf (peace be upon him) read it, Maʿārif says, he trembled and broke into tears and decided to let his secret out.

Ibn Kathir describes the same moment: when his brothers told him about the afflictions, hardship and shortages in food they suffered in the aftermath of the drought, and he remembered his father's grief for losing his two children, he felt compassion, pity and mercy for his father and his brothers — the more so, Ibn Kathir notes, since he was enjoying kingship, authority and power. So he cried, and revealed his true identity.

## "Do you know what you did?"

He does not begin with "I am Yusuf." He begins with a question: *Do you know what you did with Yusuf and his brother, when you were ignorant?* Ibn Kathir explains "what you did" as: when you separated between Yusuf and his brother. And on *when you were ignorant*, he gives Yusuf's meaning as: what made you do this is your ignorance of the tremendous sin you were about to commit. Maʿārif fills in the same clause — at a time when they were ignorant, unable to distinguish between good and bad, and quite neglectful of acting with foresight.

Notice who supplies that excuse. It is not the brothers pleading immaturity — it is the wronged man himself, in the same breath in which he names the wrong, handing them a way to bear hearing it. The question is not an interrogation designed to crush them; it is a door held open for confession.

Ibn Kathir adds: it appears, and Allah knows best, that Yusuf revealed his identity to his brothers only then **by Allah's command**, just as he hid his identity from them in the first two meetings by Allah's command. Maʿārif says the same — the restriction placed by Allah upon Yusuf (peace be upon him), that he would not disclose the truth about himself, was not going to be there anymore. So the years of concealment were not a game he was playing with his family's pain; they were obedience, held until the appointed hour. And that hour, Ibn Kathir observes, came exactly when the affliction had become harder, which is Allah's way: *Verily, along with every hardship is relief. Verily, along with every hardship is relief* (94:5–6).

The brothers, Maʿārif says, were dumbfounded. What has the ʿAzīz of Misr got to do with the story of Yusuf? Then they recollected the dream seen by young Yusuf, whose interpretation was that he would achieve some high rank and that they would have to bow down before him. As they exerted and deliberated a little more, they recognised him by some signs — and still, to confirm it further, they asked.

## "I am Yusuf, and this is my brother"

*A-innaka la-anta Yūsuf* — "Are you indeed Yusuf?" They asked it, Ibn Kathir says, in amazement: they had been meeting him for more than two years while unaware of who he really was, while he knew exactly who they were and hid this news from them.

His answer is bare and unadorned: *I am Yusuf, and this is my brother.* Maʿārif notes the purpose of the added clause: he named his brother so that they would become certain about him, and at the same time he wanted them to become sure right then of the total success of their mission — the two they had set out to search for were there before them.

Then, before a word about himself, he turns to Allah: *qad manna Allāhu ʿalaynā*, "Allah has indeed been gracious to us." Ibn Kathir: by gathering us together after being separated all this time. Maʿārif unfolds it further — Allah first gave the two brothers two qualities, patience (*ṣabr*) and the fear of Allah (*taqwā*), qualities which are a key to success and a security shield against every hardship; then He changed hardship into comfort, separation into union, and their paucity of wealth and recognition into total abundance.

## Taqwa and sabr — is Yusuf praising himself?

The ayah closes with a principle: *whoever fears Allah and is patient — then surely Allah does not waste the reward of the good-doers.* Maʿārif glosses it: whoever fears Allah and abstains from sins, and observes patience while in distress. Taqwa and sabr, it says, are two qualities which deliver a person from every disaster and distress, and the Qur'an has said in several places that prosperity and success depend on them, for example: *if you keep patience and fear Allah, their cunning shall not harm you at all* (3:120).

A surface view of the verse may suggest that Yusuf (peace be upon him) is claiming that it was because of *his* taqwa and *his* sabr that he was delivered from difficulty and given high rank. Yet no one can claim taqwa for himself; it is prohibited by definite statements in the Qur'an, for example: *do not claim purity for yourselves; He knows best who it is that guards against evil* (53:32).

Maʿārif's answer: in reality there is no claim here at all. It is a confession of the blessings and favours of Allah, for He first gave him the *tawfīq* — the enabling grace — of sabr and taqwa, and then, through it, came all blessings from Him. Read that way, the sentence is not "look what my virtue achieved" but "look what Allah gave me, and then what He gave me through it."

## Remembering the favour, not the wound

Maʿārif draws guidance from *qad manna Allāhu ʿalaynā*. Should a person be in distress or hardship, and Allah delivers him from it and showers him with blessings, then after that he should not talk about his past hardships anymore; he should remember nothing but the favour of Allah which he now has. To continue crying over past hardships after deliverance and reward is ingratitude. The Qur'an has a word for such a person: *kanūd* — *truly, man is to his Lord ungrateful* (100:6) — and *kanūd* refers to a person who does not remember favours received, but does remember hardships faced.

Therefore, Maʿārif says, Yusuf (peace be upon him) made no mention at this time of the hardships he had undergone for a long time due to the actions of his brothers. Instead, he mentioned the blessings of Allah only. Standing in front of the very men whose actions had cost him those years, holding all the power, he chose to speak of what Allah had given rather than what they had taken.

## "By Allah, Allah has preferred you over us"

They answer with an oath — *tāllāhi* — and a verdict against themselves. Ibn Kathir: they affirmed Yusuf's virtue above them, blessed as he was with beauty, conduct, richness, kingship, authority and, above all, prophethood; and they admitted their error. Maʿārif reports that they now had no choice left but to confess the wrongs they had done and admit his grace and excellence, and that in one voice they all said it, with the sense: Allah has given you the preference you deserved, and we were surely in error in whatever we did — so forgive us in the name of Allah.

Two things are precisely right in their confession. First, they do not say "you turned out to be the better man"; they say **Allah** preferred you — the excellence is recognised as a gift, not the outcome of a competition. Second, *wa in kunnā la-khāṭiʼīn*, "and we were certainly at fault" — no explanation, no softening. Naming your own wrong without decorating it is the whole substance of repentance.

## "No reproach on you today"

*Lā tathrība ʿalaykum al-yawm.* Ibn Kathir gives Yusuf's meaning as: there will be no blame for you today or admonishment, and I will not remind you after today of your error against me. Maʿārif reads it in the same spirit: far from saying much about taking revenge for your injustices against me, on this day I would not even blame you for it.

Then, Ibn Kathir says, he multiplied his generosity by invoking Allah for them for mercy: *may Allah forgive you, and He is the Most Merciful of those who show mercy.* Maʿārif's verdict on the whole declaration: it has been made from the highest level of good morals, whereby the wrongdoer was not only forgiven, but spared reproach as well.

Maʿārif calls the first half "the good news of forgiveness from his side which he let them hear" — Yusuf (peace be upon him) drops what is owed to *him*, and drops it completely, waiving even the right to bring it up again. What is owed to Allah he does not presume to settle himself; that he places where it belongs, praying for them before Allah, naming Him *arḥam ar-rāḥimīn*. He gives away everything that was his to give, and asks Allah for the rest.

## Living it

- **Never treat a door as closed.** Yaʿqub (peace be upon him) sent his sons out with the command never to despair of Allah's mercy, and the errand they took up for grain put them in front of both the men their father had sent them to find. When Allah intends a thing, its causes come together.
- **Ask, even when your capital is poor.** They came with goods that could not move themselves and still asked for the full measure. Poverty of what you bring is not a reason to stay away from the One who gives.
- **Taqwa and sabr are the two that carry you through.** Abstention from sin, and patience in distress — and if Allah grants you either, count it as His enabling grace and not your achievement.
- **Stop rehearsing the old wound once Allah has relieved you.** The one who does not remember favours received but does remember hardships faced is *kanūd*.
- **When you finally have the upper hand, drop the reproach.** Not just no revenge — no "after everything you did to me." Yusuf (peace be upon him) had every right to say it, and did not; he prayed for them instead.

passages.title: The shirt that restores Jacob's sight
passages.tafsir:
**The passage in one breath.** Yusuf, peace be upon him, has just revealed himself to his brothers and forgiven them. Now his thoughts turn to his father — and he sends back the one thing that had once carried a lie to Ya'qub: a shirt. This time it carries the truth. Ayat 93–98 follow that single garment from Egypt to Canaan and watch what it does at every stage: it is sent with a promise (93), its scent arrives before it does and is mocked in the room where it lands (94–95), it touches an old man's face and his sight returns (96), and in the space that opens afterwards a family finally says out loud what it did and asks to be forgiven (97–98). One cloth, one journey, and one claim running underneath all six ayat — that Ya'qub knew from Allah what his household did not.

## Where we stand in the story

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene. The time had come, by the will of Allah, for Yusuf to disclose his secret to his brothers, and he did. They sought his forgiveness; he not only forgave them, he did not even choose to reproach them for what they had done — he prayed to Allah for them. Meeting his father was his next concern, and given the conditions he judged it better that his father should come to him along with the family. But when he came to know that his father had lost his eyesight as a result of their separation, that became his *first* concern.

That reordering of priorities is the hinge of the whole passage. Everything that follows — the shirt, the courier, the scent, the restored sight, the request for forgiveness — flows out of a son learning that his absence had cost his father his eyes.

## The shirt: sent in ayah 93, arriving in ayah 96

**Why there was a blindness to heal.** Ibn Kathir gives the reason for the instruction in a single clause: cast it over the face of my father, his vision will return — *because Ya'qub had lost his sight from excessive crying*. The grief was not incidental to the story; it was written into his body.

**A miracle, not a remedy.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the crucial point plainly: it is obvious that putting someone's shirt on the face of a person cannot become the physical cause of eyesight returning. This was a miracle granted to Yusuf — he knew, by the will of Allah, that once his shirt was put over his father's face, Allah would give him his eyesight back. So the instruction is not an experiment and not folk medicine. *Yaʾti baṣīran* — "he will turn into a sighted man." Yusuf is reporting what Allah had let him know.

**Where the shirt came from — a reported account.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relays from the tafsir authorities Ḍaḥḥāk and Mujāhid that this was the inherent quality of that particular shirt, because it was not like ordinary clothes: it was brought from Paradise for Ibrahim, peace be upon him, at the time when Nimrud had him thrown naked into the fire. It remained with Ibrahim, then passed to Ishaq, and after him to Ya'qub, who — treating it as a sacred legacy — put it inside a tube, sealed it, and had Yusuf wear it round his neck as a *taʿwīdh* (a protective charm) to keep him safe against the evil eye. When the brothers removed Yusuf's shirt to deceive their father and he was thrown into the well without it, Jibra'il al-Amin came, opened the tube hanging at his neck, took out this shirt and clothed him in it; from then on it stayed with him. When it was needed again, it was Jibra'il al-Amin once more who told Yusuf that this was an apparel of Paradise with a unique property — that if it were placed over the face of a blind man he would become sighted — and told him to send it to his father.

**A second view.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also records a second explanation, which it attributes to a scholar it names by the honorific title Mujaddid Alf Thānī (a title of honour, not a personal name), citing it from Mazharī, the commentary Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names as its source here: that the beauty — indeed the very existence — of Yusuf was itself a thing of Paradise, so that *every* shirt which touched his body could have this property. Both explanations are offered by the commentators; the ayah itself specifies neither, and on either account the operative cause is the will of Allah.

**Who carried it — and why that matters.** According to a narration reported by al-Qurṭubī, cited in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, Yahuda (Judah) among the brothers offered to carry this shirt personally — because it was he who had carried young Yusuf's shirt smeared with fake blood, the shirt that brought so many shocks to his father. Now it should be him again, carrying a shirt in his own hands, so that amends could be made for past injustices.

Hold on to that name, because it returns three ayat later. When the passage reaches the arrival in ayah 96, Ibn Kathir reports that Ibn 'Abbas and aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk explained *al-bashīr*, "the bearer of good news," as the information itself, while Mujāhid and As-Suddī identified the bearer as Yahudha, son of Ya'qub — the same identification Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives, noting that he was the same brother who had brought the shirt from Egypt. As-Suddī adds the reason: he brought it because it was he who had brought Yusuf's shirt stained with the false blood, and so he liked to erase that error with this good act, by bringing Yusuf's shirt and placing it on his father's face. And his father's sight was restored to him.

The same man, the same road, the same kind of cloth in his hands — and this time the truth. If you are looking for what repentance looks like in action, the passage hands it to you across the span of the ayat: undo the wrong in the shape you made it, in the same place, before the same person you wronged.

**"And bring me all your family."** Ibn Kathir explains this as all the children of Ya'qub. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to something delicate in the wording: the real purpose was to have his respected father come to him, yet he did not specifically mention his father — he spoke instead of bringing the family, perhaps because he considered that asking for his father to be brought to him was contrary to etiquette. And he was already certain his father's sight would return, so no reason would remain that could stop him from coming; rather he would himself want to honour his son with the visit. It is a small choice of words that carries a whole ethic of how a son speaks about his father, even when that son holds power in Egypt.

## The scent and the room: ayat 94–95

**Before the caravan is out of sight.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the timing precisely: the caravan had barely reached outside the limits of the city when Ya'qub, far away, said to those around him — *"I do indeed sense the scent of Yusuf, if only you did not think me senile."*

'Abdur-Razzāq narrated that Ibn 'Abbas said: when the caravan departed from Egypt, a wind started blowing and brought the scent of Yusuf's shirt to Ya'qub — and he found his scent from a distance of eight days away. Ibn Kathir notes that similar was reported through Sufyān ath-Thawrī and Shu'bah, and others reported it from Abū Sinān. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds al-Ḥasan's estimate: eighty *farsakh*, nearly two hundred and fifty miles. So the shirt of the previous ayah is already at work before it has travelled a day's journey, and it is working on a sense, not on eyes.

**The question that unlocks the whole passage.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān asks the thing a thoughtful reader wants to ask, and its answer governs how we should read every miracle in these six ayat: it is a thing of wonder that this scent caused no reaction in the father's senses when Yusuf was sitting confined in a well of his own homeland. Right from here, it says, we learn that no miracle is in the control of a prophet. A miracle is not even the personal act of the prophet; it is directly the act of Allah. When Allah wills, He makes a miracle manifest itself — and when the divine will is not there, the nearest of the near recedes into the farthest.

That single sentence explains both halves of the passage at once: why a scent crosses eight days of desert here, and why it did not cross out of a well then. The variable was never the distance. It was the will of Allah.

**"If only you did not think me senile."** The word Ya'qub uses is *tufannidūn*. Ibn Kathir reports two shades of meaning from the early authorities: Ibn 'Abbas, Mujāhid, 'Aṭā', Qatādah and Sa'īd bin Jubayr commented, "if only you think me not a fool"; Mujāhid and al-Ḥasan said it means "if only you think me not old" — Ibn Kathir glosses the phrase as: except that you might think me senile because of old age. Notice what the clause reveals about the speaker. This aged prophet knows exactly how his announcement is going to sound in that room, and he makes it anyway.

**And the room answers.** Their reply comes with an oath: *"By Allah! Certainly, you are in your old ḍalāl"* — "your old error," according to Ibn 'Abbas, as Ibn Kathir reports. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains what they were pointing at: those around Ya'qub were wondering that he still seemed engrossed in his old fallacy — that Yusuf is alive and that they would meet again.

Qatādah's comment, cited by Ibn Kathir, is the sharpest reading of their intent: they meant that *because of your love for Yusuf you will never forget him*. The passage then delivers its verdict on the exchange: so they uttered a harsh word to their father that they should never have uttered to him, nor to a Prophet of Allah — and Ibn Kathir notes that similar was said by As-Suddī and others. Two wrongs at once, then: they spoke that way to a father, and to a prophet. It is worth sitting with, because these were not enemies. They were his own household, oath and all, confidently wrong about the one thing that mattered.

## Vindication, and the door it opens: ayah 96

When the bearer of good news arrived and cast the shirt over his face, his vision returned — and Ya'qub said to his children, *"Did I not say to you, 'I know from Allah that which you know not?'"*

Read that against the two ayat just before it. In 94 he announced something no one else could perceive; in 95 he was told he was in his old error. Now the claim of 94 is standing in the room with its sight restored. Ibn Kathir explains what the knowledge consisted of: that Allah would return Yusuf to him, and what he had said about sensing the scent of Yusuf. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the same content — that Yusuf is alive and that they will meet again.

And notice that he is not scoring a point about himself. His claim was never "I am clever"; it was "I know *from Allah*" — knowledge with a source outside himself. That is precisely why the vindication does not curdle into humiliation for his sons. It leaves them room to speak, which is exactly what they do next.

## The asking: ayat 97–98

**The confession.** Now, when the truth of the matter had become clear, the brothers turned to their father. Ibn Kathir describes their manner as humbleness; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls their style spiritually endearing: *"O our father! Ask forgiveness for us for our sins; indeed we have been sinners."*

Notice what they do *not* do — no excuses, no re-litigating the old story, no blaming one brother rather than another. Just *innā kunnā khāṭiʾīn*, "we have been sinners." Naming the sin without decoration is part of what makes the request sincere. And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the necessary inference from their request: it is obvious that a person who asks that Allah forgive his sins through another's prayer would be praying to Allah for that himself too. Asking a righteous person to make du'a for you is not a replacement for turning to Allah yourself; it accompanies it.

**The promise, and the delay.** Ya'qub's answer is: *"I shall pray to my Lord to forgive you."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that instead of praying for them instantly, he made a promise that he would pray for them soon.

Why the delay? Ibn Kathir reports that 'Abdullah bin Mas'ūd, Ibrāhīm at-Taymī, 'Amr bin Qays, Ibn Jurayj and several others said that the Prophet Ya'qub delayed fulfilling their request until the latter part of the night. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the reason the commentators have generally given: his purpose was to pray for them particularly, in peace and with concentration, towards the later part of the night — because the prayer made at that hour is answered specially.

**The hour itself.** For this, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites a hadith in the Ṣaḥīḥ of al-Bukhārī and Muslim: in the last third part of every night, Allah descends in all His Glory close to the firmament near the earth, and proclaims — *Is there someone who would pray to Me, and I would answer? Is there someone who would seek forgiveness from Me, and I would forgive?* What the hadith asks of us is not speculation but presence: to be awake and asking at the hour when the invitation is issued.

**The names at the end.** Ya'qub closes not with reassurance about himself but with two of Allah's names: *"verily, He! Only He is the Oft-Forgiving, the Most Merciful."* Ibn Kathir's comment is short and complete: and He forgives those who repent to Him. The father does not tell his sons they are fine. He points them past himself to the One who actually forgives, and rests his promise on Allah's own names rather than on his own goodwill — which is where the passage that began with a father's blindness finally comes to rest.

## Living it

- **Miracles are Allah's act, not a righteous man's possession.** A scent crosses eight days of desert when Allah wills, and does not travel out of a well in his own homeland when He does not. Ask Allah, not the means.
- **Repair the wrong in the shape you made it.** Yahuda carried a false shirt once and a true one after, and wanted to erase the old error with the new deed. Where you can, return to the exact place of the damage and undo it there.
- **Say it plainly.** "We have been sinners" — no framing, no defence.
- **Ask others to pray for you, and pray yourself.** The request in ayah 97 assumes both.
- **Keep the last part of the night.** A prophet waited for that hour rather than rushing his du'a. If he thought it worth waiting for, it is worth waking for.

passages.title: The family reunited and the dream fulfilled
passages.tafsir:
The family that was torn apart walks into Egypt together, and the dream a boy once told his father — the dream of ayah 4 — finally stands in front of him as fact. The three ayat form one closing scene: the arrival and the welcome (99), the dream fulfilled and the gratitude poured out over it (100), and a final du'a in which Yusuf turns from his father to his Lord and asks — not for more — but for a good ending (101).

## The caravan comes to Egypt (ayah 99)

Ibn Kathir explains that Yusuf had asked his brothers to bring their entire family, so they left Kanaan for Egypt. When Yusuf received news that they were approaching, he went out to receive them. The king ordered the princes and the notable people to go out in the receiving party with Yusuf to meet Allah's Prophet Ya'qub, peace be upon him; it is said that the king himself also went out with them.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the scene from the narrations: Yusuf had sent back with his brothers a large supply of clothes and other articles of need, loaded on some two hundred camels, so the family could prepare for the journey. When Ya'qub and his family set out, their number is given as seventy-two in one narration and ninety-three men and women in another. On the Egyptian side, Yusuf and the people of Egypt came out of the city to receive them — and with them four thousand soldiers, a guard of honour.

These figures come from narrations, not from the Qur'an.

فَلَمَّا دَخَلُوا عَلَىٰ يُوسُفَ — "when they entered upon Yusuf" — is followed by آوَىٰ إِلَيْهِ أَبَوَيْهِ, rendered by Ibn Kathir as "he took his parents to himself," and by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān as: he lodged his parents with him. Yusuf does not merely greet them at the gate. He takes them in.

## "Enter Egypt, if Allah wills, in security"

Ibn Kathir reads ادْخُلُوا مِصْرَ, "enter Egypt," as meaning *reside* in Egypt — this is not a visit, it is a home. And إِن شَاءَ اللَّهُ آمِنِينَ, "if Allah wills, in security," he connects directly to the hardship and famine they had been suffering. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a second layer: they were to enter without fear, free of the usual restrictions placed on travellers entering another country.

Notice where Yusuf places the إِن شَاءَ اللَّهُ. Two ayat later he will say to his Lord, قَدْ آتَيْتَنِي مِنَ الْمُلْكِ — "You have given me of the sovereignty"; Ibn Kathir speaks of Allah having bestowed on him prophethood and kingship. A man carrying that much authority could have promised his family safety in his own name. He hangs the whole promise on the will of Allah instead.

## "His parents" — a genuine difference among the scholars

Who exactly are the أَبَوَيْن, the "two parents"? Ibn Kathir reports both positions. As-Suddi and 'Abdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam said they were his father and his maternal aunt, since his mother had died long ago. Muhammad bin Ishaq and Ibn Jarir at-Tabari said, "His father and mother were both alive," and Ibn Jarir added: "There is no evidence that his mother had died before then. Rather, the apparent words of the Qur'an testify that she was alive." Ibn Kathir judges this second opinion to carry the apparent and suitable meaning that the story itself testifies to.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the first view: after the death of Yusuf's mother, Ya'qub married Layya, the sister of his late wife, who as Yusuf's maternal aunt and his father's married wife deserved to be called nothing but his mother.

Its footnote is careful: on this question **there is no authentic riwayah** at all. Isra'ili reports do exist, but they contradict one another, and the author of Rūḥ al-Maʿānī has himself said that the Jewish chroniclers do not subscribe to the view that Yusuf's mother died at Benyamin's birth. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Kathir opted for the weightier view — that the one raised to the throne here is his real mother.

Where the Qur'an is silent and the reports are tangled, the honest scholar says so and manufactures no certainty.

## The throne and the prostration (ayah 100)

وَرَفَعَ أَبَوَيْهِ عَلَى الْعَرْشِ — "and he raised his parents to the ʿarsh." Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and several others explained, as Ibn Kathir relates, that he raised them to his bedstead, where he himself sat; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says he had his parents sit with him on the royal throne. Either way the gesture is the same: the son given the seat does not sit above his parents. He lifts them up to it.

Then وَخَرُّوا لَهُ سُجَّدًا — "and they fell down before him prostrate." Ibn Kathir specifies that it was Yusuf's parents and his brothers, and they were eleven men.
