Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that at that moment he remembered the dream of his childhood, the sun and the moon and eleven stars prostrating to him.

## Was this prostration permitted?

Ibn 'Abbas, as reported in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, said that **this prostration was one of gratitude offered to Allah**, not to Yusuf.

Others distinguished two kinds of sajdah. Sajdah as an act of *ʿibādah* (worship) done for anyone other than Allah has always been forbidden in the sharia of every prophet. But sajdah of *taʿẓīm* — veneration — was permissible in the religious codes of past prophets. Ibn Kathir, conveying the substance from Qatadah and other scholars, says people were allowed to prostrate before men of authority when they met them, from the law of Adam until the law of ʿĪsā, peace be upon them, and that this was later prohibited in our law: prostration is for Allah alone.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the reason for the closing of that door — it is a source of shirk — and notes that this is confirmed by hadith reports from **Al-Bukhari and Muslim** that prostration for anyone other than Allah is not halal. The Qur'an itself says: لَا تَسْجُدُوا لِلشَّمْسِ وَلَا لِلْقَمَرِ, "prostrate not to the sun nor to the moon" (41:37).

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir relates that when Muʿādh bin Jabal visited the Shām area he found the people prostrating before their priests, and on his return he prostrated before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who asked him, "What is this, O Muʿādh?" Muʿādh said, "I saw that they prostrate before their priests. However, you, O Messenger of Allah, deserve more to be prostrated before." The Messenger ﷺ replied that if he were to order anyone to prostrate before anyone else among the creation, he would have ordered the wife to prostrate before her husband, because of the enormity of his right over her — and he did not order it. Ibn Kathir also relates that when Salmān al-Fārisī wished to prostrate to him, the Prophet ﷺ said: "Do not prostrate to me, O Salmān; prostrate to the Ever-Living who never dies."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes plainly: if a prostration offered as a token of respect to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ himself is not permissible, how can it become permissible before a saint, an elder, or a pīr?

## "This is the ta'wīl of my dream"

هَـٰذَا تَأْوِيلُ رُؤْيَايَ مِن قَبْلُ قَدْ جَعَلَهَا رَبِّي حَقًّا — "O my father, this is the ta'wīl of my dream from before; my Lord has made it come true."

Ibn Kathir notes that تَأْوِيل is used here to describe what became of the matter later on — its real-world outcome, not merely its verbal explanation. He points to the same usage in another ayah: هَلْ يَنظُرُونَ إِلَّا تَأْوِيلَهُ ۖ يَوْمَ يَأْتِي تَأْوِيلُهُ — "Await they just for its ta'wīl? On the Day the event is finally fulfilled…" — meaning the Day of Judgement, when what people were promised of good or evil will surely come to them. A ta'wīl, in this sense, is not a reading. It is an arrival.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws this lesson from the phrase (citing Ibn Jarir and Ibn Kathir): the fulfilment of a dream's interpretation can sometimes take a long time to materialise — as here, where it manifested itself after forty, or on another reckoning eighty, years.

Yusuf does not say "my dream came true." He says قَدْ جَعَلَهَا رَبِّي حَقًّا — *my Lord* made it true. Ibn Kathir reads it so: Allah blessed him by making his dream come true. The dream was never a prediction he owned; it was a promise Allah kept.

## How a prophet tells the story of his suffering

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws this out at length. Imagine someone in our day put through everything Yusuf was, finally meeting his parents after so long a separation. How many days and nights would he spend recounting what he had suffered?

But here both the teller and the listener are prophets of Allah. Yusuf's hardships, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, fall into three stages: (1) the injustices of his brothers; (2) the separation from his parents; (3) the pain of the prison. Look what he does with all three in one sentence:

وَقَدْ أَحْسَنَ بِي إِذْ أَخْرَجَنِي مِنَ السِّجْنِ وَجَاءَ بِكُم مِّنَ الْبَدْوِ مِن بَعْدِ أَن نَّزَغَ الشَّيْطَانُ بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَ إِخْوَتِي

**He reverses the order.** He starts from the prison — the last chapter, not the first.

**He mentions the prison only by its exit.** He says nothing about how he entered it or what he suffered inside; only that Allah *brought him out* of it, and even that framed as gratitude.

**He never mentions the well at all** — not even in passing. Al-Qurṭubī, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates, explains why: Yusuf had already forgiven his brothers' mistake and had said لَا تَثْرِيبَ عَلَيْكُمُ الْيَوْمَ, "no reproach upon you today" (ayah 92). So he did not consider it proper to mention the incident of the well in any form, lest his brothers be put to shame. Forgiveness that keeps a receipt is not forgiveness.

**He turns the separation into a reunion.** He was, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, "supposed to" dwell on that long and trying separation — and he sets all of it aside, taking up only its final part: "and He brought you from the badw," from the countryside, into this city. Ibn Jurayj and others, cited by Ibn Kathir, note that they lived a bedouin life and raised cattle, in the Arava and Ghūr area of Palestine in Greater Syria. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sees a hint of blessing in the phrase: Allah brought his father from a countryside where the conveniences of living are scarce into a city, with royal honours.

**He assigns the blame to Shayṭān.** "After Shayṭān had sown enmity between me and my brothers." He sweeps the whole thing away, even making it easy for them by suggesting his brothers were not the kind of men who would do such a thing — they were deceived.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls this the elegance of the prophets: not only are they patient against pain and hardship, they invariably find in every condition an occasion to be grateful to Allah. And it contrasts this with our habit: thousands of blessings showered over us that we mention to no one, and one hardship we go about crying over all our lives. The Qur'an names that habit: إِنَّ الْإِنسَانَ لِرَبِّهِ لَكَنُودٌ, "human beings are, to their Lord, very ungrateful" (100:6).

## "My Lord is Laṭīf to whatever He wills"

إِنَّ رَبِّي لَطِيفٌ لِّمَا يَشَاءُ. Ibn Kathir explains: when Allah wills something, He brings forth its reasons and the elements of its existence, then wills it into existence and makes it easy to attain. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds: when Allah intends to do something, He has His subtle ways of arranging things and causes secretly, in a manner that no one can get the slightest inkling about.

That is the word Yusuf reaches for at the end of a life he could not read while he was living it. The well, the prison, the rift Shayṭān sowed between him and his brothers — at the time each was only hardship, and each turned out to be a thread. Laṭīf names a plan so fine you can only see it from the far end.

He closes with إِنَّهُ هُوَ الْعَلِيمُ الْحَكِيمُ. Ibn Kathir: **al-ʿAlīm** — He knows what benefits His servants; **al-Ḥakīm** — wise in His statements, actions, decrees, preordainment, and in what He chooses and wills. Yusuf ends the account of his own life not with what happened to him, but with who his Lord is.

## The du'a of a man at the summit (ayah 101)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out the shift: in the previous verses Yusuf was addressing his father. Now, having achieved so great an objective, he is at peace, and devotes himself to praising Allah and supplicating before Him — praise first, then request.

رَبِّ قَدْ آتَيْتَنِي مِنَ الْمُلْكِ وَعَلَّمْتَنِي مِن تَأْوِيلِ الْأَحَادِيثِ — "My Lord, You have indeed bestowed on me of the sovereignty, and taught me something of the interpretation of dreams." Both gifts are named as *given* and *taught*, never as achieved. Then فَاطِرَ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ أَنتَ وَلِيِّي فِي الدُّنْيَا وَالْآخِرَةِ — Creator of the heavens and the earth, You are my walī, my protector, in this world and in the Hereafter. And then the request: تَوَفَّنِي مُسْلِمًا وَأَلْحِقْنِي بِالصَّالِحِينَ — "cause me to die as a Muslim, and join me with the righteous."

Ibn Kathir observes that this is the invocation of Yusuf, the truthful one, to his Lord — made after Allah's favour upon him was complete. And he asks that as Allah has perfected His bounty on him in this life, He continue it into the Hereafter: that when he dies, he dies as a Muslim, as ad-Ḍaḥḥāk said, and that he be joined to the ranks of the righteous — with his brethren the Prophets and Messengers, may Allah's peace and blessings be on them all. Tafsīr Mazharī, cited in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, notes that "the righteous" here can be the prophets themselves, since they are divinely protected (maʿṣūm) against all sins.

Ibn Kathir offers two possibilities: that Yusuf, peace be upon him, said this supplication while dying, or that he begged this of Allah long before he died. In connection with the first he cites what is recorded **in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs** from 'Ā'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her: that while he was dying, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ raised his finger and said three times, "O Allah, to ar-Rafīq al-Aʿlā" — the uppermost, highest company.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the portrait: this du'a shows us the servants of Allah who have the honour of being accepted by their Creator. They may be enjoying the highest ranks, with all sorts of power and office beneath their feet, and never wax proud over any of it. If anything they fear such things may be taken away — and so they keep praying that the blessings given them, physical and spiritual, remain and even increase, right through the hour of death.

**A note on asking for death.** Since Yusuf asks for death *in a particular state* — adhering to his īmān and Islam — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān clarifies that making a du'a for death under particular conditions is not prohibited. The prohibition of wishing for death in the sound and authentic ahadith is aimed at something else: going about asking for death out of depression at worldly hardships, or simple lack of patience. The Prophet ﷺ said that no one should ask for death because of some hardship, and that if one has to say something, let him say: "O Allah, keep me alive as long as life is better for me, and give me death when death is better for me."

## After the last ayah

With ayah 101 the Qur'an's telling of Yusuf's story reaches its completion. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is explicit that **what happened afterwards is not reported in the Qur'an, nor in any *marfūʿ* hadith** — that is, as the tafsir itself glosses the term, a hadith "with its chain of reporting authorities ascending to the Holy Prophet himself." Most commentators relay what follows from historical or Isra'ili narrations, which contradict one another. So hold it loosely:

- Ḥasan's narration, reported in Tafsīr Ibn Kathir, that Yusuf was seven when his brothers threw him into the well, remained separated from his father for eighty years, lived twenty-three years after meeting his parents, and died at a hundred and twenty.
- Muhammad ibn Ishaq's report, as in the narrations of the People of the Book, that the separation lasted forty years, and that Ya'qub lived seventeen years in Yusuf's company in Egypt.
- Al-Qurṭubī's report from the annals of historians that Ya'qub died after twenty-four years in Egypt, having instructed Yusuf that his body be sent back to his home country and buried beside his father Isḥāq.
- The report of Ibn Ishaq, based on a narration of ʿUrwah ibn Zubayr, that Mūsā was commanded not to leave Yusuf's body in Egypt, located his grave, and carried it to Canaan in Palestine to bury him beside Isḥāq and Ya'qub.

Ibn Mas'ūd's figure for the number of Banī Isrā'īl who left Egypt with Mūsā carries a footnote: Ibn Khaldūn criticised that narration in his *Muqaddimah*. Background colour, never creed.

## Living it

**Honour your parents visibly.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān derives from ayat 99–100 that paying due respect to parents is obligatory (wājib).

**Tell your story the way Yusuf told his.** From وَقَدْ أَحْسَنَ بِي, "He favoured me," Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the rule: when a person is delivered from a disease or a disaster, the way of the prophets is to show gratitude to Allah for the deliverance and to leave the remembrance of the disease or disaster behind. Mention the exit, not the pit.

**Cover the people who wronged you once you have forgiven them.** Yusuf would not name the well in front of his father so that his brothers would not be shamed.

**Ask for the ending, not just the next thing.** At the highest point of his life Yusuf asked for a death upon Islam and the company of the righteous. That is the one request that outlives every other answered prayer.

passages.title: News of the unseen that most still reject
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

The story of Yusuf (peace be upon him) is over. Now Allah turns from the story to the one reciting it, and speaks directly to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. Three short ayat answer three questions in sequence: where did this account come from (102), how did people respond to it (103), and what is the Messenger asking in return for it (104)? Read together they are one thing — a proof of prophethood placed in the hand of the Prophet ﷺ, and, in the same breath, a consolation for his heart when that proof is rejected anyway.

## The moment behind the words

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports from Imam al-Baghawi that the Jews and the Quraysh had joined hands to test the truthfulness of the Prophet ﷺ. Their challenge was specific: tell us everything about Yusuf (peace be upon him), exactly as it happened to him, if you are truthful in your claim to prophethood. He told them what he had learnt through divine revelation. And they stayed exactly where they were, sticking to their disbelief and denial.

That is the setting for these three ayat. The test was passed and the verdict was ignored. Maʿārif adds that this shocked the Prophet ﷺ. Ayah 103 comes immediately after, and once you know why, it stops reading like a general observation about humanity and starts reading like a hand placed on a grieving shoulder.

## Ayah 102: "You were not there"

**The argument is built out of absence.** Allah does not say "this is true because We say so." He says: *dhālika min anbāʾ al-ghayb nūḥīhi ilayk* — "That is from the stories of the unseen which We reveal to you" — and then removes every other way the Prophet ﷺ could have come by it: *"You were not (present) with them when they arranged their plan together, and (while) they were plotting."*

Ibn Kathir spells out what that absence covers: you did not witness their conference nor see them, when they arranged their plan to throw Yusuf into the well and were plotting against him. Then he lines this ayah up with its sisters elsewhere in the Qur'an, where the same argument is made in the same shape: *"You were not with them, when they cast lots with their pens"* (3:44); *"And you were not on the western side, when We made clear to Musa the commandment"* (28:44); *"And you were not at the side of the Tur when We did call"* (28:46); *"And you were not a dweller among the people of Madyan, reciting Our verses to them"* (28:45). Four times: you were not there, you were not there, you were not there. The conclusion each time is the same — as Ibn Kathir puts it, "We taught you all this through Our Revelation which We sent down to you."

**Why the Qur'an does not bother ruling out books and teachers.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the obvious objection: absence from the scene proves he was not an eyewitness, but a man can still consult books of history or hear something from a teacher. Why does the ayah settle for "you were not there"?

Because in Arabia at that time nobody needed to be told the rest. The whole peninsula knew that the Prophet ﷺ was *ummiyy* — that is, he did not learn to read and write from anyone. Everyone knew he had lived his whole life in Makkah al-Muʿazzamah. Maʿārif goes through his travels one by one: one trip towards Syria with his uncle Abu Talib, on which he came back home while still en route; and a second, a business trip, where he finished his work and returned in a few days — in that trip too, no chance of meeting some scholar or going to an educational institution. And the story itself dates back thousands of years before his time. So the case closes itself: there is no way he could have known it in the manner he did except that it be divine revelation itself. Maʿārif notes that the Qur'an makes the point explicit elsewhere anyway: *"You did not know them (events) before this (the revelation of the Qur'an), neither you nor your people"* (11:49).

Notice too *why* Allah reveals it, in Ibn Kathir's reading: not as a display of information, but "because it carries a lesson, for you to draw from and a reminder to those who defy you." Ibn Kathir adds that Allah taught His Messenger the news of what occurred in the past, which carry lessons for people to draw from, "so that they acquire their safety in their religious affairs as well as their worldly affairs." The whole surah — the brothers, the well, the plotting, and the end Allah gave Yusuf over the very people who tried to harm and kill him: the better end, triumph, the sovereignty and wisdom, that is, prophethood — was given to be *used*, not merely admired.

## The distinction the ayah is built on: news of the unseen, not knowledge of the unseen

This is where Maʿārif ul Qurʼān slows down, and it is the most important thing in the passage for a Muslim's creed.

**The wording repeats across the Qur'an.** The same statement, *dhālika min anbāʾ al-ghayb nūḥīhi ilayk*, appears in the same words in 3:44 with the story of Sayyidah Maryam, and with a slight change of wording in 11:49 — *tilka min anbāʾ al-ghayb nūḥīhā ilayk* — with the story of Nuh (peace be upon him). A fixed formula, attached each time to a story no living person witnessed.

**Now look at the noun.** The Qur'an says *anbāʾ* al-ghayb — reports, news, of the unseen — and says they are *revealed* to him. Maʿārif builds on the difference between that and *ʿilm* al-ghayb, knowledge of the unseen, and the difference is not a quibble.

Allah does communicate to His prophets a great deal of news of the unseen through *waḥy* (revelation). Maʿārif states that our Messenger ﷺ, known as the head of all the messengers, was blessed with a special portion of it, more than that which was given to all the past prophets — which is why he was able to inform this Ummah of many events due to happen right through the Day of Qiyamah, some briefly and some in detail, of the kind gathered in the chapters on tribulations (*Kitab al-Fitan*) in the books of hadith.

But receiving news is not possessing knowledge. Maʿārif quotes the decisive ayah: *"No one in the heavens, or on the Earth, knows the unseen except Allah"* (27:65). Knowledge of the unseen — *ʿilm al-ghayb* — is the unique attribute of Allah, His and no one else's. To take an apostle, messenger, prophet or angel as a sharer in that attribute, Maʿārif warns, amounts to equating him with Allah; it is what the Christians do when they declare a messenger to be a divine son and a partner in divinity.

So the honest way to speak is the Qur'an's own way. The Prophet ﷺ was told what Allah chose to tell him — and what he was told was true, precise, and beyond any human means of obtaining. That is an enormous rank. In the terminology of the Qur'an, it is simply not the same thing as knowing the unseen. Maʿārif observes that common people do not understand this fine difference and tend to take the news of the unseen as the knowledge of the unseen — which is why, when someone holds to the Qur'an's terminology and says that no one other than Allah can claim to know what is unseen, they would prefer to differ rather than accept the truth as it is. Honouring the Prophet ﷺ does not require giving him what belongs to Allah alone.

## Ayah 103: "even if you are keen"

*Wa mā aktharu al-nāsi wa law ḥaraṣta bi-muʾminīn* — "And most people will not believe — no matter how keen you are."

Read it in order: the proof has just been established (102), and the very next sentence concedes that the proof will not move most of them. Maʿārif is blunt about it — the proofs of his being a prophet were clear, he longed for their faith, he tried his best, and still most were not going to believe. The problem was never the strength of the evidence.

Ibn Kathir places the ayah beside two others that make the same point about the majority: *"And if you obey most of those on the earth, they will mislead you far away from Allah's path"* (6:116), and *"Verily, in this is an Ayah, yet most of them are not believers"* (26:8). Numbers are not a measure of truth in the Qur'an's reckoning. A believer who feels outnumbered is standing exactly where the Qur'an said he would be standing.

**The consolation, stated plainly.** Maʿārif draws the meaning out for the Prophet ﷺ and, through him, for every caller to Allah: your duty is to spread the call and to seek the betterment of people. That you succeed in it is not in your control, nor is it your responsibility, nor should you grieve over it.

## Ayah 104: nothing is being charged for this

*Wa mā tasʾaluhum ʿalayhi min ajr — in huwa illā dhikrun lil-ʿālamīn.* "And no reward you ask of them for it; it (the Qur'an) is no less than a Reminder unto the 'Alamin (men and Jinn)."

**No fee, so no excuse.** Ibn Kathir: you do not ask them, in return for this advice and your call to all that is good and righteous, for any price or compensation for delivering it — rather, you do so seeking Allah's Face and to deliver good and sincere advice to His creatures.

Maʿārif points out the practical edge of this: asking them for something in return could have caused them to find it difficult to listen to him or to follow him. Every excuse has been removed. What he is telling them is for their own good.

**"A Reminder."** *Dhikr* — Maʿārif renders the sense as an advice to heed and a lesson to learn from. Ibn Kathir describes its effect: by it people remember, receive guidance, and save themselves in this life and the Hereafter. And it is not rationed. Maʿārif: it is for everyone; Ibn Kathir's rendering of *al-ʿālamīn* takes in men and jinn alike. The story of one family and its old wound turns out to be addressed far beyond the household it happened in.

**The quiet last turn.** Maʿārif finds a hint in the ayah aimed straight at the grief of the Prophet ﷺ: when the purpose behind your effort is no worldly gain — when it is nothing but the reward of the Hereafter and the betterment of your people — then that purpose of yours already stands achieved. Why would you then grieve over it? The result he was waiting for was never the one he was actually working for.

## Living it

**Deliver, do not despair.** These ayat draw a line between what is asked of you and what is not. Conveying the truth and seeking people's betterment is your work. Their response is Allah's affair. Maʿārif says it in as many words: succeeding in it is not in your control, not your responsibility, and not yours to grieve over.

**Do not price the message.** The standard set in ayah 104 is that the caller seeks Allah's Face, not a price or compensation from the people he is calling. Whatever a person gives to this religion — teaching, correcting, inviting — the moment something is asked in return for it, an obstacle has been placed in front of the very people meant to hear it.

**Read the stories for what they were sent for.** Ibn Kathir's note is a whole method of reading the Qur'an: these accounts were revealed because they carry lessons for people to draw from, so that they secure their safety in their religious and their worldly affairs. Sūrah Yusuf is not history for its own sake. It ends by telling you, in ayah 104, that it is *dhikr* — a reminder — and a reminder only works on someone willing to be reminded.

**Say about the unseen only what Allah said.** Ayah 102 gives the Prophet ﷺ a rank almost impossible to overstate: Allah told him what no eye witnessed and no book preserved. Honour that rank by describing it the way the Qur'an describes it — news of the unseen, given by revelation — and leave *ʿilm al-ghayb* where the Qur'an left it, with Allah alone.

passages.title: Signs passed by, hidden shirk, sudden ruin
passages.tafsir:
**These three ayat move from the eye, to the heart, to the end.** Ayah 105 describes people who walk through a universe crowded with signs and never once look up. Ayah 106 describes those who do look up, admit that Allah made all of it — and then hand His rights to someone else anyway. Ayah 107 turns to both groups with the question that binds the passage together: what exactly makes you feel so safe?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the three as a deliberate sequence. Ayah 105, it says, "was a description of people who simply did not believe in the existence of Allah Taʿālā, the great Creator, and in His wisdom and power." Then "mentioned next are those who do believe in Allah as the Creator" — but who "also associate other things as partners in His Divinity." Ayah 107 then puts its question to people described in both terms: Ibn Kathir frames it as addressed to "these idolators who associate others with Allah in the worship," while Maʿārif speaks of those who are carefree "despite their denial and rebellion." Denial and diluted belief end up in the same exposed position.

## Ayah 105: a universe they walk past

The wording is not "they cannot see the signs." It is **yamurrūna ʿalayhā** — *they pass by them* — **wa-hum ʿanhā muʿriḍūn**, rendered in the sources as "while they are averse therefrom" and "they are heedless to it." The picture is of traffic, not blindness. Nothing is hidden; the person is simply in motion past it, face already averted. And the opening **wa-ka-ayyin min āyah**, "how many a sign," insists on the sheer quantity: this is not one missed clue but a lifetime of them.

Ibn Kathir answers that count by making the reader look. Allah, he says, "created brilliant stars and rotating heavenly objects and planets, all made subservient. There are many plots of fertile land next to each other on earth, and gardens, solid mountains, lively oceans, with their waves smashing against each other, and spacious deserts. There are many live creatures and others that have died; and animals, plants and fruits that are similar in shape, but different in taste, scent, color and attributes."

Notice the last item, where sameness and difference sit inside the same sentence: things "similar in shape, but different in taste, scent, color and attributes." And notice what Ibn Kathir concludes from the whole list. These are not merely proofs that *a* maker exists; he calls them Allah's "signs and proofs of **His Oneness**," closing with: "All praise is due to Allah the One and Only, Who created all types of creations, Who Alone will remain and last forever. It is He Who is unique in His Names and Attributes." The heavens do not merely argue for a Creator. They argue that He has no partner — which is exactly why ayah 106 follows.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sharpens the indictment: "these people are not of the kind who would simply not listen to a well-wisher out of their obstinacy. **They are worse.**" A man who refuses to listen to advice has at least been offered words he can argue with. These people will not learn from "the very open signs of the perfect power of Allah Taʿālā visible to them all the time," but "keep passing by them without paying any attention and without wondering whose signs they were."

And some of those signs are not beautiful at all. Maʿārif adds that among them "are many signs which remind people of punishments which descended upon past peoples, and they themselves see their overturned habitations, but they would still refuse to learn their lesson." They travel past the wreckage of nations that were destroyed and read nothing in it. Hold onto that — it is precisely why ayah 107 asks whether they feel *secure*. The evidence that ruin is possible is lying by the roadside, and they drive past it.

## Ayah 106: belief with a partner quietly attached

**wa mā yuʾminu aktharuhum billāhi illā wa hum mushrikūn** — "And most of them do not believe in Allah without associating partners with Him."

This is one of the most searching statements in the Qur'an about religion, because its subject is not the atheist. It is the believer. Ibn ʿAbbas explains: "They have a part of faith, for when they are asked, 'Who created the heavens? Who created the earth? Who created the mountains?' They say, 'Allah did.' Yet, they associate others with Him in worship." Ibn Kathir notes that the same is said by Mujahid, ʿAtaʾ, ʿIkrimah, Ash-Shaʿbi, Qatadah, Ad-Dahhak and ʿAbdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam — a remarkable agreement among the early commentators. Their faith is real as far as it goes. It simply stops short of the point where it would cost them something.

Ibn Kathir then produces the detail that makes it unforgettable: the idolaters' own **Talbiyah**, the words they called out during the Hajj season. It is recorded in the Sahih that they used to say: *"Here we rush to Your service. You have no partners with You, except a partner with You whom You own but he owns not!"* Read that twice. They deny partnership in the first half of the sentence and smuggle it back in the second — and they do it while performing an act of worship. That is the anatomy of the ayah in a single line.

(A note on names: Ibn Kathir cites his hadith sources here as "the Sahih" and "the Two Sahihs" — his shorthand for the most rigorously authenticated collections of hadith. Since that is exactly how the sources name them, this commentary keeps his wording rather than expanding it.)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names precisely where the leak occurs: those who profess belief in Allah "would do so by lacing it with Shirk. They would suggest others as partners in the attributes of knowledge and power which are exclusive for Allah Taʿālā — which is rank injustice, and ignorance." That is a useful diagnostic. Shirk rarely announces itself as an open claim to a second Lord. It arrives as a quiet assumption that someone or something *knows* what only Allah knows, or *can do* what only Allah can do.

Ibn Kathir calls this "the greatest type of Shirk," citing Allah's words, "Verily, joining others in worship with Allah is a great *Zulm* (wrong) indeed" (31:13). He then cites what is recorded in the Two Sahihs from ʿAbdullah bin Masʿud, who said: "I said, 'O Allah's Messenger! What is the greatest sin?' He said, *'That you call a rival to Allah while He alone created you.'*" The reasoning is contained in the last clause — *He alone created you*. To set up a rival to the One who is solely responsible for your existence is not merely forbidden; it is incoherent.

## The shirk that hides inside faith

Here the commentary turns from those idolaters to us. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records: "Ibn Kathir has said that included under the sense of this verse are Muslims who, despite having ʾĪmān, are involved with different kinds of Shirk." The sources then list those kinds concretely.

**Showing off in worship.** Al-Hasan Al-Basri commented on this very ayah: "This is the hypocrite; if he performs good deeds, he does so to show off with the people, and he is an idolator while doing this." He was pointing to Allah's description of the hypocrites who "stand up for As-Salah… with laziness and to be seen of men" (4:142). Maʿārif adds, from the Musnad of Ahmad, that the Prophet ﷺ said: *"The most dangerous of things I apprehend for you is the small Shirk."* When the Sahabah — the Companions — asked what that could be, he said: *"Hypocrisy is the small Shirk."* The deed is right; the audience is wrong — and that is enough to poison it.

**Oaths sworn by other than Allah.** In a hadith from Ibn ʿUmar collected by At-Tirmidhi, who said it was *Hasan* (a grading indicating the report is judged reliable), the Prophet ﷺ said: *"He who swears by other than Allah, commits Shirk."* Swearing puts something sacred behind your word. To place anything but Allah there is to treat it as holding a weight only He holds.

**Charms tied on for protection.** Ibn Kathir introduces this as "another type of hidden Shirk that most people are unaware of," and passes on a report — narrated by Hammad bin Salamah from ʿAsim bin Abi An-Najud from ʿUrwah — that "Hudhayfah visited an ill man and saw a rope tied around his arm, so he ripped it off while reciting" *this very ayah*: "And most of them believe not in Allah except that they attribute partners unto Him." He looked at a rope on a sick man's arm and recited ayah 106 over it. That is what trained insight into tawhid looks like. Ibn Kathir then reports that Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud "and other scholars of Hadith" narrated from ʿAbdullah bin Masʿud that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Verily, Ar-Ruqā, At-Tamāʾim and At-Tiwalah are all acts of Shirk."* Ibn Kathir leaves these three Arabic terms untranslated; what he does make clear is where they belong — in the same section as the rope torn from the sick man's arm, under the heading of hidden Shirk.

**Omens.** In another narration collected by Ahmad and Abu Dawud, the Prophet ﷺ said: *"Verily, At-Tiyarah (omen) is Shirk; everyone might feel a glimpse of it, but Allah dissipates it with Tawakkul."* This is one of the most merciful sentences in the passage. The involuntary flicker — the sinking feeling at a bad sign — is acknowledged as something almost nobody escapes. What is asked is not that you never feel it, but that you refuse to let it steer you, and the named remedy is **Tawakkul**: reliance on Allah.

**Vows and offerings made to other than Allah.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that "vows and offerings (*Mannat* and *Niyaz*) in the name of anyone other than Allah is also included under it, on which there is a consensus of Muslim jurists."

What unites the list is that every item is something a believing person does. This is the ayah's real force: it does not let faith and shirk sit in separate compartments labelled "them" and "us."

## Ayah 107: what makes you feel safe?

**a-fa-aminū** — "Do they then feel secure?" The question is not *will* punishment come. It is: on what grounds are you calm? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes the tone exactly — their heedlessness is "questioned and deplored," that these people, "despite their denial and rebellion, become so carefree."

Two things are named. First, a **ghāshiyah** of Allah's punishment — rendered in the sources as "the covering veil of the torment of Allah." Ibn Kathir puts the question this way: "Do these idolators who associate others with Allah in the worship, feel secure from the coming of an encompassing torment from where they perceive not?" Maʿārif says it "overtakes them from all sides." It is not a blow from one direction that you might dodge; it is something that comes down over you like a sheet. Second, the Hour itself, arriving — in the words of the translation Ibn Kathir gives — "all of a sudden while they perceive not." Maʿārif says the same: it "descends upon them all of a sudden while they are not ready for it." That closing phrase is the point: not merely that they are unprepared, but that they never see it approaching.

Ibn Kathir then places two parallel passages beside it, and they are worth reading slowly because each closes a different escape route:

- "Do then those who devise evil plots feel secure that Allah will not sink them into the earth, or that the torment will not seize them from directions they perceive not? Or that He may catch them in the midst of their going to and from, so that there be no escape for them? Or that He may catch them with gradual wasting (of their wealth and health)? Truly, Your Lord is indeed full of kindness, Most Merciful" (16:45–47). Below you, from an unwatched direction, mid-journey, or so slowly you never notice it beginning — and yet the passage closes not on threat but on Allah's kindness and mercy.
- "Did the people of the towns then feel secure against the coming of Our punishment by night while they were asleep? Or… in the forenoon while they were playing? Did they then feel secure against the plan of Allah? **None feels secure from the plan of Allah except the people who are the losers**" (7:97–99). Asleep at night, at play in the morning: the two states in which a person is least braced.

That final line is the passage's verdict. A settled, unexamined sense of immunity is not a sign of strong faith. It is named as the feeling of those who lose.

## Living it

The passage asks for three things, in the order it gives them.

**Look on purpose.** Ibn Kathir's catalogue — stars, mountains, colliding waves, fruits alike in shape and unlike in taste — is not decoration. It is an instruction to stop passing by. Ayah 105 condemns motion without attention, and the cure is small and daily: look at one created thing today long enough to ask whose sign it is.

**Audit the seam.** Ayah 106 is not aimed at people who reject Allah; it is aimed at people who affirm Him and then quietly place His knowledge or His power somewhere else. Maʿārif's phrasing gives you the test: is there anything I treat as knowing what only Allah knows, or as able to do what only Allah does? The sources then hand over specifics — worship performed for an audience, oaths sworn by other than Allah, the kind of thing Hudhayfah tore off a sick man's arm, omens obeyed, vows made in another's name. Each is a place to check, and each is checkable this week.

**Refuse false security.** Ayah 107 does not ask you to live in dread; Ibn Kathir's own proof-text ends by calling Allah "full of kindness, Most Merciful." It asks you to stop assuming that because nothing has happened, nothing can. The believer walks between hope in Allah's mercy and a healthy refusal to feel safe from His plan — and when the omen flickers or the fear rises, the answer the Prophet ﷺ named is the same one: **Tawakkul**.

passages.title: "This is my way" and the lesson of the stories
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat close Surah Yusuf by stepping out of the story and speaking straight to the Prophet ﷺ and the Makkans rejecting him: *this is my way, and it rests on clear sight* (108); *the messengers before me were men, and the ruins record what became of those who refused them* (109); *the punishment you mock as slow has always been slow — and it has always come* (110); *what you have just heard about Yusuf is no invented tale but a lesson from Allah for anyone with a mind* (111).

## Ayah 108 — "This is my way"

**A road, not a mood.** Ibn Kathir explains that Allah orders His Messenger ﷺ to say to mankind and the jinn that this is his way — "his method, path and Sunnah" — concentrating on calling to the testimony that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah alone, without partners.

**"I invite to Allah upon *baṣīrah*."** *Baṣīrah* is inward sight — insight, not hearsay. Ibn Kathir: the Messenger ﷺ calls to this testimony "with sure knowledge, certainty and firm evidence," and those who follow him call to the same with the same certainty, "whether logical or religious evidence." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: the *daʿwah* of the Prophet ﷺ — his invitation to Allah — is not based on some summary view of things; it is the outcome of insight, reason and wisdom.

**"...I and whoever follows me."** *anā wa man ittabaʿanī* — he names himself, then joins his followers to the very same *baṣīrah*. Ibn ʿAbbas said it refers to the noble Sahabah, may Allah be pleased with them — "the soldiers of Allah." Ibn Masʿud said of them: the Sahabah of the Prophet ﷺ are the best people of this whole Ummah; their hearts are pure and their knowledge is deep; they are far removed from formality; Allah chose them to accompany and serve His Messenger, so learn their morals, habits and ways, for they are the ones on the straight path.

Maʿārif notes it is also possible to take "whoever follows me" generally: everyone who carries the daʿwah of Allah's Messenger to the Ummah right up to Qiyamah. On that reading, Kalbi and Ibn Zayd held that this verse makes it *necessary* for anyone claiming to follow the Prophet ﷺ that he spread that daʿwah and make the teaching of the Qur'an available to all (Mazhari).

**"And glorified is Allah. And I am not among the idolaters."** Ibn Kathir unpacks the *tasbīḥ* — the declaring of Allah free from every defect: I glorify, honour, revere and praise Allah as far above having a partner, equal, rival, parent, son, wife, minister or advisor — glorified above everything they attribute to Him, as in *"there is not a thing but glorifies His praise. But you understand not their glorification"* (17:44). Maʿārif: earlier in the surah, mention was made of people who profess belief in Allah yet mix it with shirk, open or concealed; so here he declares he has absolutely nothing to do with shirk. The gist: *my daʿwah does not aim at inviting people to become my servants; I myself am a servant of Allah, and it is this servitude — to none but Him — that I invite people to.* And yet, since he is the *dāʿī*, the one making the call on Allah's behalf, faith in him is obligatory.

## Ayah 109 — why a man, and why the ruins

Maʿārif supplies the objection this answers: the disbelievers of Makkah pleaded that a messenger of Allah should not be a human being but an angel.

**"We sent none before you but men."** Ad-Daḥḥāk reported that Ibn ʿAbbas commented: "They were not from among the residents of the heaven (angels), as you claimed." Ibn Kathir gathers the parallels — *"they ate food and walked in the markets"* (25:20); *"nor were they immortals"* (21:8); *"Say: I am not a new thing among the Messengers"* (46:9). Maʿārif adds the principle: for human beings, a prophet has always been a human being. What sets him apart is not his species but that the *waḥy* — the revelation Allah sends down — comes to him directly, never the outcome of anyone's individual effort. Allah Himself chooses the servant who, in His knowledge and judgement, is fittest.

**Rijāl, and the question of women.** Ibn Kathir takes *rijāl* (men) at face value: Allah sent Prophets and Messengers from among men, and did not reveal legislative law to any woman from the daughters of Adam. He states this as the belief of Ahl al-Sunnah wa'l-Jamāʿah, noting Shaykh Abu al-Hasan ʿAli b. Ismāʿīl al-Ashʿari mentioned it as their view. His evidence: Allah's praise of the most honourable of them, Maryam, is *"His mother was a Ṣiddīqah (truthful believer)"* (5:75) — had she been a Prophet, that would have been the thing to mention.

Maʿārif notes that some scholars did identify certain women as prophetesses — naming three: Sayyidah Sarah, the wife of Sayyidna Ibrahim (peace be upon him); the mother of Sayyidna Musa (peace be upon him); and Sayyidah Maryam, the mother of Sayyidna ʿIsa (peace be upon him). Their reason was that particular words in the Qur'an about these three give the impression that angels spoke to them as Divinely commanded, gave them good news, or that they came to know something through revelation. The majority of the ʿulamā' accept that such verses prove these women had a high spiritual rank in the sight of Allah, but hold that the wording is not sufficient as proof of prophethood.

**"...from the people of the townships."** Ibn Kathir: from the people of cities — not from among the bedouins, who are among the harshest and roughest of people. Maʿārif gives the same point, attributing it to Ibn Kathir, Qurtubi and others.

**"Have they not travelled in the land?"** Ibn Kathir: have they not travelled and seen the end of earlier nations who rejected the Messengers, and how Allah destroyed them. He pairs it with *"Have they not travelled through the land, and have they hearts wherewith to understand?"* (22:46). Maʿārif fills in what they would see: the habitation of the people of Sayyidna Lut overturned, ʿAd and Thamud destroyed by various punishments — and the punishment of the Hereafter is far more severe. The lesson, says Ibn Kathir, is that Allah destroyed the disbelievers and saved the believers, "and this is His way with His creation."

**"And the home of the Hereafter is better for those who have taqwa."** Ibn Kathir: just as We saved the faithful in this life, We also wrote safety for them in the Hereafter — as in *"We will indeed make victorious Our Messengers and those who believe in this world's life and on the Day when the witnesses will stand forth"* (40:51). Maʿārif: a good end in the Ākhirah depends on taqwa, the fear of Allah and abstention from sins — in short, strict adherence to the commandments of the Sharīʿah. The closing rebuke, *"do you not then understand?"*, names the failure as one of *reason*: preferring this world's short-lived comfort over the everlasting blessings to come.

## Ayah 110 — the long delay, and the hardest word in the surah

**Why this verse comes here.** Maʿārif explains the doubt being removed: the Makkans had heard warnings of divine punishment from the Prophet ﷺ for a long time and seen nothing arrive, which made them bolder. The answer: Allah, in His mercy and wisdom, often keeps granting respite to erring and sinning people, and that respite can at times run fairly long — long enough that the defiant grow more daring and aggressive, which causes a certain anxiety to prophets.

**The word the scholars weighed.** The verse says the Messengers reached the end of hope *wa ẓannū annahum qad kudhibū*. Ibn Kathir records that there are two recitations of this word. One is with a *shadda* — the Arabic mark that doubles a letter — giving *kudhdhibū*, meaning they were betrayed by their people; this is how ʿA'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, recited it. The other is without the doubling: *kudhibū*. (Maʿārif adds that the doubled form derives from *takdhīb*, "falsification" — being declared a liar.)

**ʿA'ishah's answer, recorded by al-Bukhari.** Al-Bukhari relates that ʿUrwah b. az-Zubayr asked ʿA'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, about the verse — denied, or betrayed? She said, "betrayed." ʿUrwah pressed: they were *sure* their people betrayed them, so why the word "thought"? She said, yes, they were sure. Then he put the other reading to her — *and they thought that they were denied (by Allah)*? She said, "Allah forbid! The Messengers did not suspect their Lord of such a thing." Her own explanation: the verse concerns the Messengers' *followers*, who had faith in their Lord and believed their Messengers; their period of trial was long and Allah's help delayed, until the Messengers gave up hope for the conversion of the disbelievers among their nation and suspected that even their followers were shaken in belief — and then Allah's help came to them.

**The other explanation, from Ibn ʿAbbas and the Salaf.** Ibn Jurayj narrated from Ibn Abi Mulaykah that Ibn ʿAbbas read the light form; and Ibn ʿAbbas said to him that they were human beings, then recited *"...even the Messenger and those who believed along with him said, 'When will come the help of Allah?' Yes! Certainly, the help of Allah is near!"* (2:214). ʿA'ishah did not agree with this and rejected it, saying: nothing that Allah promised Muhammad ﷺ but that he knew for certain it would come, until he died. And she recited the doubled form: *"and they thought that they were betrayed."*

Ibn ʿAbbas's own reading of the sense keeps the doubt away from the prophets altogether: "When the Messengers gave up hope that their people would accept their messages, and their people thought that their Messengers had not said the truth to them, Allah's victory came."

Ibn Jarir at-Tabari narrated from Tamim b. Hadhlam that he heard ʿAbdullah b. Masʿud comment on this ayah: the Messengers gave up hope that their people would believe in them, and their people thought, when the respite was long, that the Messengers were not given a true promise.

Ibn Jarir at-Tabari narrated from Ibrahim b. Abi Hamzah al-Jazari that a young man of Quraysh came to Saʿid b. Jubayr: how do you read this word, for when I pass by it I wish I had not read this Surah? Saʿid gave the same explanation — the Messengers despaired of their people believing in them, and those to whom the Messengers were sent thought the Messengers were not truthful. When Muslim b. Yasār asked Saʿid the same question and received the same answer, he stood and embraced him: "May Allah relieve a distress from you as you relieved a distress from me!" Ibn Kathir notes this was reported from Saʿid b. Jubayr through various chains, that it is also the tafsir of Mujahid b. Jabr and several other Salaf scholars.

**A mistaken estimate, corrected.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān follows the well-known *qirā'ah* — an established, transmitted way of reciting the Qur'an — namely *kudhibū*, and says the tafsir it has chosen is the most sound and the freest from doubts. It reproduces a paraphrase from *Bayān al-Qur'ān*, the tafsir of Maulana Ashraf ʿAli Thanavi: past communities were given long respite, until the messengers despaired that Allah's punishment would fall on such people and that the truth would show itself in the manner and at the time they had hoped; and they thought that, in determining the time of the Divine promise, they had been wrong in their estimation. It was in that state of despair that Allah's help came: the punishment fell on the disbelievers as promised, those whom Allah willed were saved, "because Our punishment is not averted from the guilty."

**Why a prophet may misjudge a time.** Maʿārif then explains: the essential sense of *kudhibū* is to find one's own estimation or thinking wrong, which is a kind of *ijtihādī* mistake — a conclusion reached by personal reasoning — and some such mistake can issue forth from the blessed prophets. But there is a difference between prophets and other *mujtahids*: when an ijtihādī mistake issues from a prophet, Allah does not let him stay by that mistake; He makes him aware of it and enables him to see reality clearly.

The proof offered is Hudaybiyah. The Qur'an states that this event rests on a dream the Prophet ﷺ saw: that he was performing *ṭawāf* — the circling of the Kaʿbah in worship — of the Baytullah with his Sahabah. The dream of a prophet is itself an imperative form of revelation, so the event was certain. But the dream identified no particular time. The Prophet ﷺ, by his estimation, thought it would happen that same year; he set out for Makkah with his Sahabah for ʿUmrah — but the Quraysh confronted them en route and they could not perform the intended ṭawāf and ʿUmrah. The full unfolding came two years later, in the Hijri year 8, in the Conquest of Makkah. So the dream was true and certain; the *time* he had taken from signs and estimation was not — and that mistake was compensated right then.

Maʿārif adds that *qad kudhibū* in this verse carries the same sense. This tafsir is reported from Sayyidna ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbbas, and ʿAllāma al-Tībī said this report is sahih (sound) because it has been mentioned in the Sahih of al-Bukhari (Mazhari).

On the doubled reading, *kudhdhibū*, Maʿārif gives the parallel sense: the prophets had determined an estimated time for the punishment, and when it did not come then, they had apprehensions about their own believers — lest they should declare them false on the basis that what they had said had not turned out to be true.

**The consolation underneath it all.** Ibn Kathir: Allah sends His aid and support to His Messengers, peace be upon them, when distress and hardship surround them and they are eagerly awaiting His aid. Relief arrives at the last edge of endurance.

## Ayah 111 — the lesson of the stories

**ʿIbrah for ūlū al-albāb.** There is *ʿibrah* — a lesson drawn by taking heed — for *ūlū al-albāb*, those possessed of understanding. Ibn Kathir: the stories of the Messengers and their nations, how Allah saved the believers and destroyed the disbelievers, are a lesson for "men of understanding, who have sound minds." Maʿārif observes that "their stories" may point both to the stories of all the prophets in the Qur'an and to the story of Sayyidna Yusuf in particular, since through it it becomes absolutely clear how the obedient servants of Allah are supported and helped: taken out of a deep well and seated on a high throne — while the practitioners of ill-will and deception end up in sheer shame.

**"It is not a forged statement."** Ibn Kathir: this Qur'an could not have been forged; it truly came from Allah. **"But a confirmation of that which was before it"** — the previously revealed Divine Books: the Qur'an testifies to the true parts that remain in them and denies and refutes the forged parts that were added, changed and falsified by people, accepting or abrogating whatever Allah wills of them. Maʿārif adds: this very story of Sayyidna Yusuf is mentioned in the Torah and the Injil too; and Hadrat Wahb ibn Munabbih said there is no Scripture which does not have the story of Sayyidna Yusuf in it (Mazhari).

**"And a detailed explanation of everything."** Ibn Kathir lists what that covers: the allowed and the prohibited, the preferred and the disliked; the acts of worship, the obligatory and the recommended; major facts regarding existence and about matters of the future. And, he says, the Qur'an tells us about the Lord, the Exalted and Most Honoured, and about His Names and Attributes, teaching us that Allah is glorified from being similar in any way to the creation. Maʿārif adds: the details of everything human beings need in religion — worship, dealings, morals, social living, government, politics.

**"A guide and a mercy for people who believe."** Ibn Kathir: with it their hearts are directed from misguidance to guidance and from deviation to conformance, and with it they seek the mercy of the Lord of all creation in this life and on the Day of Return. Why restricted to believers? Maʿārif answers that only they can enjoy the benefit: the Qur'an is nothing but mercy and guidance in itself, including for disbelievers, but it is through their own misconduct and disobedience that this mercy and guidance has become heavy and unwholesome for them.

**The frame the whole surah was built in.** Shaykh Abu al-Mansur said the purpose behind the whole of Surah Yusuf, and the story narrated in it, is to comfort the Prophet ﷺ: to tell him that the sufferings he endured at the hands of his own people were the lot of the prophets before him too — and that in the end Allah enabled His prophets to overcome, and in his case too, that is what was going to happen.

## Living it

- **Call with baṣīrah** (108): the call of the Prophet ﷺ was "not based on some summary view of things" but on insight, reason and wisdom. Learn a thing before you call people to it.
- **The verse includes you.** On the view of Kalbi and Ibn Zayd, "and whoever follows me" obliges anyone claiming to follow the Prophet ﷺ to spread the daʿwah.
- **Do not read delay as abandonment.** Ibn Kathir: Allah's aid reaches His Messengers when distress and hardship surround them. Hudaybiyah shows the difference between a promise failing and an estimated *timing* being wrong.
- **Take the story as ʿibrah.** Ibn Kathir ends his tafsir of this surah asking Allah to make us among those whose faces radiate with light on that Day.
